<a id="HWN-132"></a>
## HWN-132 — local note 132

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 162](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/162?lang=ar)

An objector might say that the preceding reasoning eliminates at most the definite article of prior mention (*lām al-ʿahd al-dhikrī*). It does not prove that every type of definiteness is impossible, since the absence of one special class does not imply the absence of the entire general class.

The first reply is contextual. The author was contrasting this introduction with the first division, which was definite by virtue of having been mentioned. For that limited contrast it suffices to identify the missing ground of definiteness. A second reply appeals to the other possible readings: in this location neither universal comprehensiveness, a familiar technical introduction, quiddity considered simply as such, nor an unspecified individual instance would be suitable. Since the alternatives are contextually unavailable, the particular reason of previous mention can be cited without rehearsing the others.

The glossator clarifies the form of the objection: the proposed conclusion seems broader than the evidence, which excludes only one member of the class. He suggests two ways to restore a proper relation between evidence and conclusion. Either restrict what the conclusion itself is claiming, or treat the stated evidence as a conspicuous part of a larger argument whose remaining premises are sufficiently obvious to have been omitted.


**Reading / scope note:** Contains quotation and subsequent explanation signed by Muḥammad ʿAlī; excludes a formal logical error only under the contextual restriction made explicit.


---


<a id="HWN-133"></a>
## HWN-133 — local note 133

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 162](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/162?lang=ar)

An objection says that “the first division” simply means the questions of logic. If “logic” means those same questions, the two expressions differ only in their wording, not their referent. One cannot literally place something *in* itself merely by changing its name: a contained thing and its container must be distinct.

The principal commentary answers by distinguishing a book's title from what is titled. The “first division” may designate the heading or organized literary part, while logic denotes the discipline's subject-matter. Those are different enough for a relation of inclusion. The quoted marginal critic finds the remaining elaborate explanations unnecessary: they distinguish words, meanings, graphic inscriptions, pairwise combinations, triple combinations, acquired logical disposition, the science of all logical problems or a substantial body of them, and the problems themselves. In his judgment this enumeration mostly multiplies expressions without advancing the explanation.


**Reading / scope note:** A substantial editorial criticism from al-Taqrīb, not an agreed conclusion of the principal commentary.

<a id="HWN-134"></a>
## HWN-134 — local note 134

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 162](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/162?lang=ar)

The objection is that the contained and the container would become identical, which is impossible for a literal relation of containment. A thing cannot contain itself in exactly the same respect in which it is contained. A different conceptual consideration or a genuinely different referent is required if the wording is to be defended.


**Reading / scope note:** One-sentence categorical distinction; later notes qualify the issue for metaphorical containment.


---


<a id="HWN-135"></a>
## HWN-135 — local note 135

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 162](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/162?lang=ar)

Most of the proposed ways of interpreting containment can be made intelligible. One exception occurs when “the first division” means the meanings of the logical propositions and “logic” means the propositions themselves. If the propositions are just those meanings, the phrase reduces to “these meanings in these meanings,” and the objection of self-containment returns.

An attempted solution says that “the first division” denotes a universal whose only instance lies in logic, so the sense would be “this universal is in this particular.” A critic regards that as contrived. Another solution treats the first division as a part of logic, because the discipline is not exhausted by the questions in this literary division. The intended relation would then be “this particular part is in the wider whole.” Such a part–whole relation is clearer than making a universal literally present inside its own single instance.


**Reading / scope note:** Reports competing resolutions of the same container/contained argument; the part–whole reading is not automatically valid if 'logic' means only exactly the same selected problems.

<a id="HWN-136"></a>
## HWN-136 — local note 136

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 162](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/162?lang=ar) · [Qum 163](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/163?lang=ar)

The three twofold combinations mentioned are (1) expressions together with meanings, (2) expressions together with graphic inscriptions, and (3) meanings together with inscriptions. This enumerates the three pairs that can be formed from the three basic levels of a book—its verbal wording, what that wording signifies, and its written marks. The source begins the enumeration at the end of Q162 and completes its final item at the beginning of Q163.

<a id="HWN-137"></a>
## HWN-137 — local note 137

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 163](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/163?lang=ar)

The word malaka (“acquired disposition”) denotes a quality that has become settled so firmly in the person who possesses it that it cannot be readily removed at will. If a quality does not yet have that stability and the person can easily rid himself of it, it is called a ḥāl (“state”). This understanding of malaka is one of the common senses in which knowledge is spoken of. The glossator wonders why a particular marginal commentator on al-Muṭawwal did not include it.

A further objection concerns the familiar metaphor that expressions are the moulds of meanings. If a book or its division is treated as verbal expressions *contained in* meanings, while meanings themselves are treated as *contained in* verbal expressions, does each become both container and contained by the other?

The reply distinguishes standpoints. The “container” of words can be their *explanatory function*: expressions are arranged to disclose meanings, which may also be disclosed without those particular expressions. In that respect the work of explaining meanings provides a governing framework for the expressions. Conversely verbal expressions can be described as moulds of meanings because the understanding obtained from them expands or contracts with the expressions, and meanings are received through their formulation.

It is impossible for one and the same thing to be container and contained of itself *in the same respect* under the same literal relation. But the two descriptions here concern different relations and are partly metaphorical, so the alleged contradiction does not follow.


**Reading / scope note:** Malaka vs ḥāl and two distinct 'container' respects. Speaker ends with ʿAbd al-Raḥīm signature.

<a id="HWN-138"></a>
## HWN-138 — local note 138

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 163](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/163?lang=ar)

The difference between “knowing all the questions” and “the questions themselves” is that in the first case the questions are considered under the illumination of being known or disclosed, while in the second they are considered simply as questions in themselves, without considering their disclosure to any particular knower. The same contents are thus distinguished by whether their epistemic relation is included in the conception.


**Reading / scope note:** Quoted al-Taqrīb note distinguishes knowledge-as-disclosure from known propositions considered apart from their epistemic status.


---


<a id="HWN-139"></a>
## HWN-139 — local note 139

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 163](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/163?lang=ar)

Most combinations of the seven possible referents of “the first division” and five possible meanings of “logic” can be interpreted straightforwardly. A problematic class remains where the first division is taken as meanings, either alone or combined with another element, while logic is taken as the problems themselves, whether all of them or a substantial selection. The problems themselves are those meanings. The result then seems to be “meanings are in meanings,” merely returning to the objection the explanation was supposed to escape.

One answer distinguishes the division from the whole discipline: the first division comprises only a part of logic, since not every possible logical question appears in it. Therefore a particular subset can be said to be within the wider class. But this does not solve the case where “logic” denotes only the substantial body of problems actually in the very same division; then the division is not a proper part of that body but the same thing.

Another proposed answer distinguishes unrestricted meanings from meanings of a special kind. On this reading one says in effect that the meanings of the book serve to explain this particular kind of meaning, namely logical meanings. This is compatible with the earlier restriction to specific words and meanings, the glossator says, when each statement is taken under its proper conceptual aspect. Merely considering a thing under an aspect does not bring into existence a second independent thing.


**Reading / scope note:** Source explicitly rejects a first attempted part–whole repair in the narrow case and distinguishes conceptual consideration from numerically distinct things.


---


<a id="HWN-140"></a>
## HWN-140 — local note 140

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 163](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/163?lang=ar) · [Qum 164](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/164?lang=ar)

Even when one of the thirty-five combinations—seven possible things meant by the first division multiplied by five possible senses of logic—has been given a formally defensible container/contained relation, one further requirement remains. The actual words must yield an idiomatic and intellectually appropriate sentence.

For example, “the words in the disposition” may avoid the strongest logical objection to containment, but it does not read naturally in the present literary construction. One should instead speak of “words *for acquiring* the disposition,” “words *for explaining* the meanings,” or “words *for attaining* the body of problems.” The supplied verbal noun—explanation, acquisition or attainment—establishes the correct relation between the otherwise mismatched terms.

This corrective procedure must be performed for each of the thirty-five theoretical combinations rather than assuming that, once an abstract relation of inclusion has been proved possible, the author's wording is already stylistically appropriate. The point is the difference between **logical coherence of a proposed relation** and **idiomatic suitability of its linguistic expression**.

# Introduction to Logic

**H-INTRO · printed pp165–187 · local notes1–82**


<a id="HWN-INTRO-001"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-001 — local note 1

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 165](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/165?lang=ar)

On the explanation “that is, this is an introduction”: the word *muqaddima* is a predicate of an omitted demonstrative subject, “this.” This follows the basic order that the subject is definite and the predicate indefinite. Others instead make “an introduction” the subject, with an omitted predicate: “an introduction [is concerned] with defining logic, explaining the need for it, and stating its subject.” An objection arises that a completely indefinite noun cannot ordinarily serve as the subject of a statement. Several replies are given. One can treat the indefiniteness as specially qualified by the tanwīn of magnification—signalling the many benefits of this introduction—or of diminution—signalling the brevity of its expressions. Alternatively place the omitted predicate before it: “In the definition of logic, the need for it, and its subject, there is an introduction,” like “In the house is a man.” A more general response judges the admissibility of an indefinite subject by whether the sentence conveys information, not by a fixed list of formal qualifications. Thus “A tree prostrated” and “A star fell just now” can inform the hearer, whereas a bare “A man is standing” may lack informative force in the relevant context.

A further objection targets the original analysis “this is an introduction.” Does the demonstrative not designate the three matters mentioned—the definition, need, and subject—whereas the introduction is not identical with those matters but is an exposition *about* them? Even granting this distinction, one need not take “this” to point to the three items themselves; it can point instead to the specifically arranged words and meanings that introduce them. The same response is available to those who understand the suppressed subject as “these matters.”


**Reading / scope note:** Entire p165 numbered note1 in first pass; the objection concerns reference and identity, not just definite-vs-indefinite forms.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-002"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-002 — local note 2

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 165](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/165?lang=ar) · [Qum 166](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/166?lang=ar)

‘Three matters are explained in it’: the relation of containment can be understood as in the earlier expression ‘the first division is in logic.’ The author’s commentary on the Talkhīṣ also offers another approach. An introduction to a science comprises what intelligent entry into it depends upon, such as knowing its definition, end and subject. An introduction to a book is a portion of discourse placed before the main purpose because of its connection and usefulness to it. On the proposed analysis these need not be identical, so the alleged identity of container and contained is avoided. Al-Sharīf objects in his marginalia that ‘introduction to a book’ is a new convention unsupported by the received terminology.

ʿAbd al-Raḥīm replies that authors conventionally call their preliminary discourse an introduction just as they call portions of a work an art, chapter or section. They may substitute other names—pattern, admonition or indication, as the Shaykh does in the Ishārāt—or call the opening a ghurra, as some teachers have done. Such designations are not restricted by a fixed rule that would make every new name impermissible. Al-Zamakhsharī’s Fāʾiq itself says muqaddima first names the group advancing before an army, from a verb meaning to advance, and is then extended to the beginning of anything, including a book or science.

A separately introduced comment by Muḥammad ʿAlī gives another explanation. Each of the three preliminary matters is a part of the introduction, as a particular inquiry can be ‘in’ a chapter. The present commentator similarly takes the introduction as the book’s prefatory discourse, useful whether or not the discipline strictly depends on it, rather than the science’s necessary preliminaries. These two repairs differ: the first understands a science’s introduction and treats the three matters individually as parts within it; the second understands the book’s introduction and can treat the whole complex of three matters as its content.

Thus the source preserves several analyses of what the word ‘introduction’ designates and what kind of containment is asserted, rather than one undisputed identification.


**Reading / scope note:** The digital text’s first proposal calls the science-introduction the container of the book-introduction, an orientation requiring checking. The ensuing two-speaker discussion is preserved without silently reversing that wording.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-007"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-007 — local note 7

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 166](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/166?lang=ar) · [Qum 167](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/167?lang=ar)

Muqaddima is taken from the vanguard of an army, the group which advances before it. This may be a conventional transfer, making the new use literally correct within the convention, or a metaphor like calling a brave man a lion. The shared feature is a part of something placed before the remainder.

Al-Khaṭṭāʾī suggests avoiding either transfer or metaphor by taking the original expression as an adjective whose noun was omitted, then applying it to a group of meanings or words preceding the science or the rest of a book. Its feminine ending can mark a shift from adjective to noun, or agreement with an understood feminine noun such as ‘group.’ But the distinction needs care. If it remains adjectival—something feminine possessing the property of advancing—its application to the prefatory group is literal insofar as that group is an instance of the general description, and figurative insofar as the word is applied under a specially established designation. If it is a noun whose underlying descriptive sense merely explains why the name was chosen, like flask or wine, literal application requires proof that the original language assigned it to this prefatory group. What is evidently established is its assignment to the army’s advance group.

ʿAbd al-Raḥīm separately repeats the alternatives: conventional transfer through resemblance, metaphor, or an adjective with an omitted qualified noun. The feminine ending can reflect substantivisation or an underlying feminine ‘group.’

The common pronunciation has kasra on the dāl, making an active participle. Yet these matters were put first by the author and appear to require a passive participle with fatḥa. The answer takes the verb qaddama in the intransitive sense ‘advance,’ as the author’s shorter commentary indicates: the preliminary matters themselves precede the rest. An objection invokes the usual morphological rule that this intensive form makes an intransitive verb transitive. The rule may be predominant rather than exceptionless. Alternatively, retain its transitive sense and regard the prefatory group as putting itself forward because it has a reason for precedence, or as placing the person who knows it ahead of one who does not by enabling an informed beginning.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-008"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-008 — local note 8

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 167](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/167?lang=ar)

The commentator signals that *muqaddima* also has two other uses. First, it is a proposition made a component of a syllogism or other proof. Second, it is something on which the validity of an argument depends—for example, in the first syllogistic figure, the minor premise's being affirmative and the major premise's being universal. The second use is broader than the first, since it includes conditions of an inference as well as its constituent propositions.


**Reading / scope note:** The two logical senses of premise are distinct from the earlier book/science introduction distinction.

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 167](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/167?lang=ar)

The words “what is intended by it here” specify that this occurrence means *the introduction to the book*, not the introduction to the science, as the term is used in some other works. The glossator has already distinguished them and directs the reader back to that discussion.

The definition of the present introduction as a “portion of discourse” is the definition of a book's introduction. That is why the author does not say that the science's problems necessarily depend on it, as one would when defining a science's introduction. The small word “here” is thus significant. Al-Sayyid al-Sharīf makes an analogous observation: in syllogistic reasoning the word “premise” means either a proposition entering the proof or something on which its soundness depends, including conditions such as affirmative minor, its actuality and universal major in the first figure.

## HWN-INTRO-011 — local note 11

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 168](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/168?lang=ar)

This means “from verbal discourse,” as is clear from the context. A *ṭāʾifa* is a group or portion. Some authorities put its minimum at three or four, others at two or three. Its form is among adjectives that have come to be used substantively, as though the original expression were “a group which separates itself from something.”

It is reported from Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās, however, that a *ṭāʾifa* may denote even one person or more. This accords with al-Jawharī's general explanation of it as a “piece of something.” Qurʾān 9:122, which speaks of a party going forth from every group to acquire religious understanding, is interpreted as allowing a single person, or a pair, to comprise the party. The plural pronoun in the following words does not require each individual *ṭāʾifa* to contain a plurality; it can refer to the multiple parties collectively conveyed by the context.


**Reading / scope note:** Lexical reports and Qurʾānic exegesis are the glossator's cited authorities, not independently authenticated interpretations.

## HWN-INTRO-012 — local note 12

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 168](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/168?lang=ar)

It is obvious that the principal topic is connected to the *meanings* conveyed by that group of expressions, not to the expressions considered merely as sounds or letters. Likewise, what is beneficial for the subject is the meanings, not the words simply as words. Hence one may supply an omitted genitive: “because the purpose is connected with *their meanings*, and *their meanings* are beneficial to it.”

Alternatively no omission is needed. Since expressions are the means through which knowledge is communicated and received, the connection and benefit are attributed to them figuratively. On the first analysis there is figurative omission (*majāz al-ḥadhf*), and on the second there is figurative attribution (*majāz fī al-isnād*).

<a id="HWN-INTRO-019"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-019 — local note 19

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 169](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/169?lang=ar) · [Qum 170](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/170?lang=ar)

The author divided knowledge without first defining it, although division is a judgement concerning something and apparently presupposes apprehending it. The commentator gives three excuses. First, conception under some aspect suffices: ordinary recognition of what this discipline calls knowledge is enough to divide it, just as grammarians divide exception into connected and disconnected without first defining it exhaustively. Second, the definition is so familiar that brevity permits its omission. Third, the concept of knowledge is immediately evident, as reported from al-Rāzī. It is among the states found by inward awareness, like hunger, thirst, satiety and repletion. Another argument is that ordinary people unfamiliar with logical definition can answer whether they know a particular thing; they must therefore understand the question, including knowledge.

The glossator initially objects to both arguments. Introspection establishes at most that a real definition is unnecessary; a verbal explanation locating the word’s assigned meaning among the mind’s stored concepts may still be needed. Immediate awareness of knowledge does not itself teach that this particular word was assigned to it. The ordinary-speaker argument applies either to someone who knows the assignment or someone who does not. The former can answer, but definitions also serve those ignorant of assignments; and if knowing the assignment made every real nature clear, knowledge would have no special status. The latter cannot necessarily understand the question or answer it.

On reconsideration, the arguments aim only to establish the concept’s immediate intelligibility and lack of need for a real definition, not a verbal one. The introspective objection therefore misses the point. For the second, choose the hearer who knows the assignment: knowing a word’s usage does not invariably entail knowing the thing’s real nature, especially for an untrained person, or the theory of definition would be unnecessary. Even so, answering the question shows only enough understanding of the assigned meaning to answer; it does not establish full grasp of the real nature. Reflect.

A further claim says knowledge cannot be defined, because everything is known through it and knowing it through something else would be circular. Again, this could concern only a real definition, since we apprehend things without knowing the word ʿilm or its assignment. Even as an objection to defining the general concept, the circle is not established: the universal knowledge to be defined differs from the particular cognitions through which particular things are apprehended.

Finally, why mention assent before conception when conception is naturally prior, either as a component on al-Rāzī’s account or as a condition on the philosophers’ account? The order here concerns the concepts: assent is positive and thus deemed nobler than conception understood privatively. What is prior in nature can be later in this order of dignity.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-021"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-021 — local note 21

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 171](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/171?lang=ar)

The “judgmental relation” (*nisba ḥukmiyya*) is explained as the complete reportable relation, affirmative in an affirmative proposition and negative in a negative one. Some instead maintain that the relation must be an affirmative restrictive relation in either case, lest the negative judgment turn into an affirmative assertion concerning nonoccurrence.

That objection works only if a restrictive relation is itself made the explicit subject of a further judgment—for example, “the relation of nonestablishment between the terms does not obtain.” It does not apply when one simply conceives the complete predicative relation expressed in “Zayd is not a writer” and then assents to it.

The correct analysis, the writer contends, treats the judgmental relation as complete and reportable. Philosophers agree that conceiving a judgmental relation precedes the occurrence of judgment. The relation must therefore be conceivably complete before assent is added. One can conceive a subject, predicate and complete predicative link without assenting and later assent without having separately entertained an additional restrictive relation between them. Introspection supports this distinction.


**Reading / scope note:** Contrast between complete assertoric relation and restrictive relation is the focus; avoid treating the writer's claim of philosophical unanimity as verified consensus.


---


<a id="HWN-INTRO-022"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-022 — local note 22

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 171](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/171?lang=ar)

There are three views of the reality of *taṣdīq*. The philosophers say it is the very act of assent and judgment. Al-Rāzī and his followers treat it as a compound of four items: the conception of what is judged about (subject), of what is attributed (predicate), of the predicative relation between them, and assent. The author of *al-Kashf* and his followers treat it as the first three taken in the condition of judgment's accruing to them; this is known as the newer school.

Thus under the first view judgment is identical with assent; under the second it is one part of assent; under the third it is external to the three conceived elements and attaches to them as an accident. Taftāzānī selects the first when he writes “knowledge, if it is assent to a relation, is taṣdīq.” Further detail belongs in longer treatises, not this brief gloss.


**Reading / scope note:** Direct three-school map of taṣdīq: simple judgment; compound of four; three cognitions with judgment as accident.


---


<a id="HWN-INTRO-023"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-023 — local note 23

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 171](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/171?lang=ar) · [Qum 172](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/172?lang=ar) · [Qum 173](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/173?lang=ar)

Two questions must be separated. The first concerns the reality of assent. The philosophers define it as apprehension with acceptance directed to a complete reportable relation. It is a kind of apprehension intrinsically different from conception, not merely an apprehension of a different object. Al-Rāzī and his followers instead make assent a compound of four: conception of the subject, predicate and relation, together with judgement. The commentator’s omission of the relation either reflects his limited purpose of identifying the difference or follows a later explanation. On the first account assent is simple with three prerequisites; on the second it is composite.

The philosophers’ convention better suits their division of knowledge according to methods of acquisition. Particular methods are too numerous to enumerate, but they fall into two general kinds. Dividing knowledge correspondingly allows a regulated account: judgement is acquired through argument, while the remaining conceptions are acquired through explanatory statements. Al-Rāzī’s aggregate has no single distinctive method, since its conceptions are acquired through explanation and its judgement through argument.

Some reconcile the accounts by saying judgement is simple when considered comprehensively and composite when analysed, because its relation presupposes its terms. The source objects that al-Rāzī explicitly distinguishes them as composite and simple. His Mulakhkhaṣ says that when a conception receives an affirmative or negative judgement, the aggregate is assent. Judgement is therefore only a component of assent for him, whether judgement itself is analysed as simple or composite.

The second question concerns the proposition’s components. Earlier philosophers give three: subject, predicate and complete affirmative or negative reportable relation. Apprehending that relation with assent is judgement, expressed as occurrence or nonoccurrence. Later philosophers give four: subject, predicate, a positive restrictive relation, and that relation’s occurrence or nonoccurrence. Their reason is that doubt contains conception of a relation without judgement; apprehending whether it obtains adds something. The objection replies that the same relation can be apprehended without assent and with assent without increasing the proposition’s components.

A possible reconciliation considers one relation under two aspects. Without assent it belongs to conceived knowledge and is called the predicative relation; with assent it belongs to assented knowledge and is called judgement on the philosophical account. Counting four follows conceptual distinction, counting three underlying identity. The commentary on the Maṭāliʿ accordingly says there are four components upon detailed analysis.

The present author is said to choose the earlier account on both questions: assent is judgement itself, and its object is the complete reportable relation rather than another occurrence/nonoccurrence component. Calling that relation the proposition’s final component points to a three-part proposition, whose only earlier prerequisites are conception of its two terms. Without ‘final,’ a fourth component after the relation would remain possible. An objector could supply an omitted ‘occurrence of’ in the author’s wording, producing four components. His later explicit threefold analysis of propositions blocks that reconstruction. None of this conflicts with simple assent: a proposition and assent are not the same thing. Further disputes exceed the scope of this gloss.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

## HWN-INTRO-025 — local note 25

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 173](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/173?lang=ar)

The philosophers agree that assent itself is judgment and is not a compound containing the three prior conceptions. They disagree, however, about the composition of the *proposition*. The earlier philosophers count three constituents: the subject, the predicate, and the complete affirmative or negative assertoric relation. Later philosophers add a fourth: the occurrence or nonoccurrence of that relation.

Taftāzānī chooses the former position, since he makes the object of assent the predicative relation itself, rather than a distinct “occurrence” or “nonoccurrence” of the relation as the later account would.

## HWN-INTRO-031 — local note 31

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 174](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/174?lang=ar)

The words “the author will indicate” forestall an objection. His description of judgment as assent to the relation alone does not, merely on its face, prove he accepts the earlier philosophers' three-part proposition. One might supply a suppressed genitive and coordination: “assent to the occurrence or nonoccurrence of the relation.” Such omissions are not unknown in eloquent Arabic. For example, Qurʾān 16:81 mentions garments guarding against heat, from which cold may also be understood, and Qurʾān 87:9 commands reminding if it benefits, with a disputed understanding of the unmentioned contrary case.

The reply is that the author later explicitly treats the proposition as having three constituents. It would then be illegitimate to impose the four-part interpretation on this earlier wording, since the hypothetical ellipsis would explain him in a way he does not accept. Changing his position or silently assuming he is merely reporting someone else's is implausible. The apparent wording also deserves interpretive priority unless a reason for an alternative reconstruction is established.


**Reading / scope note:** The Qurʾānic examples are alleged parallels for possible ellipsis; their exegetical strength is not established here.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-032"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-032 — local note 32

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 174](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/174?lang=ar)

The promised indication occurs where the author says that if a categorical judgment attributes something to something else or denies it, the proposition is affirmative or negative; the judged-about is its subject (*mawḍūʿ*), what is attributed its predicate (*maḥmūl*), and what signifies the relation its copula (*rābiṭa*). He says nothing about “occurrence or nonoccurrence of the relation” as an additional fourth constituent, either expressly or by implication.


**Reading / scope note:** Quoted future-text concordance. Actual Taftāzānī matn should be checked as a separate T-family source.

## HWN-INTRO-033 — local note 33

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 174](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/174?lang=ar)

That is, a restrictive relation may be genitive or relational, like the preceding example; or adjectival, as in “a standing man”; or another incomplete construction, such as “the one whose father struck [someone].” Such relations are not identical with an independent complete report.


**Reading / scope note:** Clarifies technical *nisba taqyīdiyya* as an incomplete relation.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-034"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-034 — local note 34

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 174](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/174?lang=ar)

A person who conceives a predicative relation can have several distinct states. First, the conceived image may influence the soul, stirring attraction or repulsion, even when the intellect recognises that the opposite is true. Rhetorical phrases such as “wine is flowing ruby, delightful,” or “honey is bitter and nauseating,” produce this *takhyīl* (imaginative impression).

If it does not have that effect, and the two sides—being and nonbeing—appear evenly balanced with no preference, the state is *shakk* (doubt). If one side is preferred without certitude, the less likely side considered is *wahm* (conjecture) and the more likely side *ẓann* (opinion). Where there is definite judgment, the author distinguishes cases in which the negative side is fixed and those in which the positive side is asserted. He further distinguishes judgments corresponding to reality from those which do not; an entrenched false judgment is *jahl murakkab* (compound ignorance), whereas a judgment agreeing with reality is *yaqīn* (certainty) when immune to further doubt or *taqlīd* (unexamined acceptance) when susceptible to it.

The resulting classification is said to have eight forms. It is not acceptable to label every one as assent in the relevant technical sense. Imaginative impression, doubt, and mere weaker apprehension lack judgment; the glossator also sets apart the negative case as he has defined it. The remaining forms are treated as assent. Therefore “assent” in the original division must be taken broadly enough to embrace probable opinion (*ẓann*) rather than only the highest certitude (*yaqīn*). The proposed eightfold count is a local classification of mental states; its labels are not automatically equivalent to those of all other logic schools.


**Reading / scope note:** Source eightfold taxonomy; exact distribution of 'falsehood' vs 'compound ignorance' merits further clarification but sequence/conditions are rendered.


---


<a id="HWN-INTRO-035"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-035 — local note 35

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 175](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/175?lang=ar)

The clarification “in the sense of division” prevents a misunderstanding of the author's sentence. Because the form *iftiʿāl* is often intransitive, one might take *iqtisām* to mean “accepting division,” then insert an omitted preposition before “necessity and acquisition.” That would yield: conception and assent are divided by necessity and acquisition.

But, the glossator argues, al-Zamakhsharī's *Asās al-Balāgha* also uses *iqtisām* transitively in the sense of actively dividing. There is then no reason to supply the omitted preposition. Conception and assent *divide* necessity and acquisition. This does not mean conception is assigned wholly to one and assent wholly to the other—as though one person were allotting two different sorts of property to separate recipients. Rather, each of conception and assent receives a share in each of the two kinds. It resembles the way a noun is divided into definite and indefinite, declinable and indeclinable, explicit and pronominal, simple and construct forms.

On the intended reading, then, both conception and assent can be immediate and both can be acquired. The syntactic construction conveys the intended logical division, but not by taking the whole of necessity as conception and the whole of acquisition as assent, or conversely.


**Reading / scope note:** Transitivity of *iqtisām* used to preserve both taṣawwur and taṣdīq under both necessary and acquired cognition.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-036"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-036 — local note 36

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 175](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/175?lang=ar)

Many verbs belonging to the pattern *iftiʿāl* govern their objects directly: for example, verbs meaning “carry it,” “take it back,” “cut it out,” or “pluck it.” Their direct transitivity need not be explained artificially by positing that they incorporate the meanings of other transitive verbs. The author regards that manoeuvre as an arbitrary complication.


**Reading / scope note:** Explicitly MODERN printed attribution to al-Karmī. Count as a printed numbered item but never as sixteenth-century al-Yazdī or early glossator speech.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-037"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-037 — local note 37

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 175](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/175?lang=ar)

The immediate or necessary is what is obtained without discursive inquiry (*naẓar*); the acquired or theoretical is what is obtained through inquiry. This formulation differs from the familiar definitions: necessary knowledge is what does not *depend* on inquiry, and theoretical knowledge what does depend on it. The distinction matters for knowledge that is ordinarily acquired discursively but might also be attained in a sudden intuition (*ḥads*) or by a specially endowed intellect. On the dependence formulation, that particular occurrence would cease to be theoretical and the definitions would fail either to include all the intended cases or to exclude the others. Describing how knowledge actually occurs—without or through inquiry—avoids the immediate ambiguity.


**Reading / scope note:** A conceptual objection about *dependency* vs *mode of acquisition*, not an independent proof of a metaphysical 'sacred soul'.


---


<a id="HWN-INTRO-038"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-038 — local note 38

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 175](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/175?lang=ar) · [Qum 176](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/176?lang=ar)

The surface wording could seem to mean that conception and assent divide necessity and acquisition, making the first pair the *dividers* and the second pair what is *divided*. The principal purpose, however, is to show that each of conception and assent is divisible into immediate and acquired kinds. This can be understood implicitly in the stated division. If both conception and assent each take shares from the two classes, each must have an immediate kind and an acquired kind, just as a noun divides into definite/indefinite or other opposing grammatical classifications.

The main assertion is thus conveyed by implication (*iltizām*) and by indirect expression (*kināya*), rather than explicitly saying that conception and assent are each of two kinds. The commentator calls an indirect expression better and more eloquent than a bare statement because the conclusion is approached through something entailing it: in favourable cases, the existence of a necessary concomitant provides evidence for the intended meaning. One must nevertheless preserve the difference between an implication that actually follows and a rhetorical interpretation merely alleged to follow.


**Reading / scope note:** The note crosses Q175–176; this is its first-pass full argumentative summary, not independently scanned.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-039"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-039 — local note 39

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 176](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/176?lang=ar)

Two explanations of *kināya* were already contrasted in the book's preface: al-Sakkākī and his followers define it as mentioning what necessarily accompanies something while intending the thing accompanied, with the literal meaning still potentially intended; another group reverses that relation. The present construction can support either explanation, because the two relevant divisions entail one another when the terms are understood correctly.
The glossator criticizes an interpretation which reduces the matter to simply reversing the order of a sentence, as in the proverbial “I presented the she-camel to the pool” instead of “I presented the pool to the she-camel.” Reversal is not in principle incompatible with indirect expression; one can use a reversal *and* speak by kināya. The critic might have intended indirect expression effected by a reversal, but that is not the same as defining kināya as reversal itself.


**Reading / scope note:** A distinction between structural inversion and indirect predication; explicitly preserves possibility of both.


---


<a id="HWN-INTRO-040"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-040 — local note 40

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 176](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/176?lang=ar)

Why is an indirect expression said to be more eloquent and beautiful than explicit speech? One answer likens it to establishing a claim by evidence. From the existence of the thing accompanied (*malzūm*) one may infer its necessary concomitant (*lāzim*), because the one cannot exist without the other. That explanation works readily for the account of kināya in which the thing accompanied is mentioned and the concomitant intended.

For al-Sakkākī's direction of inference—from the concomitant to the thing it accompanies—the explanation is less straightforward. A concomitant may be more general than the thing for which it is a concomitant, and the existence of what is general does not prove a specific instance. The argument can be repaired if the concomitant and its referent are coextensive or otherwise mutually entailing. Al-Sakkākī is cited as recognising the dependence of the inference on that equality. The full theory of rhetorical evidence would require more discussion than this note permits.


**Reading / scope note:** A rigorous scope qualification: a necessary consequence need not be convertible unless coextensive.


---


<a id="HWN-INTRO-041"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-041 — local note 41

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 176](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/176?lang=ar)

The verb *jashima* means to undertake something with exertion or hardship. In the causative form *jashshamahu* or *ajshamahu*, it means to impose that burdensome task upon another person. This explains the earlier phrase about the effort required to construct a proof.


**Reading / scope note:** Short lexical item; no historical speaker identity beyond quoted al-Taqrīb heading.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-042"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-042 — local note 42

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 176](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/176?lang=ar) · [Qum 177](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/177?lang=ar)

The customary argument establishes that some conceptions and assents are immediate and others theoretical. They cannot all be immediate, since some plainly require inquiry. Nor can all be theoretical. Acquiring one would then require another, that another a further cognition, and so on. If the sequence returns to its starting point, it is circular; if it never terminates, it is an infinite regress. Circularity would make a cognition precede itself: if A depends on B, B on C and C on A, the chain of priority returns to A. Regress would require apprehending infinitely many prerequisites.

An objection distinguishes infinitely many cognitions at one time or within finitely many times from cognitions distributed over an infinite past. An eternal soul might successively possess an unending series of preparatory cognitions, each preparing the next, without their simultaneous presence. If the proof claims simultaneous or finitely timed apprehension, the entailment is denied; if merely an infinite temporal succession, its impossibility is denied. The reply says this defence relies on the philosophers’ eternal-world and eternal-soul doctrines, rejected elsewhere; the present argument proceeds on the opposing assumptions.

A further limitation is crucial. The proof assumes conceptions cannot be acquired through assents or assents through conceptions. Without that restriction, every conception could be theoretical yet terminate in an immediate assent, or every assent theoretical yet terminate in an immediate conception. The argument establishes the twofold division within each class only if the additional restriction is justified.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.


---


<a id="HWN-INTRO-043"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-043 — local note 43

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 177](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/177?lang=ar)

The point is to establish that immediate cognitions really occur. Reality is often disclosed to us spontaneously through ordinary dealings with the world. We encounter heat without seeking to know it, conceive what heat is, and learn of fire; we then judge that fire is hot, without having first constructed a deliberate proof. Thus a conception and a judgment can arise without paid effort or systematic inquiry. Thousands of similar everyday examples are available.

Theoretical cognition is equally evident: the very need for canons of inference and methods of evaluating proofs is to acquire and establish conclusions that do not simply arrive of themselves.


**Reading / scope note:** An appeal to spontaneous experience, not an independently established formal classification of particular sensings.


---


<a id="HWN-INTRO-044"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-044 — local note 44

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 177](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/177?lang=ar)

By the conception of heat and cold is meant the intellect's grasp of the *universal concept*, acquired by means of particular sensations of heat and cold, not those particular sensations themselves. Heat itself can be present in the bodily organ which bears the power of touch. Its being present in that physical way is not, on this commentator's theory, knowledge, since knowledge is the form received in the intellect from the object.

There is no inconsistency between calling these concepts immediate and later giving the properties or characteristics of heat and cold in a scientific discussion. The latter treatment explains their attributes and judgments concerning them, rather than supplying for the first time the elementary apprehension needed to think of them.


**Reading / scope note:** Historical distinction between the causal occasion in sensation and the universal concept abstracted by intellect.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-045"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-045 — local note 45

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 177](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/177?lang=ar) · [Qum 178](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/178?lang=ar)

The note describes an angel, in the inherited cosmological account, as a luminous upper-world body capable of taking different forms except those of a dog and pig; a jinn is described as a fiery lower-world body capable even of those forms. The spirit, by contrast, is described as an immaterial substance connected to the body as rose-water is connected to a rose.

These are quoted definitions within a premodern theological/cosmological vocabulary, not empirical anatomical propositions or universally agreed metaphysical definitions.


**Reading / scope note:** Short source crosses Q177–178; its cosmological assertions are faithfully attributed without modern factual endorsement.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-046"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-046 — local note 46

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 178](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/178?lang=ar)

For the philosophers, assent is necessary or theoretical with respect to the act of judgment alone; they do not include the prior conceptions of the two terms and their relation in this classification. For al-Rāzī, by contrast, assent is a compound of four elements. Its being necessary therefore requires all four to be necessary; it is theoretical if at least one of its components is theoretical, even when the others are not. The same consequence holds for the followers of the view associated with the author of *al-Kashf*.

The extension of “necessary assent” is accordingly broader on the philosophers' simple-act account than on the composite accounts, while “theoretical assent” is broader on the composite accounts. A change in what counts as the *thing classified* changes the extension of its necessary and theoretical species.


**Reading / scope note:** Formal inclusion claim derives from different definitions of assent; source does not count all species as identical.


---


<a id="HWN-INTRO-047"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-047 — local note 47

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 178](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/178?lang=ar)

The definition of inquiry (*naẓar*) as “considering an intelligible to obtain an unknown” would, the critic argues, be clearer if it said “considering something known to obtain something unknown.” The latter immediately conveys the thought that an item already disclosed is used to discover something concealed. The phrase “the intelligible” instead suggests what has already been apprehended by the rational faculty, without making the inferential transition as transparent.

The principal commentator gives several reasons for choosing “intelligible.” First, “knowledge” (*ʿilm*) is used in multiple senses, such as a form in the intellect, assent and certainty, and equivocal language in a definition is undesirable. The critic regards the list as verbal proliferation: knowledge properly refers to the disclosure of reality. Second, reasoning proceeds in intelligibles, especially universals, not bare particulars; an isolated particular is too determined to serve as a universal mediating term by which another is inferred. Third, the term maintains balanced rhyme with “the unknown.”

The critic suspects that the third reason was the chief motive. He adds that a particular is neither a suitable general means of acquiring a distinct particular nor usually something acquired by using another particular as a middle, because the individuating conditions separate them. The argument concerns the logical role of middle terms, not the claim that particular events can never be known by signs in ordinary life.


**Reading / scope note:** Rendered substance of the quoted al-Taqrīb note; traditional inference distinction is source-attributed.


---


<a id="HWN-INTRO-048"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-048 — local note 48

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 178](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/178?lang=ar)

“Through inquiry” should mean through an act of deliberate intention, as the wording and final purpose suggest. The definition is therefore not refuted by a case of sudden intuition (*ḥads*), in which the arranged premises arise all at once; in such an event the apprehension is not brought about by a deliberately chosen discursive procedure, but occurs without that voluntary direction.


**Reading / scope note:** Intention distinguishes formal inquiry from sudden intuition; no independent psychometric claim.


---


<a id="HWN-INTRO-049"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-049 — local note 49

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 178](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/178?lang=ar)

The intelligible under consideration may be a conception or an assent; and the assent may be certain, probable or even mistaken in the specified sense. The expression is broad enough to include one known item or several, since a definition may employ a single term or a composite explanation. The definite article is therefore generic, indicating the class rather than a single preselected item.


**Reading / scope note:** Short scope clarification; note50 starts on Q178 but continues beyond, left for next stage.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-050"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-050 — local note 50

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 178](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/178?lang=ar) · [Qum 179](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/179?lang=ar)

The unknown sought may be conceptual or assertoric. A conceptual unknown is acquired from conceptual materials: to understand human, we consider animal and rational and arrange them. An assertoric unknown is acquired from assertoric materials: to know that the world is originated, we consider that it changes and that everything changing is originated.

The starting materials must already be known, so that they can be considered. The result must not be known in precisely the respect in which inquiry seeks it, or one would be acquiring what is already possessed. It must nevertheless be known under another aspect, so that the inquirer can distinguish it among meanings and direct a voluntary search toward it.

Al-Rāzī raises a dilemma. If the object is already apprehended, seeking it seeks what is already possessed; if it is wholly unapprehended, no search can be directed toward it. The usual reply distinguishes a known aspect from an unknown one. His further objection is that under the known aspect it still cannot be sought as unknown, and under the unknown aspect the mind still has no apprehended object toward which to direct the search. The source expressly leaves Sharaf al-Dīn al-Marāghī’s objection to this argument, the reply and their detailed discussion outside the present book.


**Reading / scope note:** Full coverage of the printed numbered note; the debate which the source itself declines to supply is not an untranslated omission in this edition.

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 179](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/179?lang=ar)

The statement about departing from the word “known” supplies an answer to the objection that the author did not define inquiry as considering the known to obtain the unknown, even though knowledge and ignorance are the natural opposites.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-052"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-052 — local note 52

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 179](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/179?lang=ar)

“Knowledge” has several technical uses. It may signify a form present in intellect, encompassing conception and assent; it may also mean firm, unshakable, reality-conforming conviction, or belief in a broad sense including opinion, compound ignorance and imitation. A definition using such a shared expression without an indicator risks being read in the wrong sense. That is the reason advanced for choosing “intelligible” instead of “known.”


**Reading / scope note:** The list reports distinct inherited usages; it does not make compound ignorance genuine knowledge in every technical vocabulary.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-053"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-053 — local note 53

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 179](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/179?lang=ar)

A particular can be apprehended through the five outward senses or through the inward powers traditionally enumerated as common sense, imagination, estimation, the compositive power and memory. Simply arranging several particular sensations does not produce another particular sensation or a universal as a logical inference. Nor does joining universals as such yield a determinate individual. On this account particulars are neither logical premises acquiring another particular nor conclusions acquired as particulars. “Intelligible” therefore points toward universals, whereas “known” can cover both particular and universal objects.


**Reading / scope note:** A historical restriction on *formal inferential acquisition*, not a denial of ordinary knowledge of particulars through signs.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-058"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-058 — local note 58

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 180](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/180?lang=ar)

The reading ‘the judgements of its subject’s particulars are learned from it’ has the reported alternative ‘are discovered by it’; both amount to the same. Make the universal rule the major premise of a readily obtained minor which predicates the rule’s subject of a particular falling under it. The particular judgements potentially contained in the rule are thereby brought into explicit actuality. To determine Zayd’s grammatical status in ‘Zayd struck,’ establish ‘Zayd is an agent’; add ‘Every agent is nominative’; infer ‘Zayd is nominative.’ Apply the pattern throughout the sciences.

The applications under a rule need not all be theoretical. Otherwise ‘The first figure is productive’ would be excluded, since its individual inferential judgements are immediately evident, although the rule is admitted among logic’s questions. ‘Judgements are learned from it’ therefore means its suitability to yield them: were they not already immediate, they could be acquired through the rule. Reflect.


**Reading / scope note:** The alternative wording is source-reported and not independently manuscript-certified.

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 181](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/181?lang=ar)

Contradictory results of reasoning can belong to different persons, since thinkers disagree; but they can also arise within one person's intellectual history, as the same inquirer changes judgments at different times. <a id="HWN-INTRO-063"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-063 — local note 63

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 181](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/181?lang=ar)

When a person directly recalls having reasoned to one conclusion and then to its opposite, the conflict of the judgments is accessible by introspection. In disputes between different people, words alone do not guarantee that their internal beliefs contradict: a speaker may utter a position for display or some other reason. Error also affects conception, as shown by disagreement about *ḥadd* and *rasm*. The author's emphasis on assent may rest on its greater obviousness or on leaving the parallel conceptual case to analogy.


**Reading / scope note:** A distinction between contradictory utterances and actual opposed assents; it does not make all self-reports infallible.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-064"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-064 — local note 64

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 181](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/181?lang=ar) · [Qum 182](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/182?lang=ar)

‘There must be a universal rule’: lā budda can be explained as no separation from it, or no substitute for it, with the accompanying preposition interpreted accordingly. Although the practical aim is to distinguish the correctness of a particular thought in detail, no teacher can enumerate every such particular case. The discipline therefore supplies the universal rule to which one can turn when examining any particular inference.

An objection says that a universal rule would be necessary only if inquiry were the sole way of acquiring knowledge. The soul might instead be freed from distractions and directed toward the universal world, receiving truth through disclosure or another route. The reply restricts the claim: it is not that every person requires the rule for every kind of knowledge, but that the reflective inquirer, precisely as reflective inquirer, needs it.

Another objection says the methods and their conditions might already be immediately known; error could result simply from failing to attend to whether a particular inference is sound. The reply is that immediate rational awareness alone does not reliably distinguish error from correctness, since sincere intelligent seekers of truth do nevertheless err in acquisition. The stated need concerns the disciplined regulation of such inquiry.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-066"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-066 — local note 66

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 182](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/182?lang=ar)

Why begin the proof that logic is needed by dividing cognition into conception and assent? Would it not suffice to distinguish knowledge acquired by reflection from that which arises without reflection? The answer is that the author wants to establish the need for logic in both its parts: the way leading to unknown conceptions and the way leading to unknown judgments. A genus can have two kinds without each species itself exhibiting both kinds. Without the more detailed initial divisions, one could suppose all conception immediate while only assent required acquisition, or conversely. The desired twofold need would not follow.


**Reading / scope note:** The note later queries whether the final premise proves need for logic itself or need to learn it; its logic is a distinction of conclusions.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-067"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-067 — local note 67

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 182](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/182?lang=ar)

The argument has three premises in its outward presentation but arguably four in substance, because the second combines two propositions: conception and assent each divide into immediate and acquired kinds, and theoretical knowledge is obtained from immediate knowledge.


**Reading / scope note:** A structural unpacking of the argument, not a new manuscript reading.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-068"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-068 — local note 68

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 182](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/182?lang=ar) · [Qum 183](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/183?lang=ar)

The familiar counterargument says logic is acquired, yet cannot be needed to acquire theoretical knowledge. If it were not acquired it would be immediate, making study unnecessary. But if acquired logic were required for every acquisition, obtaining it would require another rule, and that another, producing circularity or infinite regress. One cannot simply propose termination in an immediate logical rule while simultaneously assuming that the whole collection called logic is acquired.

The answer denies both extreme assumptions. Logic is not theoretical in every part, nor immediate in every part. The first figure supplies an immediately evident element; the other three figures provide theoretical elements established from it by the stated reductions. The acquired portions thus terminate in immediate portions without making all study unnecessary.

The objection can also be formulated the other way: to avoid circularity and regress, logic must be immediate, so learning it is unnecessary. Even if granted, this establishes only lack of need to learn it, not lack of need for the principles themselves. A person may already possess an immediate or previously acquired rule and still depend on it in obtaining further theoretical knowledge. This distinction is difficult and deserves reflection.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-073"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-073 — local note 73

**MODERN EDITORIAL REFERENCE — not full translation** · [Qum 184](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/184?lang=ar) · [Qum 185](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/185?lang=ar)

Modern editorial reference: al-Taqrīb, p19, supplies the numbered discussion of a science’s subject and various proposed classes of intrinsic and foreign accidents. The separately introduced historical quotation by Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī immediately following it is translated in full below, rather than being treated as part of the modern author’s numbered voice.


### Separately attributed unnumbered passage

**Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī, independently introduced extended gloss after no.73**

Know that accidents divide into intrinsic and extrinsic accidents. What belongs to a thing may belong through its own essence, through a broader or coextensive constituent, or through an external factor that is equal, broader, narrower or disjoint in extension: seven cases. Three are agreed to be intrinsic: belonging through the essence, as wonder to humans as human; through a coextensive constituent, as speaking through rationality; or through a coextensive external property, as laughter through wonder. Three are reported as agreed to be foreign: through a broader external factor, as occupying space belongs to a white thing because it is a body; through a narrower factor, as laughter belongs to animal because it is human; or through a disjoint factor, as heat belongs to water through fire or sunlight. The remaining case is disputed: belonging through a broader constituent, as occupying space belongs to humans through body and voluntary movement through animality.

Later writers count this last case as intrinsic; earlier writers count it as foreign, followed by some later investigators. The principal commentator’s definition follows the latter. Further discussion exceeds the place available.

A science investigates intrinsic accidents because its purpose is to explain its own subject’s conditions. Intrinsic accidents truly are conditions of that subject. Foreign accidents are primarily conditions of other things, to which they belong intrinsically; they should therefore be investigated in the sciences whose subjects are those other things.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-INTRO-075"></a>
## HWN-INTRO-075 — local note 75

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 185](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/185?lang=ar) · [Qum 186](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/186?lang=ar)

The inquiry returns to the science’s subject in several ways. It may make that general subject the subject of a question and establish an intrinsic accident, as natural philosophy attributes a natural place to body. It may make a species the subject, as touch is attributed to every animal. Here it may establish an intrinsic accident or a feature belonging through a broader factor, provided the generality does not exceed the science’s subject—for example the jurist’s treatment of every intoxicant as prohibited.

It may also make an intrinsic accident or a species of such an accident the subject of a question, establishing its intrinsic property or a property mediated by something broader under the same restriction. The example is the asserted intermediate rest between two rectilinear motions. Thus the science investigates either its general subject’s intrinsic accidents or intrinsic accidents of things specifically belonging within that subject. This answers the objection that sciences discuss properties mediated by narrower factors although such properties are not intrinsic accidents of the unrestricted general subject. A further discussion and another answer will follow.

## HWN-DALALA-006 — local note 6

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 189](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/189?lang=ar)

Logic needs an account of signification because technical rules concerning definitions distinguish whole, partial and implicative meanings. In a complete essential definition, an external implication cannot replace the defining content; the use of constituent meanings likewise has restrictions. The five predicables belong to the study of simple meanings, requiring a prior distinction between simple and compound expressions. Figurative and equivocal expressions are normally avoided in definitions unless a clarifying indicator is present. Univocal and gradated terms also matter: some allow a gradated expression to function as a genus while others deny it. These controversies explain the conventional introductory study of language.


**Reading / scope note:** First-pass paraphrase of the note's instructional dependency chain, not certification of every reported technical opinion.

The difference must therefore rest on the relevant nature producing or prompting the sign, so that the indication is attributed to nature.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-013"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-013 — local note 13

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 189](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/189?lang=ar) · [Qum 190](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/190?lang=ar)

The interjection aḥ may have fatḥa or ḍamma on the hamza. A derivative verb describing someone’s making that sound is said to be a later formation rather than an original lexical verb. Natural signs also include akh, with variants in the hamza and doubling of the final consonant, for pain; uff for vexation; and awh for suffering. Al-Sharīf elsewhere gives a particular pronunciation of akh for regret, and in another gloss omits the doubling qualification and associates it with sadness. The present writer prefers the account he has given.


**Reading / scope note:** The exact historical vocalisations remain tied to the searchable spelling and need independent print checking; the competing lexical reports are not collapsed.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-014"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-014 — local note 14

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 190](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/190?lang=ar)

A rapid pulse indicating fever is an example of nonverbal natural indication. The commentaries on the Maṭāliʿ and the Muṭawwal appear to allow only conventional and rational nonverbal signs, making five types in total. The present writer defends the sixth: flushing with embarrassment, paling with fear, and a pulse-movement indicating a bodily condition are natural nonverbal signs.

One may object that these are rational signs—effects indicating causes, or one co-effect indicating another. But the same analysis can be applied to cries of pain. Nor can the distinction simply be that nature compels bodily effects but not the utterance; intense pain may also compel a cry. The correct account allows both indications under different grounds. Where the causal connection is rationally known, the sign supports rational indication. A person unfamiliar with that rational connection may nevertheless pass to the meaning through experience of nature’s customary behaviour. That indication is not based on the rational relation; even supposing that relation absent, the habituated passage could remain.

Nonverbal natural indication is therefore evident in an animal pawing the ground on seeing barley, a listener moving rhythmically in response to pleasing music, or expressions of face and brow accompanying pain. The relevant issue is how the sign leads the observer, not merely whether its physical occurrence has a cause.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-015"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-015 — local note 15

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 190](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/190?lang=ar) · [Qum 191](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/191?lang=ar)

The meaningless sound dīz heard behind a wall indicates a speaker by reason. A meaningful utterance would also do so, and most writers therefore say ‘utterance’ without restriction. A meaningless example prevents a beginner from mistaking the indication for lexical convention. Convention assigns a word to its meaning, not to the existence of whoever speaks it. Another explanation says that using a meaningful word would give two indications, conventional and rational, obscuring the example’s purpose.

The wall likewise makes the sound’s evidential function clear. A visible speaker can also be known by sight, making the sound’s indication comparatively unobtrusive. The lexical aside gives the singular and plural forms of the Arabic words for wall.

Al-Sharīf says in two glosses that a visible speaker is known by vision, while a speaker behind a wall is known through the sound’s rational indication. The natural interpretation is not that rational indication disappears in the visible case, but that knowledge is not obtained from the sound alone: sight accompanies it. His stated purpose of making the indication evident, and his contrast with the wall-case, support that interpretation.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 191](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/191?lang=ar)

Their exhaustiveness is supported by surveying cases, not a strict contradiction-based proof that no additional relation is possible. By contrast, conventional verbal signification divided into whole, part and external concomitant is treated as exhaustive by conceptual disjunction.


**Reading / scope note:** Distinguishes an empirical classification from an alleged rationally exhaustive partition.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-018"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-018 — local note 18

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 191](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/191?lang=ar)

The author divides conventional verbal signification without redefining it, relying on the earlier general definition and division. Quṭb al-Dīn defines it as an expression being such that whenever uttered its meaning is understood because its assignment is known. The last condition excludes natural verbal indication, where understanding proceeds from nature rather than an assignment, and rational verbal indication, which can occur without an assignment or without knowing it. Hearing an utterance behind a wall indicates a speaker equally to someone who knows the language and someone who does not.

‘Whenever uttered’ is universally stated because the signification considered in this art is general. Understanding a meaning on a particular occasion through a contextual indicator is not, for these logicians, enough to make the expression generally signify it. Grammarians and legal theorists may instead attend to ordinary communicative understanding, which is why they also invoke customary concomitance. Finally the definition says ‘knowledge of its assignment,’ not ‘knowledge of its assignment to that meaning’: the latter would restrict the definition to whole-meaning signification and exclude the other two species.
