<a id="HWN-DALALA-021"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-021 — local note 21

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 191](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/191?lang=ar) · [Qum 192](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/192?lang=ar)

A word may indicate an external concomitant, as human indicates the capacity for laughter. The first kind is called correspondence because expression and complete meaning agree; the second inclusion because the indicated constituent is within the assigned meaning; the third implication because the external indicated item accompanies that meaning. Each names the resulting indication from its grounding relation. Iltizām is preferred to mere luzūm because the stronger formation suits the strongest relevant concomitance.

Each definition should include ‘insofar as it is such’: the complete assigned meaning as complete, the constituent as constituent, and the external concomitant as external concomitant. Otherwise the species overlap incorrectly when one expression has several assignments. If a word is assigned independently to a whole and to its part, its indication of the part within the whole is inclusion, although the part is also a complete meaning under the other assignment. Conversely, direct use under the part’s own assignment is correspondence, though the item happens to be a constituent elsewhere.

Similarly, with separate assignments to something and its concomitant, indication of the concomitant from the former is implication, not correspondence, although the same item is directly assigned elsewhere. Directly indicating the concomitant under its own assignment is correspondence, not implication. If the word is assigned to the accompanied thing, its concomitant, and their aggregate, indication of the concomitant as part of the aggregate is inclusion although it is external relative to the first thing; indication of it as that first thing’s external concomitant is implication although it is a part under the aggregate assignment.

The author is dividing in a manner suggesting definitions, rather than supplying exhaustive definitions of each species, and leaves familiar aspect-conditions implicit. Extended commentaries discuss the remaining questions; the brevity of this work does not require reproducing them all.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-022"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-022 — local note 22

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 192](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/192?lang=ar)

Implication is indication of something external to the assigned meaning, but a word cannot indicate every external thing indiscriminately, or one expression would signify infinitely many unrelated meanings. An additional condition is therefore required. Correspondence and inclusion need only knowledge of the assignment: understanding the whole brings understanding of its part.

If an expression has several independent assignments, or its one assigned meaning has several constituents, a hearer acquainted with those assignments can understand all those senses or parts when it is uttered. Each complete sense is indicated by correspondence and each constituent by inclusion, even if the hearer does not know which the speaker intends. Signification does not simply depend on current intention, since established meanings can be understood without being intended. No single word has infinitely many separate assignments or one meaning composed of infinitely many constituents in the relevant sense. Thus the infinity problem does not demand a further restricting condition for correspondence and inclusion as it does for implication.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-027"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-027 — local note 27

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 193](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/193?lang=ar) · [Qum 194](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/194?lang=ar)

Indication of a constituent as constituent presupposes indication of the named whole, and indication of what lies outside a named meaning as outside presupposes that named meaning. One explanation says inclusion and implication require an assignment, and assignment supplies correspondence, so the two require correspondence. Another says they are subordinate to correspondence and a subordinate cannot exist without what it follows.

That second explanation is insufficient. A thing considered precisely as ‘what is followed’ likewise presupposes a follower; it would appear to establish the reverse dependence too. Nor can subordination simply mean later occurrence: apprehending a part precedes apprehending a whole, and apprehending a positive capacity can precede apprehending its privation. More plausibly the subordination concerns purpose: lexical assignment primarily aims to indicate the assigned meaning, and indicates its parts or concomitants secondarily. But a secondary intended stage may occur without achieving the principal goal, as someone travels partway and returns before reaching his destination. Purpose-subordination alone does not prove inseparability.

An objection invokes a word used for a constituent or concomitant with an indicator blocking intention of the whole. The reply distinguishes intention from signification: the indicator blocks intending correspondence, not its underlying occurrence for someone who knows the assignment.

A further test concerns the grammarians’ three components of a verb’s meaning: action, relation to an agent, and time. Hearing the verb without its agent seems to convey the action but not the relation, which requires both relata, apparently giving inclusion without correspondence. Three replies are offered. Correspondence may be present hypothetically: it would occur if the agent were stated. Alternatively, the assumed isolated utterance is not a correct use in eloquent discourse, on which the relevant understanding depends. Or the verb is assigned to action qualified by time, while the relation to the agent is not a constituent of its assigned meaning. Consider these alternatives carefully.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-028"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-028 — local note 28

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 194](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/194?lang=ar) · [Qum 195](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/195?lang=ar)

Definitions of the three significations differ. On the familiar majority account, correspondence indicates the whole real assigned meaning whether intended or not; inclusion indicates its part, and implication its concomitant, equally without requiring present intention. Another account admits a whole assigned meaning actually or constructively and requires, in all three cases, that the word be used primarily for its assigned meaning. Its part or concomitant may then be intended secondarily.

Under the second convention, a word used primarily for a part or an external concomitant is classified as correspondence in that use, not inclusion or implication. Under the majority’s account the same use may retain the latter names. Dependence of inclusion and implication on correspondence is therefore evident under the second definition, because use of the whole or accompanied meaning is built into it. Under the majority’s definition the dependence is less evident: familiar extended use or a diverting contextual indicator may direct the word toward part or concomitant without an actual whole-meaning indication in the intended sense. The author, choosing that account, answers with ‘even hypothetically,’ as explained by the commentator. The full dispute exceeds this brief passage.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-032"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-032 — local note 32

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 195](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/195?lang=ar) · [Qum 196](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/196?lang=ar)

Correspondence can occur without inclusion if the assigned meaning has no part, and without implication if it has no suitably rational or customary concomitant. But merely showing that such an absence is possible does not establish its actual occurrence. Lack of knowledge of entailment is not knowledge that entailment fails. Some accordingly accept non-entailment of inclusion from examples such as a point or unity, whose lack of parts supplies an actual case, while treating implication differently.

Another argument appeals to inward awareness: were a further concept necessarily apprehended whenever any concept is apprehended, we could not think of anything while inattentive to everything else. Al-Sharīf says this proves non-entailment only if that introspective claim is sound.

A regress argument says that if every concept necessarily carried a further concept, apprehending one would require infinitely many at once. The reply allows the chain to close reciprocally, as with fatherhood and sonship. Mutual mental implication does not itself make each cognition causally depend on the other in a vicious circle. Nor does the actual termination of the series require that termination itself be conceived, with another attendant concept.

An attempted repair considers the aggregate of a thing and its concomitant. If the aggregate has none, the desired counterexample is found; if it has one, add it and continue. But conceiving the two members does not entail conceiving their aggregate as an aggregate, so the new regress does not follow.

Al-Rāzī instead argues that every essence has an evident concomitant, at least that it is not what is other than itself. If ‘evident’ means that the concomitant’s conception necessarily arises from conceiving the essence, the universal claim is denied: we often think of something without thinking of another thing or of their difference. If it means that conceiving both and their relation makes the connection evident, that broader evident concomitance is admitted but is insufficient for the stricter implicative signification at issue.

A final objection says that an apprehended thing must be distinguished from others, requiring apprehension of those others. The reply distinguishes being differentiated in itself from explicitly apprehending that differentiation. Otherwise every conception would already require an assent, which the source rejects. The thing must be distinct, but the thinker need not separately judge or conceive its distinction from every other thing.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-033"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-033 — local note 33

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 196](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/196?lang=ar) · [Qum 197](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/197?lang=ar)

The commentator now compares inclusion and implication. The author left this relation unstated because it could be inferred by comparison from ‘not conversely.’ Neither need entail the other. A composite assigned meaning may have parts but no relevant external concomitant, allowing inclusion without implication. A simple assigned meaning may have a mentally necessary correlate without parts, allowing implication without inclusion; the source proposes the sun as a body with light as its correlate.

An opposing argument says that understanding the whole as whole and its part as part necessarily brings understanding of composition, which is outside the assigned meaning; inclusion would therefore entail implication. The reply identifies a confusion between something bearing an attribute and that thing explicitly considered under the attribute. What is understood may be the object which happens to be a whole and the object which happens to be a part, without their being conceived as whole and part. Only the latter explicit considerations require the further concept of composition.

Moreover, if those explicit concepts of wholeness and parthood necessarily arose, they would themselves already be external concepts sufficient for the opponent’s purpose. The extra appeal to their entailment of composition would be unnecessary. Reflect.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-036"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-036 — local note 36

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 197](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/197?lang=ar)

The division into simple and compound is not being applied to every object called a “sign” or to the entire earlier sixfold classification. <a id="HWN-DALALA-037"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-037 — local note 37

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 197](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/197?lang=ar) · [Qum 198](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/198?lang=ar) · [Qum 199](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/199?lang=ar)

In defining a compound as an expression whose part is intended to signify a part of its meaning, the signification meant is correspondence, as al-Kātibī and others specify. It is not inclusion or implication alone, their conjunction, or an unrestricted notion covering all three. Otherwise an expression composed of two independently meaningful elements could be compound relative to its whole assigned meaning yet simple relative to a simple included part or simple external concomitant, which has no parts to be indicated.

A commentator objects that being compound under one meaning and simple under another is harmless. ‘ʿAbd Allāh’ is simple as a personal name and compound as ‘servant of God’; ‘rational animal’ can likewise be a name or a description. Why should differences between correspondence and inclusion or implication be less allowable?

A preferable rationale for prioritising correspondence is then offered. Composition under an included meaning entails composition under the whole: a part of a part is a part. Composition under an implied meaning likewise presupposes corresponding signification of the relevant expression-parts. But composition under the whole does not entail composition under its included or implied meanings, which may be simple. Correspondence is therefore the more fundamental criterion. An objection reverses the reasoning for simplicity, since simplicity under the whole entails simplicity under the other senses, not conversely. The answer gives priority to the positive concept of composition over the privative concept of simplicity. This establishes preference for the criterion rather than, by itself, absolute necessity.

The earlier objection can also be answered by distinguishing two assignments from one. Proper-name and descriptive uses involve different assignments, whereas the disputed correspondence/inclusion/implication comparison concerns one assignment and one use. The permitted change of classification in the former case does not automatically license indistinct classification in the latter. ‘Intended’ must also mean a legitimate intention under linguistic convention: arbitrarily intending a syllable of Zayd to signify part of his meaning does not make the name compound; nor does such arbitrary intention alter a multiword phrase already used as a single proper name.

The familiar difficulty concerns verbs. Their material letters appear to signify action and their form, constituted by vowels, pauses and letter-order, time. A verb would therefore have a part signifying a part of its meaning, although it is ordinarily counted simple. The standard answer restricts ‘part’ to an audible component ordered in hearing; a purely formal configuration is not separately audible.

But an imperative or a verb with an implicit subject is counted compound with that subject, although one component is unspoken. The reply extends audible to what is grammatically supposed or capable of being heard: the implicit ‘you’ in an imperative and ‘he’ in the appropriate verbal clause satisfy that condition.

The glossator finds the answer unstable. If form is conceded to be a component of the verb, which is an utterance, denying that component is audible threatens the claim that the whole is an utterance. Better deny that the form is a separately countable part of the verbal expression. This also blocks the renewed argument that the remaining material alone indicates a part of the meaning: once the proposed form/material division is rejected as a division into expression-parts, the relevant objection has lost its premise.

More fundamentally, all these difficulties assume that the verb’s meaning is the aggregate of action, time and relation to an agent. On the writer’s preferred account, it is a simple configuration abstracted from those three. The material-and-form expression jointly signifies that simple configuration; one need not grant that its material separately signifies action and its form separately time. The counterexample then does not arise in the proposed form.

Finally, although the simple is naturally prior to the compound, the definition considers the concepts as a possession-and-privation opposition. Privation is understood through what it lacks; the positive concept is also considered nobler. The author therefore presents compound before simple in this conceptual division without denying the natural priority of simpler components.


**Reading / scope note:** This preserves the source’s alternative defences and its preferred account rather than treating every proposed solution as jointly accepted. The philosophical theory of verbal form is reported, not independently established.


---


<a id="HWN-DALALA-038"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-038 — local note 38

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 199](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/199?lang=ar) · [Qum 200](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/200?lang=ar)

The relevant ‘part’ is an audible component ordered in hearing, actually or in grammatical supposition. This answers the objection that verbs would all be compound because their material signifies action and their formal configuration signifies time. The form is not independently audible and ordered as another expression-part. It also allows an imperative’s implicit subject, since ‘strike!’ is grammatically equivalent to ‘strike, you!’

One may instead deny that form is a part of the verb at all in that sense. A formal configuration, as ordinarily understood, is not itself an utterance; combining an utterance with something not uttered would not make both independent audible parts. Otherwise the classification of verbs among words and their study in grammar and morphology would become problematic.

A further difficulty remains with audible present-tense prefixes indicating person and with the alif indicating participation in the relevant verbal pattern: these are both heard and semantically functional. Expressions with the definite article, feminine suffix or relational suffix present no identical problem, because logicians may regard them as compound; nothing in their own wording establishes that all are simple. A grammatical commentary’s calling them simple may concern their taking one inflection, or simply a different grammatical convention. Grammarians’ classifications are not automatically authoritative for the logicians’ different criterion.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-039"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-039 — local note 39

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 200](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/200?lang=ar)

The original Aristotelian definition of a compound was commonly stated as an expression whose part indicates a part of its meaning. Later writers added that this indication must be **intended**, because a multiword expression such as “ʿAbd Allāh” may be used as a single proper name without intending its components separately to signify a servant and God. The logician's attention to semantic unity explains why this case differs from a grammatical division based on word count alone.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-040"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-040 — local note 40

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 200](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/200?lang=ar) · [Qum 201](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/201?lang=ar)

Requiring that the partial signification be intended implies that signification is broader than intention. Someone who knows a word’s assignment and has the corresponding meaning available conceives that meaning upon conceiving the word, even if the speaker does not intend it. A hearer familiar with several senses of an equivocal word may apprehend them all although only one was intended.

Others make signification dependent on intention. The Shaykh says in the Shifāʾ that a word does not signify simply by itself; otherwise it would have an invariable allocation of meanings which it could never exceed. If ʿayn is intended for a spring, it signifies the spring; if for a coin, the coin. Without intention it signifies nothing in this sense; some logicians would not even call an uninterpreted sound a meaningful utterance. Al-Ṭūsī similarly says in the commentary on the Ishārāt that conventional signification belongs to an utterance used with an intended meaning which the hearer understands. Other possible meanings, in the same or another language, are not thereby what it signifies on that occasion.

Later writers strongly object. Granting that sound does not signify intrinsically does not make intention the only alternative: established assignment may supply the relation. The commentary on the Maṭāliʿ appeals to evident experience that recalling an assigned word evokes its meaning whether intended or not, and an equivocal expression evokes its known senses. A contextual indicator determines the intended one, but intention and signification are very different facts.

The glossator judges the dispute largely verbal, depending on whether signification is defined as passage from word to meaning insofar as intended, or passage without that restriction. The Shaykh and his followers need not deny the occurrence of the broader mental associations; later writers need not claim that every evoked sense is thereby apprehended as the speaker’s intended one. Either extreme would be unreasonable. Compare their formulations with this definitional distinction in view.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 201](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/201?lang=ar)

If it means *capable of being intended*, a proper name composed of words might be counted compound simply because its components could be used independently under another assignment. ## HWN-DALALA-044 — local note 44

‘In the grammarians’ convention, a verb’ seems to identify the logical kalima and grammatical fiʿl in both directions. Neither unrestricted equivalence is secure. Defective verbs are grammatical verbs but can be logical instruments rather than kalimāt. Conversely, names of verbs are called kalimāt by al-Sharīf while grammarians classify them as nouns.

One may accept the first counterexample, given the division of copulas into temporal and non-temporal, yet dispute the second. Names of verbs do not indicate time through their own morphological forms: other nouns with comparable patterns do not indicate time. They plainly count as kalimāt under a definition such as ‘what can serve as predicate alone but not as subject.’ They might also be accommodated under the present definition by saying that they signify expressions whose forms indicate time, and are consequently treated as though their own forms did so.

The more exact reply follows the present author’s own definition and denies that these verb-names are kalimāt for him. The commentator can also be read as asserting only that every logical kalima of this defined kind is a grammatical verb, not that every grammatical verb is a logical kalima. The defective-verb counterexample then does not refute what was actually claimed. Reflect.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-064"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-064 — local note 64

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 205](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/205?lang=ar) · [Qum 206](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/206?lang=ar)

Some answer the objection by saying that dividing a universal into classes does not require every class to occur within every species under that universal. The classes need only be found across the species collectively. Thus dividing simple expression into proper, univocal, gradated and the other kinds need not put every kind within noun, verb and particle separately.

The glossator agrees with that logical principle but says it does not solve this case. The problem is not that verbs and particles lack some resulting classes; it is that, under the assumed account, they belong to none of them. If they remain within the subject divided, the enumeration is not exhaustive.

The correct response is that the relevant unity and multiplicity of meaning are themselves not ascribed to verb and particle in this nominal conceptual sense. The later class-names depend on that qualification, so the effective division concerns nouns alone. One may still object that the original subject is ‘simple expression’ without restriction. The answer is that its division is conditional upon the meaning’s being one or many in the specified respect, as the conditional particle and context indicate. Verbs and particles lacking that qualification are not members of the effectively restricted subject. This final clarification is presented by the writer as an expansion of his earlier brief remark.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-068"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-068 — local note 68

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 206](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/206?lang=ar)

Assignment requires the assigner to conceive some meaning, since it establishes a relation between expression and meaning. If a particular meaning is conceived and a word or words assigned to it, the assignment is specific because its grounding conception is specific, and the assigned meaning is specific too.

If a universal meaning containing relative or absolute particulars is conceived, the assigner may select an expression or expressions for that universal itself: both assignment and assigned meaning are general. Alternatively, the universal conception may direct attention collectively toward its particular instances, and the expression may be assigned to their specific meanings. Their general apprehension through the universal suffices for this act: the assignment is general in its grounding consideration while the assigned meanings are particular.

The dispute about pronouns, demonstratives, relatives, article-definite expressions and related forms is whether their assignment follows the second or third pattern. The author prefers the second, so they initially enter ‘one in meaning’ and must then be excluded from proper names by the further qualification ‘by assignment,’ as the commentator explains.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-072"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-072 — local note 72

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 208](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/208?lang=ar) · [Qum 209](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/209?lang=ar)

On ‘there is therefore no need to exclude them’: under the first interpretation, demonstratives and similar expressions are already excluded from proper names, on the author's own position, by ‘with its individuation,’ meaning its particularity. The further qualification ‘by assignment’ would therefore be redundant under this interpretation too. Restricting this difficulty to the last interpretation, as the wording apparently does, is not satisfactory.

The objection applies to the author's words as the glossator explains them, even if the passage is interpreted through a rhetorical shift of reference (istikhdām). It can, however, be repaired by taking ‘meaning’ initially as the meaning genuinely assigned, while the pronoun in ‘with its individuation’ refers instead to what the expression is used for, whether literally or figuratively. On that shifted interpretation, ‘by assignment’ can exclude demonstratives and the like, since what they are used for is plainly an individuated particular.

Two further matters remain. First, an indefinite expression intended to denote some individual or other, alternatively and indeterminately, seems to have one particular meaning individuated by assignment; yet it is certainly not called a proper name. Do not answer that its meaning is not particular by assignment, because it has indeterminate range and can apply to many, like ‘human’ and other universals, and because some writers call it universal. The predicability of many which is absent from the particular and present in the universal is inclusive predicability, not alternative application: predicability of many under one utterance and one intention, not merely under different possible uses. ‘Some individual or other’ cannot be predicated of many in the former sense, whereas ‘human’ can. This also explains why a figure seen at a distance is judged a true particular, although the intellect allows that it may be one among many things. Its actual referent is one personal individual; the alternatives occur in the observer's mind because that referent is unidentified. Calling an indefinite expression universal is figurative, considering its unrestricted range and treating it in that respect like a universal predicable of many. Alternatively, it is considered without its indefinite tanwīn; under that consideration it is indeed universal rather than particular, because it is assigned to the unrestricted universal nature. Understand this.

Second, a proper name can be a name of an individual or a name of a kind. Zayd and ʿAmr exemplify the first; Usāma for the lion, Thaʿāla for the fox and Umm ʿArīṭ for the scorpion exemplify the second. The author's definition is confined to the first class. Either names of kinds must be included among univocal or gradated terms, contrary to the established nomenclature, or they are included neither there nor among proper names, leaving an unclassified middle and defeating exhaustiveness.

One defence says that these are not proper names in logical usage, although they are proper names for grammarians. Logicians attend to meanings, and their meanings are universal. Grammarians attend to verbal rules: these expressions take the rules of proper names, including exclusion of the definite article, qualification by definite adjectives and an ensuing indefinite in the accusative as a circumstance. The two terminologies therefore differ because their considerations differ. Another answer says that names of kinds are assigned to a quiddity considered as one under the condition of mental unity; they therefore fall under proper names for logicians too. Reflect: this is a difficult point on which many have stumbled.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-073"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-073 — local note 73

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 209](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/209?lang=ar) · [Qum 210](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/210?lang=ar)

On ‘this universal meaning is predicated equally of those individuals’: an objection asks whether the equality required for univocal predication and the inequality required for gradated predication are considered objectively or merely in intellectual supposition. If objectively, hypothetical universals seem to be neither univocal nor gradated, since they have no actual individuals among which equality or inequality could obtain. If merely by intellectual supposition, whether or not that supposition agrees with reality, two established rules are disrupted.

First, the writers affirm that ‘human’ is univocal because its predication is equal across individuals, whereas ‘existence’ is gradated because its predication differs. If the criterion were arbitrary intellectual supposition, neither assertion could be made decisively. They should instead say that whatever the intellect supposes equal across its individuals is univocal, and whatever it supposes unequal is gradated, whether the concept is human, existence or anything else. Second, they hold that a gradated concept cannot be essential to the individuals beneath it, since an essential does not vary with different individuals. That argument would fail if gradation meant merely a difference supposed by the intellect: the intellect can suppose an essential to vary too, even though its supposition is false.

The answer can choose the objective interpretation. Hypothetical individuals do not prevent the equality or inequality from being objective. The claim means that, were the thing to possess realised individuals, its predication of them would objectively be equal or unequal. This does not depend on those individuals actually existing.

Thus the individuals considered in univocal and gradated predication may be external, as with human; mental, as with a supposed partner of God; or some external and some mental, as with necessary existent and sun. Retain this distinction.

The univocal is named mutawāṭiʾ because its individuals agree in its predication, tawāṭuʾ meaning agreement. The gradated is named mushakkik because its individuals agree in the underlying meaning while differing in one of the respects to be explained. Considering their agreement, an observer may take it for a univocal expression; considering their differences, he may take it for one expression independently assigned to several meanings. It therefore causes doubt: is it univocal or equivocal?


**Reading / scope note:** The cases involving hypothetical or mental individuals concern conceptual predication, not a claim that impossible things exist externally.


---


<a id="HWN-DALALA-074"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-074 — local note 74

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 210](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/210?lang=ar)

On ‘this concept is predicated of some …’: the first clause explains priority (awwaliyya), while the following alternative explains greater appropriateness (awlawiyya). Existence exemplifies both. Its obtaining in, and predication of, the Necessary precedes its obtaining in, and predication of, the contingent. It is also more complete, more established and stronger in the Necessary than in the contingent; its predication there is therefore more appropriate. Under the first consideration it exemplifies priority, and under the second greater appropriateness.

The two differences are distinct: something posterior may be stronger and more established than something prior. Existence in celestial motion and in generated bodies is the example. Its predication of the motion is prior to its predication of the bodies, yet it is weaker and less stable in the former than in the latter.


### Separately attributed unnumbered passage

**Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm, separately introduced Q210**

ʿAbd al-Raḥīm, separately introduced: qualifying the precedence as causal shows that essential precedence is intended. Mere temporal precedence, as among human individuals, does not count: it concerns the parts of time rather than how the concept itself obtains in its individuals. Causal precedence here means that this concept cannot be predicated of some individuals before first being predicated of certain others. Existence obtains in the Necessary before it obtains in the contingent in such a way that the latter obtaining is impossible without the former, because the Necessary is the principle of everything else. It is not required that the concept be stronger or more established in the prior individual. Existence in the generated bodies of our world is stronger than in the celestial motion essentially prior to them. Strength is required only for the other criterion [the searchable closing word repeats ‘priority’; the intended contrast appears to be ‘greater appropriateness’].


**Reading / scope note:** The two signed voices are separated. The second passage's final الأولية is retained as a reading query rather than silently certified as الأولوية.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-076"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-076 — local note 76

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 210](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/210?lang=ar)

<a id="HWN-DALALA-078"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-078 — local note 78

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 210](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/210?lang=ar) · [Qum 211](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/211?lang=ar)

“Primary assignment” means that the expression is assigned to this meaning independently at the outset, rather than first assigned to another and later transferred to the present meaning through common use. <a id="HWN-DALALA-083"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-083 — local note 83

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 212](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/212?lang=ar) · [Qum 213](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/213?lang=ar)

On ‘under the second alternative’: namely, the expression is not assigned to each of those meanings initially by a distinct assignment. Several cases are possible. It may have no assignment to any of them, primary or secondary; it may be assigned to all through one collective secondary assignment; to all through several secondary assignments; to all through one collective primary assignment rather than several assignments; or to some primarily and to others secondarily. Negating a composite condition may negate all its elements or only some.

The first case is impossible. We have no expression used in several meanings which has no primary or secondary assignment to any of them, since assignment here includes legally instituted assignment.

Of the remaining cases, the first is exemplified by ambiguous referential expressions according to the older grammarians: they are assigned to the particular referents for which they are used through one collective secondary assignment. You may object that those writers acknowledge an initial assignment to a universal quiddity; how can this exemplify secondary assignment to all the meanings? The answer is that ‘meaning’ here denotes what the expression is actually used for, not every meaning without restriction. Although these expressions are assigned to a universal quiddity on that account, they are never used for it. They are therefore figurative uses with no actual literal use.

The second surviving case is a transferred expression which different arts have transferred repeatedly to different meanings, with use of its original assigned meaning wholly abandoned. Its current meanings have several secondary assignments. The third is again exemplified by ambiguous referential expressions, but according to the later grammarians' account, already indicated in our earlier gloss. The fourth comprises literal and figurative uses, and transferred expressions whose use in the original meaning has not been wholly abandoned.

A word counts as transferred (*manqūl*) when its second use becomes sufficiently familiar to convey its meaning without a contextual indicator. <a id="HWN-DALALA-086"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-086 — local note 86

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 213](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/213?lang=ar) · [Qum 214](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/214?lang=ar)

Abandonment of the former use means that the word is no longer used for that meaning literally and without contextual indicators; it does not mean that the former use disappears altogether. Otherwise two objections arise. First, listing every transferred expression among expressions with several meanings would be inconsistent: if the new meaning is one and the old use wholly abandoned, it no longer has several meanings, since ‘meaning’ here concerns what the word is used for. Second, we plainly find transferred expressions still used for their earlier meanings. Ṣalāt, for example, is transferred in legal usage to prescribed ritual elements, yet is also used in that usage for its earlier meaning, supplication.

The answer is clear. Although ṣalāt is used for unrestricted supplication in legal discourse, it is not used for it literally and without an indicator. When uttered without indicators in that discourse, the second meaning—the prescribed ritual elements—is immediately understood. Relative to the original convention, the transferred expression is literal in the first meaning and figurative in the second; relative to the second convention, the reverse holds. Understand this.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-088"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-088 — local note 88

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 214](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/214?lang=ar)

A literal expression (ḥaqīqa) is an expression used for what it was assigned to signify, under that very consideration. ‘Used’ excludes an expression never employed for any meaning: technically it is neither literal nor figurative. ‘For what it was assigned’ excludes a figurative expression used for something to which it is assigned neither in the convention governing the conversation nor in another convention, such as ‘lion’ in ‘I saw a lion shooting’ or in the bathhouse example. Some say that it also excludes a mistaken use, such as saying ‘Take this horse’ while pointing to a book. That depends on taking use broadly enough to include incorrect use. If use means use conforming to linguistic convention—the principal and most familiar case—the condition ‘used’ already excludes the mistake.

The consideration-clause excludes a figurative use for something to which the expression was assigned in another convention, but not in the convention of the present conversation. For example, a speaker operating within grammatical terminology may use fiʿl for an event without further qualification. It is linguistically assigned to that meaning, so it is an expression used for an assigned meaning; but this use does not proceed under that assignment. Within the grammatical convention it proceeds from another meaning connected with it.

Originally, ḥaqīqa has the pattern faʿīl in an active sense, from a thing's becoming established, or in a passive sense, from establishing something. It was transferred to an expression fixed or established in its original place; its feminine ending marks the transfer to substantive usage on either derivation.

The author of the Miftāḥ says the ending can instead mark grammatical femininity on either derivation. This is straightforward on the active interpretation: faʿīl used actively agrees with masculine and feminine, whether its qualified noun is expressed or omitted—‘a graceful man,’ ‘a graceful woman,’ or ‘I saw a graceful one,’ with the appropriate masculine or feminine form. The Qurʾānic ramīm predicated of bones does not contradict this: according to the Kashshāf it is a substantive naming decayed bones, not an active adjective; alternatively, it is passive.

The passive derivation is less straightforward, because faʿīl used passively normally has one form for masculine and feminine, as with a wounded man or woman. One must suppose that, before its terminological transfer, ḥaqīqa qualified a feminine noun which was left unexpressed. A passive faʿīl used substantivally then distinguishes masculine and feminine to avoid ambiguity, as with ‘a wounded one’ or ‘a slain one.’ But this would apparently restrict literal expression to a simple word, since the omitted qualified noun is kalima, whereas it is commonly recognised that literal expressions may also be compound. One might claim that the Miftāḥ writer does restrict it, as suggested by his definition in terms of a word used for its assignment without reinterpretation. In any case, this is an unnecessary complication: the earlier account of the ending as marking substantive transfer suffices.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-DALALA-089"></a>
## HWN-DALALA-089 — local note 89

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 214](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/214?lang=ar) · [Qum 215](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/215?lang=ar)

A figurative expression (majāz) is an expression used outside the meaning assigned to it in the user's convention, with an indicator preventing that assigned meaning from being intended. The use-condition excludes expressions not used for any meaning, which are neither figurative nor literal. Use outside the assignment excludes literal use. Specifying the user's convention includes a use for a meaning assigned in some other convention but not the one governing the present use, as explained earlier. The blocking indicator excludes kināya: an indirect expression may be used beyond its assigned meaning while that assigned meaning remains possible.

Some add that the use must be correct, excluding a mistaken utterance such as ‘Take this horse’ while pointing to a book, which supplies an indicator against the literal meaning. That additional condition is needed only if ‘use’ is broad enough to include incorrect use. The author and glossator did not enumerate all the qualifications of literal and figurative expression because their aim here is division, giving an approximate indication of the definitions, not their full formal statement.

Majāz is a mīm-prefixed verbal noun taken actively, from passing beyond a place. It is transferred to an expression used outside its assignment because the expression passes beyond its original place, its assigned meaning. A passive interpretation is also possible: speakers carry the expression beyond its original place. The active interpretation is preferable, since the passive requires an understood ‘by means of it.’

Another derivation takes majāz as a path: one makes something a route to one's purpose, and the expression is a route to apprehending its meaning. The difficulty is that this loses the opposition to ḥaqīqa, so named because it stays fixed or established in its original place rather than passing beyond it. A different objection—that literal expressions would also have to be called majāz because they too are paths to understanding—is not decisive. A motive making a name suitable differs from a meaning required when a description is predicated. The descriptive condition must apply consistently; a naming motive need only explain why one label was preferred when assigned. It does not require every other thing sharing that motive to receive the same name.

Thus Ḥārith, used descriptively of someone who ploughs, ceases to be an appropriate description when the relevant ploughing ceases. Used as his proper name, it continues to apply even when the original naming motive has disappeared. Retain this distinction; it is useful in many later contexts.

Literal and figurative use in verbs and particles is ordinarily considered through their syntactic correlates and in dependence on them, as in ‘the situation spoke,’ or the Qurʾānic expression that Pharaoh's people took him up so that he became their enemy and sorrow. One investigator in legal theory adds that this concerns lexical material: grammatical form itself can also admit literal, figurative, equivocal and transferred uses—for example, a past form used to report or perform, a present form for present or future time, and a command for obligation or recommendation.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

# Concepts, four relations and five predicables

**H-MAFAHIM · printed pp216–252 · local notes1–153**


<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-001"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-001 — local note 1

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 216](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/216?lang=ar)

The distinction in question is due to the perspective under which the same item is considered, like the earlier difference between *ṣidq* and *ḥaqq*. It does not necessarily posit two numerically independent things.


**Reading / scope note:** Short programmatic distinction at the beginning of the new H-MAFAHIM section.


---


<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-002"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-002 — local note 2

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 216](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/216?lang=ar)

On the words ‘Know that what is understood from an expression …’: the apparent implication is that a concept (mafhūm) and a meaning (maʿnā) are identical in themselves. A meaning, according to the definition given, is the mental form considered insofar as an expression has been assigned to it. A concept would therefore also be a mental form. It would follow that universality and particularity are attributes of the form, although they are attributes of what the form represents. It would also follow that, in distinguishing universal from particular, what matters is whether conceiving the form prevents [its being predicated of many] or does not prevent it, whereas what matters is whether conceiving what it represents prevents this or does not.

This difficulty is not removed by the investigator al-Sharīf’s remark in his marginalia on the commentary on the Maṭāliʿ. After the commentator’s words ‘a concept is what occurs in the intellect,’ he says that ‘what occurs’ means what is of a kind to occur in the intellect, whether or not it actually occurs. For the thing of a kind to be present in the mind is the form, not what the form represents. Moreover, ‘what occurs’ means what actually occurs, since universality and particularity are mental attributes: what has not actually occurred in the mind is neither universal nor particular. Unless, that is, ‘universal’ is taken to mean what need not actually be universal but is of a kind to be universal, whether actually so or not; the same would apply to ‘particular.’

The difficulty can, however, be removed as follows. ‘Mental form’ is used both for a quality occurring in the intellect which serves as a mirror for apprehending what the form represents, and for the known quiddity distinguished in the mind by means of that form, considered with respect to its presence in the mind and its mental existence. It is the latter that is divided into a universal, whose predication of many can be supposed without impossibility, and a particular, whose predication of many cannot be so supposed.


**Reading / scope note:** Supersedes the Stage112 partial English, which remains in its immutable source file. This is full coverage of the digital numbered note, not a photographed witness. The digital wording ‘سواء حصل بالعقل أولا’ and the repeated potential/actual phrasing are retained in Arabic; the English reads the evident contrast ‘whether or not it occurs.’ The distinction is between a particular cognitive quality and the represented quiddity considered in mental existence; it does not establish that every school uses ‘mental form’ identically.

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-003"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-003 — local note 3

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 216](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/216?lang=ar)

The word *maʿnā* can be derived as a noun from the verb “to intend,” or as a lightened passive-participial form meaning what is intended. The first derivation is preferred because it avoids assuming several sound changes and deletions required by the second.


**Reading / scope note:** Traditional morphological derivation, not independent comparative etymology.


---


<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-004"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-004 — local note 4

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 216](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/216?lang=ar) · [Qum 217](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/217?lang=ar) · [Qum 218](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/218?lang=ar)

On ‘supposition here means the intellect's allowing’: this answers the objection that we do not grant the impossibility of supposing a particular to be predicable of many. Why could one not suppose Zayd to apply to numerous individuals? That seems no stranger than supposing a human with several heads or none. If supposition is included in the division, as the author includes it, a thing seems to become a division opposed to itself, since every particular could supposedly apply to many. If supposition is omitted, the particular's definition includes too much and the universal's too little, because universals without realised instances—such as a supposed partner of God or the phoenix—cannot actually be predicated of anything.

The answer is that ‘supposition’ does not mean merely making an assumption. It means the intellect's allowing and accepting the possibility under consideration. More will be said about this.

Two familiar discussions arise. First, the universal's definition appears not to exclude everything foreign to it, and the particular's not to include every particular. A figure seen at a distance might be identified as one among many things; would it therefore be universal, although it is a true particular? Also, the concept of each particular agrees with representations of that thing in many people's minds and could be supposed predicable of them; would it therefore be universal?

The first difficulty is answered by the earlier distinction: the predicability used in these definitions is inclusive, not alternative. The distant figure's possible identification with many candidates is alternative; its actual referent is a single individual. An indefinite expression intended for some individual or other is likewise particular, despite its unrestricted range. Calling it universal is figurative. The second difficulty is answered by distinguishing original existence from derivative representational existence. The individual thing's presence in several minds belongs to the latter. The same distinction answers the objection that an abstracted image of a particular would place one real particular in several subjects. What is impossible is one particular's original existence in several subjects; derivative representation resolves into several distinct individual occurrences. Reflect.

The second discussion reverses the charge: the particular's definition appears too broad and the universal's too narrow. Suppose a universal applied to two, three, four or five individuals, but not beyond five. Would it count as particular because ‘many’ is alleged to begin at six? This objection derives six from the grammatical claim that a plural comprises at least three units and that the least thing called ‘many’ is two. A further objection says that kathīrīn is a masculine rational plural, so a universal applying to nonrational things would satisfy the particular's definition rather than the universal's. ‘Multiplicity’ would therefore be preferable to ‘many individuals,’ as the author himself uses it in the five predicables.

The first answer denies a universal whose applicability cannot reach six or more: every universal has indefinitely many individuals, at least mentally, and the definition's predicability embraces external and mental instances. The second answer notes that a masculine rational plural, though assigned primarily to rational beings, can also be used more broadly or specifically of nonrational things. Another reply to both objections says that writers on intelligible matters attend to the conveyed concepts rather than the niceties of grammatical convention. One should not be astonished to find their illustrative expressions disregarding an ordinary agreement rule.

The particular and universal are named through their relation to part and whole. Ordinarily a particular is a whole containing a universal as a constituent: Zayd comprises humanity and external individuation; human comprises animal and rational; animal comprises the growing body, and so forth through body and substance. Part and whole are relative notions. The ‘particular’ is the whole considered in relation to its part; the ‘universal’ is the part considered in relation to its whole. ‘Ordinarily’ excludes the property and common accident, which lie outside the quiddity of their individuals and are not constituents. Genus and differentia, by contrast, constitute the species, and the species enters the individual. — Muḥammad ʿAlī.

A separately introduced explanation by ʿAbd al-Raḥīm states the problem briefly. One might suppose Zayd himself to apply to many and thus satisfy the universal's definition. But farḍ has two senses: assumption, as conveyed by conditional expressions, and intellectual admissibility. The latter is intended: understanding the concept does not prevent the intellect from allowing it to be affirmatively predicated of many. An individual's individuation cannot simply be disregarded while retaining that very individual; disregarding it removes the individuality in question. Things genuinely distinct from an object may be left out of consideration without that result. As for the distant figure which might be Zayd, ʿAmr or Bakr, its possible identifications are alternative, whereas the universal is predicable of many together.


**Reading / scope note:** The last separately attributed passage contains a compressed or defective ‘لا يقال’ transition in the digital text. The English preserves its intelligible distinction without claiming to restore the omitted objection. The purported grammatical minimum of ‘many’ is a reported objection, not an endorsed arithmetic or linguistic rule.

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-005"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-005 — local note 5

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 218](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/218?lang=ar) · [Qum 219](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/219?lang=ar)

On ‘a partner of the Creator’: this is a universal with several mentally conceived instances, although external instances are impossible.

You may object that supposition has just been explained as the intellect's allowing and accepting, whereas the intellect does not allow a partner of God to exist, much less several. This would instead be one of the merely hypothetical universals without instances in reality itself, mentally or externally. Dividing the universal into impossible and possible would then divide a thing into itself and something foreign to it.

The reply denies that the intellect cannot provisionally allow such existence or multiplicity. Otherwise many rational people, held responsible for fundamental beliefs and practical obligations, would never have adopted it. Intellectual allowance here does not mean the conclusion of correct reasoning, but what the intellect initially admits before that reasoning. Under this first, unexamined consideration—called the foolish first view—it can admit things whose external existence is impossible.

What, then, of hypothetical universals such as ‘not-possible in the general sense,’ ‘non-thing,’ ‘nonexistent’ and ‘what is absent’? Are they included in the division? One answer excludes them: the rules need be general only according to the purposes of this art, and its practitioners have no purpose in hypothetical universals without external instances. A second answer includes them.

The objection to inclusion is that they cannot be supposed predicable of many, since nothing can satisfy such descriptions without a coincidence of contradictories. The reply extends predicability to both what obtains in reality itself and what obtains under intellectual supposition. But would that not also make Zayd universal, since one could suppose him predicable of several people just as one supposes ‘non-thing’ predicable of things? The author distinguishes supposing an impossible situation from a supposition which is itself impossible. Supposing what is impossible is not itself necessarily impossible, whereas an impossibility remains impossible. Reflect: the distinction is subtle.


**Reading / scope note:** The digital closing sentence prints ‘فرض ممتنع’ for both contrasted cases, leaving the intended syntactic distinction unmarked. The following explicit maxim supports the distinction rendered, but the precise wording needs a printed-source check. The two proposed treatments of empty hypothetical universals are not collapsed into one answer.


---


<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-006"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-006 — local note 6

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 219](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/219?lang=ar)

On ‘that is, it is not impossible’: this can mean special possibility, the removal of necessity from both sides, or general possibility, the removal of necessity from the opposite side.

Four notions are in view: general possibility, special possibility, necessary existence and impossibility. The latter three can fall under the first when the side from which necessity is removed is allowed to vary. General possibility removes necessity from one side while leaving the other unconsidered: either from a thing's existence without deciding about its nonexistence, or from its nonexistence without deciding about its existence. If necessity is removed from existence, nonexistence may be necessary, giving the impossible, or not necessary, giving the specially possible. If necessity is removed from nonexistence, existence may be necessary, giving necessary existence, or not necessary, again giving special possibility.

An objection to ‘or its instances are possible’ says: if general possibility is intended, it cannot be opposed to ‘or they are impossible,’ because impossibility is itself one case of general possibility. A species cannot be a coordinate alternative to its genus. If special possibility is intended, the subsequent division cannot include necessary existence among its cases.

The answer is that general possibility is intended, but the objection confuses its two directions. Impossibility falls under general possibility which removes necessity from existence. The possibility intended here instead removes necessity from nonexistence; impossibility is not one of its cases. — Mullā ʿAlī Akbar al-Ahrī.


**Reading / scope note:** The direction from which necessity is removed is essential. The passage does not claim that one fixed affirmative possibility operator simultaneously includes both the necessary and the impossible.

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-007"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-007 — local note 7

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 220](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/220?lang=ar)

The intellect does not reject an instance's appearing in external reality. Under that preliminary condition, either one instance must exist while the rest cannot, or instances may remain possible whether or not actually present. The writer suggests it would be clearer to divide the cases explicitly into universally impossible, one necessary instance, and the different possible patterns, rather than relying on an ambiguous “or they are possible.”


**Reading / scope note:** Clarifies the classification of universal concepts by possible instance numbers.

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-009"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-009 — local note 9

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 220](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/220?lang=ar)

On ‘or another instance is impossible, as with the concept of necessary existent’: the earlier explanation of intellectual allowance answers the objection that necessary existent must be particular because the intellect forbids its application to many. Correct reasoning does not permit more than one instance, but the initial unexamined consideration can admit multiplicity. Otherwise people would not have adopted associationism, refutation would not require proof, and the theological purpose of sending messengers to correct it would not arise in the manner described.

A further objection says that necessary existent cannot be included among universals with possible instances, because only one instance is possible, not several. The possibility and impossibility in ‘its instances are impossible or possible’ must concern external reality; every universal must already allow mental instances if it is to be opposed to the particular.

The answer distinguishes two senses of intellectual impossibility: impossibility both under sound reflection and under the initial consideration, and impossibility under sound reflection alone. In the division, the author intends the first sense of impossibility and the possibility opposed to it. That possibility can therefore include what is impossible under the second sense. Negating a composite condition may remove one constituent rather than all. Necessary existent falls among universals with possible instances in this qualified sense. Reflect.

Another answer takes the plural ‘instances’ generically for the kind ‘instance,’ which can cover one or many. That is straightforward for a plural made definite by the article, the glossator observes, but less straightforward for the genitively determined plural used here. A further answer treats ‘its instances are impossible’ as a universal affirmative, because the genitive construction is exhaustive where no particular antecedent is intended. ‘Or they are possible’ then negates that universal affirmation. Negating a universal affirmative can yield a particular negative rather than a universal negative. Understand the scope distinction.


**Reading / scope note:** The source distinguishes preliminary conceptual allowance from demonstrated metaphysical possibility. It does not assert multiple necessary existents. Rival grammatical and quantifier-scope answers remain distinct.

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-012"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-012 — local note 12

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 221](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/221?lang=ar)

On ‘that is, any two universals’: the definite article in ‘the two universals’ is exhaustive and therefore embraces all universals. There is a difficulty: the discussion concerns only universals having an instance in external reality, as we shall indicate.

The four relations were considered between two universals, rather than between two concepts, because two concepts may both be universal, both particular, or one universal and the other particular. Had the author said ‘the two concepts,’ one might suppose that every kind of relation occurs within each of these three classes. That is not so. All four occur between universals in the sense that there are two particular universals between which disjointness obtains, two others between which equality obtains, and so forth.

Between two particulars, on this explanation, only disjointness occurs. Between a particular and a universal, only disjointness or unrestricted inclusion occurs: if the particular is an instance of this universal, it is absolutely narrower than it; if it is not an instance, it is disjoint. By saying ‘the two universals,’ the author indicates that the other two classes are not in the same position. This is what can be gathered from some writers. The truth, however, is that the restriction indicates that the principal purpose is to learn the relations of universals to one another.

As for the assertion that only disjointness occurs between two particulars: if the disjointness concerns their joint predicability, as it properly should, we do not grant that they are disjoint in this technical sense. How could we? Disjointness, as the glossator will state, resolves into two universal negatives; but the two negatives formed from particulars are singular propositions. Apply the same consideration to a universal and a particular. If, instead, ‘disjointness’ is broad enough to concern either joint predicability or the existing things themselves, we do not grant that particulars can only be disjoint. Under that interpretation, the four relations can occur between them, and between a universal and a particular.


**Reading / scope note:** The note first reports a rationale and then rejects part of it; the English retains both voices. ‘Particular universals’ here means two specifically selected universal concepts, not concepts simultaneously universal and logically particular. The treatment of particulars is source-specific, not a modern set-theoretic claim.


---


<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-013"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-013 — local note 13

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 221](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/221?lang=ar) · [Qum 222](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/222?lang=ar)

On ‘one of the four relations must obtain between them’: this points to an answer to an objection. Someone says that partial disjointness is a kind of relation in general, yet falls under none of the four divisions; the division is therefore not exhaustive. The answer is that the particular relation actually obtaining between two universals can only be one of the four. Partial disjointness, considered merely as such, does not obtain between two concepts without further determination; when specifically determined, it is not a fifth relation set over against the four. Perhaps this is what is meant by the answer that the purpose is to exhaust the species of relation, excluding partial disjointness because it is a genus of total disjointness and overlap. Calling these a species and a genus is nevertheless somewhat strained. Whether partial disjointness is essential to both, and whether their distinction rests on specific differentiae rather than accidents—as in subdivisions of a species—requires consideration.

A difficulty remains. The claim that every two universals must bear one of the four relations is not beyond weakness. ‘Non-thing’ and ‘not-possible in the general sense of possibility’ are two universal concepts, yet none of the four relations obtains between them. They are not totally disjoint: as will be explained, the contradictories of two disjoint terms must be partially disjoint, whereas ‘thing’ and ‘possible’ are certainly equal in extension. Nor are the former two equal in extension, since neither is predicable of anything at all, so that they cannot be jointly predicated. Nor do they stand in unrestricted inclusion or overlap. As will be explained, the positive broader term must be predicable together with the contradictory of the narrower; neither of these two can be predicated together with the other's contradictory, or two contradictories would coincide.

One possible answer restricts the claim: every two universals, each of which is predicable of something in reality itself, must bear one of the four relations. This would not contradict the requirement that the art's rules be general and comprehensive. Their generality is required according to the purposes pursued in the art, and its practitioners have no purpose in merely supposed universals without any instances in reality itself, either externally or mentally. But that answer conflicts with the unrestricted rule that ‘the contradictories of equal terms are equal,’ as will be discussed. ‘Thing’ and ‘possible’ are equal in extension, while their contradictories, ‘non-thing’ and ‘not-possible,’ are not equal according to the account just given.

The preferable answer therefore extends the predicability used in defining the four relations to both real and hypothetical predicability. There is necessarily hypothetical universal predicability in both directions between ‘non-thing’ and ‘not-possible’: whatever is supposed to have ‘non-thing’ predicated of it also has ‘not-possible’ predicated of it, and conversely.

Observe also that the four relations obtain not only among simple terms and expressions treated like them, such as restrictive compounds, but among propositions. In simple terms they are considered with respect to ṣidq in the sense of predication of something, as will shortly be explained. In propositions ṣidq means obtaining in reality and in reality itself, that is, agreement with it. In the predicative sense ṣidq takes ʿalā: ‘animal is predicable of human,’ meaning that it is attributed to it. In the sense of obtaining and existing it takes fī: ‘this proposition is true in reality and in reality itself.’

Predicability of something is not conceivable of propositions as such: ‘Zayd is striking,’ considered just as that proposition, is predicated neither of a simple term nor of a proposition. Conversely, truth in the sense of obtaining—that is, agreement with reality itself—is not conceivable of simple terms or what is treated like them. This is evident for simple terms; for expressions treated like them, the explanation will come in the definition of a proposition, God willing. Since the purpose here concerns ṣidq as predication, rather than every sense of ṣidq, the relations have been restricted to universals. There is thus no difficulty.


**Reading / scope note:** The Q221→222 seam is joined at ‘لا تكون / مقابلة’. This note preserves the rejection of the first proposed restriction and the author's preferred extension to hypothetical predicability. Do not substitute modern vacuous universal truth for the author's explicit account without argument. ‘Partial disjointness’ is his broader condition, not automatically the modern relation ‘overlap’.

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-017"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-017 — local note 17

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 223](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/223?lang=ar)

If you object, ‘Sleeping and waking are equal in extension, yet neither is universally predicable of the other,’ I reply: what is required for two equal terms is that each be predicable of every individual of the other. It does not follow that both must be predicated together at one time. Waking and sleeping are each universally predicable of the other, but not at the same time; that does not prevent their being equal in extension.

Some instead say that the equality is between ‘sleeping at some time’ and ‘waking at some time.’ Of someone asleep, even while sleeping, it is true that he is awake at some time, although not that he is awake while sleeping. Likewise, of someone awake, even while awake, it is true that he sleeps at some time. On this account, each equal term is predicable of every individual of the other at the time when the other is predicated of that individual. Apply the same analysis to the predicability required in unrestricted inclusion and in overlap.


**Reading / scope note:** Two temporal analyses are preserved. The English ‘at some time’ renders the contextual force of ‘في الجملة’; it is not a claim that every possible organism must sleep. No independent historical modal proof is certified here.

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-018"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-018 — local note 18

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 223](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/223?lang=ar)

Marjiʿ, with kasra on the jīm, is here a mīm-prefixed verbal noun, not a noun of place; otherwise it could not govern the complement introduced by ilā (‘to’).

You may object that the author's commentary on the Talkhīṣ apparently takes marjiʿ as a noun of place which nevertheless admits ilā. Explaining the text's words ‘eloquence resolves into avoiding [error],’ he says: ‘It is what must obtain for eloquence to be able to obtain, just as one says that truth and falsehood resolve into the judgment's agreement or disagreement with reality: that through which the two are realised and attained.’ I reply: a noun of place undoubtedly cannot govern such a complement, because it is a purely nonverbal noun without the capacity to govern.

The author's wording may instead employ istikhdām, a shift in the sense resumed by a pronoun, as some investigators have explained. Marjiʿ has two meanings: returning, and the place of return. The first occurrence intends the first meaning, while its pronoun resumes the second. The cited explanation explains that second meaning and thereby clarifies the first.


**Reading / scope note:** The digital string ‘والألم’ is preserved in Arabic and read contextually as ‘وإلا لم’ in translation. This is a flagged reading, not an unrecorded manuscript emendation. The reported grammatical rule is the glossator's position.

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-019"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-019 — local note 19

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 223](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/223?lang=ar)

On ‘disjointness resolves into two negatives’: marjiʿ, with kasra on the jīm, is a mīm-prefixed verbal noun meaning returning, not a noun of place meaning the place of return. Its governing ilā is evidence of that. The mīm-prefixed verbal noun generally takes the pattern mafʿal, with fatḥa on its middle radical, in every conjugational class, apart from irregular forms such as marjiʿ, maghfira, mafāza, maʿdhira and maʿṣiya.

Know that the glossator's account of what the four relations resolve into concerns quantity and quality. As regards modality, disjointness resolves into two universal perpetual negatives: disjointness between universals consists in their never being jointly predicated, whether such joint predication is possible or not. Equality resolves into two universal general-absolute affirmatives, because equality between universals consists in their actual joint predicability, whether that predicability is necessary or not. Unrestricted inclusion resolves into one universal general-absolute affirmative and one particular perpetual negative. Overlap resolves into one particular general-absolute affirmative and two particular perpetual negatives.

Thus the affirmatives are absolute, and the negatives perpetual.


**Reading / scope note:** The source's modal qualifiers are translated explicitly. ‘General absolute’ and ‘perpetual’ are technical traditional modalities, not interchangeable with unqualified modern categorical propositions. This record translates the classification; it does not certify the 46 unrelated modal theorem cases.
