<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-022"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-022 — local note 22

**Inherited first pass** · [Qum 224](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/224?lang=ar)

On ‘that is, everything of which one of the contradictories is predicated’: the point is that once equality between, for example, human and rational has been established, equality must also obtain between their contradictories, non-human and non-rational. Thus every non-human must be non-rational, and every non-rational thing non-human. Were these not true, their contradictories would be true: some non-human is not non-rational, and some non-rational thing is not non-human. It would then be true that some non-human is rational and some non-rational thing is human, because both contradictories cannot be absent. One positive term would therefore be predicable without the other, since contradictories cannot coincide. That contradicts the assumption.

An objection is raised: the truth of ‘Some non-human is not non-rational’ and ‘Some non-rational thing is not non-human’ does not entail the truth of ‘Some non-human is rational’ and ‘Some non-rational thing is human.’ As will be explained, a negative proposition with a negative predicate does not entail the corresponding affirmative proposition with a positive predicate. Do you not see that ‘Zayd is not a non-writer’ does not require ‘Zayd is a writer’ to be true? Zayd might be nonexistent, in which case he is neither a writer nor a non-writer.

Do not reply that the subject here exists, since non-human and non-rational apply to realised existents such as trees and stones, and that the negative with negative predicate and the positive affirmative are mutually entailing when the subject exists.

We answer that the discussion is not specifically about non-human and non-rational and similar cases. It concerns the contradictories of equal terms without restriction. What of ‘thing’ and ‘possible in the general sense’? They are equal through being predicable of all concepts, while their contradictories—‘non-thing’ and ‘not-possible’—are predicable of nothing at all, as explained earlier. The proof then certainly fails. If you say, ‘Were “Every non-thing is not-possible” not true, “Some non-thing is not not-possible” would be true, and hence “Some non-thing is possible”,’ the stated denial applies: the subject is certainly not existent.

One answer restricts the discussion to cases where the two equal terms do not embrace all things, mentally and externally. Their contradictories must then apply to something existent, externally or mentally, completing the proof and blocking the objection. As explained earlier, general rules need be general only according to the intended aims and purposes of the art.

But this restriction is needed only on the earlier assumption that predicability is confined to real predicability. On our preferred extension to real and hypothetical predicability it is unnecessary: the objection does not arise and therefore needs no answer. The assertion that a negative proposition with a negative predicate is broader than the positive affirmative holds when predicability and existence are confined to real predicability and existence. Once both are extended to the real and the hypothetical, apparently no difference remains between the two. Reflect.


**Reading / scope note:** The text's transition from failure of the two universals to the two respective particular negatives is reproduced as stated; its exact dialectical quantification is not silently repaired. ‘Negative predicate’ here renders maʿdūl al-maḥmūl and must be distinguished from a negative copula. The existential-import objection is essential; ordinary modern double-negation simplification would obscure it. Hypothetical existence is the author's proposed repair, not an independent modern proof.

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-042"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-042 — local note 42

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 226](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/226?lang=ar)

On ‘that is, just as between the contradictories of the broader …’: this removes a possible difficulty. A comparison apparently requires its point of resemblance already to be known in the object with which something is compared, as in ‘Zayd is like a lion.’ Here it is not known: it has not previously been established whether the contradictories of two disjoint terms are partially disjoint. How, then, can the contradictories of overlapping terms be compared with them?

The answer is that, as the rhetoricians explain, a comparison's purpose may concern either the thing compared or the thing with which it is compared. The stated requirement applies only to the first kind; the present example belongs to the second. Here the relevant characteristic need not previously be known in the comparison's second term. It resembles the verse, ‘Dawn appeared, its bright brow like the caliph's face when he is praised.’ Dawn's brightness and radiance are compared with the caliph's face, although that characteristic had not previously been established of his face. This is called an inverted comparison: what is really being compared in the verse is the caliph's face, and here it is the contradictories of disjoint terms. The comparison has been reversed to suggest that their possession of the characteristic is greater. Reflect. —Muḥammad ʿAlī


**Reading / scope note:** The opening word of the verse is uncertain in the digital source; the translation conveys the comparison without treating that reading as an established emendation.

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-046"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-046 — local note 46

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 227](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/227?lang=ar)

‘This’ may be the predicate of a suppressed subject, giving ‘the matter is this,’ or a subject with a suppressed predicate, giving ‘this is as stated.’ Alternatively hā may be an imperative verbal noun meaning ‘take,’ with dhā as its object. Or hā may be an attention particle, with an imperative understood: ‘take,’ according to the usual explanation, or ‘know,’ as suggested by the subsequent ‘and know also.’

This is an abrupt transition approaching a skilful transition, like the Qurʾānic words following the description of the people of Paradise: ‘This; and for the transgressors there is an evil return.’ The author reports Ibn al-Athīr as saying that ‘this’ in such a position effects a separation better than a conjunction: it forms a strong connection when leaving one discourse for another. He then calls it a division of discourse better than a smooth transition.

It follows that the claim in some marginalia that ‘this’ is the grammatical subject of ‘is correct’ is inappropriate. It prefers what is unpalatable when something agreeable is available; moreover there is no reason to employ an overt demonstrative when a pronoun would suffice. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 227](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/227?lang=ar) · [Qum 228](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/228?lang=ar)

On ‘the first is the intention of brevity …’: had he explained the contradictories immediately after the positive terms, the greatest possible brevity would have been to say, after ‘if the two universals are wholly separate they are disjoint,’ ‘and their contradictories are partially disjoint’; and then here, after ‘otherwise they overlap,’ ‘and their contradictories are like those of disjoint terms.’ Compare that with the book's actual wording.

You may object: once postponement is chosen, it would be better and shorter to say, ‘Between their contradictories and those of disjoint terms there is partial disjointness,’ avoiding the suggestion of a comparison with something unknown. I reply: coordinating with a pronoun governed by a preposition without repeating that preposition is permitted by some grammarians but not by the majority. The latter also appears to be the author's position in some of his investigations. Reflect.

The author repeats ‘their contradictories’ in all the other cases, and doing so here would avoid the suspicion of comparing with a case whose rule has not yet been explained. <a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-050"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-050 — local note 50

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 228](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/228?lang=ar)

On ‘insofar as it is abstracted from the specificity of its two instances’: this qualification is needed because, insofar as partial disjointness exists within one of its two kinds, its conception requires only that particular kind.

You may object: a general notion considered as general does not require conceiving any of its instances, still less all of them. Conceiving animal as animal does not require conceiving human, horse or another animal. Likewise partial disjointness, abstracted from its two particular kinds, should not require conceiving either, still less both.

I reply: what is intended is not partial disjointness considered simply in itself, but considered as existing—not within a specified kind, but within an unspecified one. Considered thus, conceiving it does depend upon conceiving the two kinds.

Why did they consider it in this respect rather than simply in itself? Because, as indicated at the beginning, the purpose here is to explain the relations actually obtaining between universals. That is why they restricted them to four, although partial disjointness differs conceptually from those four. When they say that the contradictories of overlapping or disjoint terms are partially disjoint, they mean partial disjointness as realised, without specifying the kind in which it is realised, not merely partial disjointness in itself.

This also exposes the weakness of the objection that the fourfold classification is defective because partial disjointness is conceptually different from the four. The aim is not relations merely in themselves, but relations as realised. Under that consideration partial disjointness is nothing other than overlap or total disjointness, as the glossator has explained. —Muḥammad ʿAlī

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-053"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-053 — local note 53

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 228](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/228?lang=ar) · [Qum 229](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/229?lang=ar)

This answers a possible objection: the externally existing instance of the concept ‘necessary existent’ does not have a universal quiddity under which it falls, although it is a real particular. It would therefore be incorrect to say that every real particular falls under a general concept. The usual answer is to deny that it lacks every such concept: concept, thing and entity are universal concepts, and it falls under each.

That answer, however, rests on looseness of expression. Otherwise God—blessed and exalted—does not fall under any universal quiddity in which another thing shares. Were He to do so, He would be composed of what is shared and what distinguishes Him; He would depend on each component and on another agent composing them, and would thus be originated, as established in theology. Exalted is He far above what the wrongdoers say.

You may object: it is necessarily known in religion that ‘existent,’ for example, is applied to the eternal God and also to other existents. We answer that this is verbal, not conceptual, community of meaning. The existence belonging to Him differs from that belonging to other created things. The same applies to ‘thing,’ ‘entity,’ ‘concept’ and similar expressions, as sincere reflection reveals; otherwise the previous unacceptable consequence would follow.

Although this is not the place for that discussion, we have indicated it briefly lest a beginner adopt the other account as his doctrine and thereby go astray and mislead others. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī


**Reading / scope note:** This is the glossator's theological rejection of shared conceptual predication, not an editorial assertion that all philosophical or theological schools agree.

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-056"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-056 — local note 56

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 229](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/229?lang=ar) · [Qum 230](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/230?lang=ar)

An investigating glossator says: the preceding explanation assumes that the author's pronoun ‘it’ refers to the particular, as is apparent; the present discussion assumes that it refers to ‘the narrower.’ The latter interpretation is remote. The author did not intend to define or explain the relative particular. Were he doing so, he would be defining it by itself if ‘narrower’ meant simply ‘the specific,’ without comparative force. If it retained comparative force, he would define it through something whose conception depends on its conception, since conceiving ‘narrower’ depends on conceiving ‘specific,’ which is the relative particular itself. He intended only to identify what the expression ‘particular’ is applied to; hence the glossator says, ‘The word particular, just as it is applied ….’ No objection arises that needs an answer. The pronoun should therefore refer to the relative particular. End of that glossator's words; may his station be elevated.

I say that al-Sharīf also gives this argument in his marginalia on the commentary on the Risāla in a corresponding case. It shows only that the relative particular cannot be given a real definition through ‘the narrower,’ as both discussions apparently suppose. A real definition must yield the quiddity of the defined thing through the defining quiddities, as in defining human through rational animal. Here the quiddity of ‘narrower’ does not yield that of ‘relative particular’: they are one and the same kind of thing.

Animal and rational, by contrast, differ from human, which is composed of them. Considered individually they are clearer and better known than human as such, and thus yield it. Human as composed of their two quiddities was unknown, while each quiddity separately was known. Conceiving them and their composition therefore yields the human quiddity that had not previously been apprehended.

The argument does not show that a verbal explanation through ‘narrower’ is impossible. If the concepts of relative particular and narrower were identical, such an objection might also be made to verbal explanation; but they are not. At most they have the same external instances, and that is required of a definiens and definiendum. The case is like explaining ghaḍanfar as ‘lion.’ Nothing shows that the present interpretation depends on ‘narrower’ being a real definition of relative particular; it rather appears to be a verbal explanation. Nevertheless, just as a broader term cannot receive a real definition through a narrower one, it cannot receive a verbal definition through it either. —Muḥammad ʿAlī

## HWN-MAFAHIM-060 — local note 60

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 230](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/230?lang=ar)

On ‘from it one learns that the particular …’: from the fact that the narrower term meant here is broader than the narrower term discussed earlier, one learns that relative particular is broader than real particular. The narrower term here may be universal or a real particular; it explains ‘relative particular.’ Since the breadth of the explanation entails the breadth of what is explained, one learns that a relative particular may be universal or a real particular. This is the sense in which the relation between the two particulars is learned by implication.

This works if it is a real definition. If it is a verbal explanation, as intended, there is a difficulty: a verbal explanation may be broader, so the breadth of the explaining term does not entail the breadth of the term explained. The desired conclusion is therefore not established. Understand. —ʿAbd al-Raḥīm

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-061"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-061 — local note 61

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 230](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/230?lang=ar) · [Qum 231](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/231?lang=ar)

For a thing to be so ‘in reality itself’ means that it is so according to itself: amr here means the thing. Its existence does not rest on someone's supposition or consideration; it obtains in itself. The connection between sunrise and the existence of daylight, for example, obtains in itself whether or not anyone supposes it, or any supposer exists at all. Reality itself is absolutely broader than external reality: everything externally existent exists in reality itself, but not conversely. It overlaps with the mental, since falsehoods can be considered and believed—for example, that five is even. Such a proposition exists in the mind but not in reality itself. Cases of this kind are called genuinely mental. —ʿAbd al-Raḥīm

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-063"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-063 — local note 63

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 231](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/231?lang=ar)

Examples are ‘non-thing’ and ‘not-possible in the general sense of possibility.’ Both are universal concepts, yet neither can really be predicated of an external or mental thing. Whatever is supposed externally or mentally is a thing and is possible; their contradictories therefore cannot be predicated of a concept among concepts. No significant purpose is served by investigating merely hypothetical universals, and they fall outside our inquiry.

The fivefold division is consequently not refuted by definitions and descriptions of nonexistent things. Someone raised such an objection: predicating something of a thing presupposes the existence of the subject; if the subject does not exist, how can one claim that this predicate is essential or accidental to it? We answer that, although universals are all produced through intellectual consideration and abstraction from individuals, intellectual constructions are of two kinds. In one, that from which the concept is abstracted has a basis and reality; in the other, it is sheer invention. A universal is accordingly either abstracted or invented. Essential and accidental are considered in the first kind, not the second.

The writers restricted the discussion of the predicables to simple meanings for the reader's convenience. The five can also be considered in compound meanings; every concept, simple or compound, falls under one of the five. —ʿAbd al-Raḥīm


**Reading / scope note:** The digital source's ‘definitions of the enumerated things’ appears to intend nonexistent things in the ensuing argument; the reading should be checked against print.

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-064"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-064 — local note 64

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 231](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/231?lang=ar)

On ‘the universal, when related …’: an objection is that some universals fall under none of the divisions—for example, thing and existent. They are not species, since every thing and existent has something additional to mere thinghood and existence. They are not genera, since they are not parts of the realities: otherwise what has been designated a highest genus would not truly be highest. Nor are they differentiae, since they are not parts of the quiddities; even if they were, they would constitute the entirety of what is shared. Finally they are not properties or common accidents, since these are accidents, and thing and existent cannot be accidents. Their subject would be either thing and existent, making something accrue to itself, or non-thing and non-existent, making contradictories coincide.

The answer chooses the first alternative without accepting the consequence. Thinghood accrues to what becomes a thing through that attribution, and existence is treated similarly. Thus the alleged self-attribution does not follow. Reflect. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-065"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-065 — local note 65

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 231](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/231?lang=ar) · [Qum 232](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/232?lang=ar)

On ‘if it is the entirety of what is shared’: what is meant is the entirety of what the items share. The article is generic, so the definition covers both a plurality of shared constituents and a single shared constituent. Animal, a composite genus, is the sum of what human and horse share: every shared constituent is part of it. Substance, a simple genus, is the entirety of what intellect and human share: there is no shared constituent other than it.

Some explain the phrase only in the first sense, as ‘all the shared parts,’ giving animal as the totality of substance, body, growth, sensation and voluntary movement shared by human and horse. Their definition then fails to include simple genera.

You may object that the account excludes remote genera, which are only parts of what is shared. Growing body is not the whole shared by human and horse—animal is—and body without qualification is only a part of what they share, or of what they and a tree share. These remote genera would then fall under ‘otherwise it is a differentia.’

I reply that growing body, although not the entirety shared by human and horse, is the entirety shared by human and tree. Likewise body, although not the entirety shared by human and horse or by those and a tree, is the entirety shared by one of them and a stone. Apply the same reasoning elsewhere. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī

A separately introduced explanation by Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm follows: ‘The entirety of what is shared’ means a shared constituent beyond which there is no further shared constituent outside it. Everything shared is either that constituent itself or a part of it. Animal is the whole shared by human and horse: every shared constituent is either animal itself or something within it, such as substance, growing body, sensation or voluntary movement. Although each is shared by human and horse, none individually is the whole shared; animal embraces them all.

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-066"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-066 — local note 66

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 232](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/232?lang=ar) · [Qum 233](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/233?lang=ar)

On ‘these three are called essentials’: the usual and more frequent use of ‘essential’ is for what is internal to a quiddity. It is also sometimes used for what is not external to it. In the first usage species cannot be called essential, because it is the entire quiddity and a thing is not inside itself. In the second usage it can, since species is not external to the quiddity: a thing is neither inside nor outside itself.

A difficulty remains. Species is the essence itself; an essence is not related to itself as its own attribute, since relation requires difference. How can the adjective ‘essential’ apply to it? One answer is that this is a logical convention, and transferred technical terms need no etymological appropriateness. Even if appropriateness were required, it would suffice for it to hold in some instances.

An investigating glossator answers that ‘essence’ can mean either the reality or the individuals of which that reality is predicated. Perhaps the latter is intended: the reality can be related to its instances, just as its two constituents can be related to it. I say that, even if accepted, this separates the senses of ‘essential’ among the three essentials, which is unattractive—unless the same account is applied to all three. A similar difficulty attends making the adjectival suffix merely intensive, as in the cited poetic adjective lahdhamiyyāt. Reflect.

Avicenna is reported to have given this answer in the Ishārāt: the quiddity is not essential to itself but to numerically multiple persons. He then rejects it. If the quiddity is essential to each person, the relation is either to the person's quiddity as such, restoring the objection, or to the aggregate of quiddity and individuation. In the latter case it is only a part, not the whole, of that aggregate, contrary to the claim that species is the entire reality of its individuals.

I say that a third alternative avoids the objection: relate it to the quiddity insofar as it is joined to the person. This differs both from quiddity simply in itself and from the aggregate compounded of quiddity and individuation. No difficulty then follows. Reflect. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 233](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/233?lang=ar) · [Qum 234](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/234?lang=ar)

On ‘What is it? asks about the complete reality’: mā has two uses. Explanatory mā requests an explanation of the name—its concept and the meaning for which it was assigned. Real mā asks for the actual quiddity. When things of the same or different realities are questioned by real mā, species or genus supplies the answer. When explanatory mā is used, accidental predicates may answer, as the author expressly states in his commentary on the Talkhīṣ.

Without restricting mā, the definitions of genus as what is predicated of a multiplicity differing in reality in answer to ‘What is it?’ and species as what is predicated of a multiplicity agreeing in reality in answer to that question would admit accidental predicates. The glossator therefore indicates that only real mā is intended. Otherwise the preceding objection arises. Yet this uses an ambiguous expression in a definition without a determining indicator—unless it is claimed that, although language originally allows both senses, logical convention has restricted mā to the real question. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 234](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/234?lang=ar)

A universal's being predicated in answer to ‘What is it?’ in respect of a shared reality is different from its being a part of a quiddity. <a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-074"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-074 — local note 74

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 235](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/235?lang=ar)

On ‘the genus is proximate, as animal …’: general rules become clear to beginners through particular examples. For this reason the manuals are full of examples, and the logicians use the following universals to arrange species and genera: human, animal, growing body, body without qualification, and substance. Human is a species because it answers ‘What is it?’ about individuals sharing one reality. Each remaining term is a genus of human. Animal is the entirety shared with, for example, sheep; growing body, with plants; body, with a stone; substance, with an intellect. One quiddity may therefore have several genera, some genera of others.

A genus is proximate or remote. It must answer a question about the quiddity together with some different reality sharing that genus. If it also answers the question about the quiddity together with each of the different realities sharing that genus, it is proximate. Animal answers questions about human together with horse, sheep, camel, mule and the other animal realities. Otherwise it is remote. Growing body answers the question about human and tree, but not human and horse, although horse too shares that genus; the answer there is animal. Body answers the question about human and stone, but not human and horse, nor human and tree: the answers there are respectively animal and growing body. Substance answers the question about human and intellect, but not human together with horse, tree or stone: the respective answers are animal, growing body and body.

Growing body is called remote by one degree, body by two, and substance by three. The rule is: where there are two possible answers the genus is remote by one degree; three answers, by two; four answers, by three; and so on. The number of degrees is always one less than the number of answers, because the proximate genus counts among the answers but not among the degrees of remoteness.

Consequently the same genus can be proximate in relation to one thing and remote in relation to another, and remote by different degrees in relation to several things. Substance is proximate to body, remote by one degree from growing body, by two from animal and by three from human. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 236](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/236?lang=ar)

On ‘remote, as body, which answers …’: remoteness may be by one degree or two, and so forth.

The original Greek use of the term genus, according to the reported account, designated a character shared by many persons: thus descent from ʿAlī would be a genus of the descendants of ʿAlī. They also called a single person to whom many others were related their genus: ʿAlī himself would thus be the genus of his descendants. They regarded this as the more primary use because ʿAlī causes that common descent to be a genus; a cause is prior to its effect whether the two agree in meaning or differ. They also called crafts and occupations genera of those sharing them, and applied the term to the sharing itself. Since what logicians now call genus is one thing related to many things that share it, and originally lacked a name, a name for these similar cases was transferred to it. —ʿAbd al-Raḥīm

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 236](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/236?lang=ar)

The passage answers an objection that the definition of relative species is not exclusive: it also applies to a subclass and to a real particular. A subclass is a species restricted by universal accidental conditions, such as Turkish or Indian human. Animal, a genus, answers ‘What is it?’ about such a subclass together with horse; the same applies to a real particular.

The answer is that ‘quiddity’ here means what is predicated in answer to ‘What is it?’ It can therefore only be universal, excluding the real particular, and essential, excluding the subclass.

You may object that the subclass, being a property, is already excluded by ‘in answer to What is it?’ and needs no additional explanation. I reply that properties are of two kinds: in one, a genus answers that question about the property and something else; in the other it does not. The subclass belongs to the first and is not excluded merely by that phrase. —ʿAbd al-Raḥīm

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-079"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-079 — local note 79

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 236](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/236?lang=ar) · [Qum 237](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/237?lang=ar)

Writers disagree whether real species and relative species stand in unrestricted inclusion or overlap. The earlier writers choose unrestricted inclusion. Every real species, they say, falls under one of the ten categories, since universals are confined to them, as established elsewhere. The categories are genera, and whatever falls under a genus is a relative species. Every real species is therefore a relative species.

Later writers choose overlap. They deny that every real species falls under a category. That would be required only if every real species were contingent, which is not so. Even if it were, they deny that all possible things are confined to the ten categories: what is confined to them is the genera of possible things in the world, as they expressly state. They argue from simple natures, which have no part capable of being a genus. A genus is a part of a quiddity; what has no parts has no genus. An objection to this will follow.

The Imam argues that quiddities are either simple or composite. If simple, each is a real species without being relative, or it would be composed of genus and differentia. If composite, they must ultimately terminate in simples, and the previous argument returns. The reply is that a quiddity's simplicity does not establish that it is a species, still less a real species. It might instead be a highest or isolated genus, a differentia, or something else. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-094"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-094 — local note 94

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 239](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/239?lang=ar) · [Qum 240](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/240?lang=ar)

On ‘know that the author did not discuss …’: writers enumerate four ranks of genus and species. A genus with another genus both above and below is intermediate; with neither above nor below, isolated; with one below only, the genus of genera; with one above only, lowest. The same division applies to species.

They illustrate isolated genus by intellect, supposing the ten intellects to differ in reality and substance not to be their genus: intellect would then have neither a genus above nor a genus below. They also illustrate isolated species by intellect, supposing the ten intellects to agree in reality and substance to be their genus: intellect would then have neither species above nor species below.

The author omits these isolated cases and gives only three ranks. Either his discussion concerns ordered genera and species, while the isolated is outside the hierarchy, as appears; or their existence has not been established, as even writers who give four ranks admit. The offered examples are merely hypothetical; moreover each contradicts the assumption of the other. But an example's purpose is to facilitate understanding, whether or not it corresponds to reality, so supposition suffices—especially where no actual example is found.

You may object that the first explanation should also prevent other writers from discussing the isolated cases, since they too discuss order. Perhaps they include isolation in the hierarchy precisely as the absence of order: it considers order negatively, while the other cases consider it positively. —Muḥammad ʿAlī

[A separately introduced modern criticism by Muḥammad al-Karmī, cited to al-Taqrīb p.33, follows and is registered without reproducing its text.]


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

An order of genera requires a genus, its genus, the genus of that genus, and so on; an order of species requires a species, its species, and so on. The isolated cases contain none of this. Some count them as ranks because isolation considers the absence of order, whereas the other ranks consider its presence. —ʿAbd al-Raḥīm

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-107"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-107 — local note 107

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 242](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/242?lang=ar) · [Qum 243](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/243?lang=ar)

I say that this answer is incomplete. At most, if accepted, it shows that the already known genus cannot supply the answer, not that every genus is excluded. If a quiddity is known through a remote genus and one seeks what distinguishes it from other members of that genus, one may answer with a lower genus or a definition containing that lower genus, just as with a differentia. Only the already known remote genus and a definition containing it are excluded.

Do not reply that the intended distinction is from all the other members of that known genus, so that only a differentia can answer. We do not grant that only a differentia gives such complete distinction: a definition may also do so, particularly when the known genus is remote. This reply would at most remove the objection from genus, not the entire objection. Even if accepted, it would exclude remote differentiae and make the definition fail in inclusiveness, just as the earlier account fails in exclusiveness. Both defects are unacceptable.

Nor should one say that ‘we ask about a differentia only after knowing that the thing has a genus’ means its proximate genus, leaving no lower genus or definition containing one available as an answer. Apart from the wording not supporting that restriction, it would again exclude the remote differentia. When the proximate genus is known, only the proximate differentia distinguishes the thing from the other members of that genus; the remote differentia does not.

That is what I wrote long ago when a distinguished scholar read this book with me. I showed it to my teacher, who approved it. Now I say: just as each species is composed of its proximate genus and differentia, each genus is composed of its own proximate genus and differentia, except the highest genus, which has neither a genus above it nor a differentia. If the rule is that we ask about a differentia only after knowing the genus, then not only the known genus and a definition containing it are excluded as answers: so are an unknown lower genus and a definition containing that lower genus, since the known genus is a constituent of the latter's quiddity.

For example, if we know human under the remote genus body and ask ‘What sort of body is human in itself?’, not only ‘body’ and ‘sentient body’ are excluded, but also ‘animal’ and ‘rational animal.’ Animal includes body—it is sentient body—and bodily nature is already known to the questioner. The unknown he asks about is sentience alone. If the questioner or respondent is assumed not to know that animal includes body, animal will then function for him as a differentia rather than a genus. Reflect. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī


**Reading / scope note:** The source explicitly revises the author's earlier objection; both stages of his reasoning are preserved.

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-108"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-108 — local note 108

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 243](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/243?lang=ar) · [Qum 244](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/244?lang=ar)

One may object that a quiddity can be composed of two or more coextensive constituents. Each would then be a differentia, since it distinguishes the quiddity essentially; none would be a genus, since each is coextensive with the quiddity whereas a genus must be broader. The rule ‘what has no genus has no differentia’ would therefore be questionable.

Moreover, if that rule is accepted, differentia must mean the universal distinguishing a quiddity from other members of its genus. The constituents of a quiddity would then no longer be confined to genus and differentia. For a quiddity compounded of coextensive constituents, each constituent is not a genus, for the reason given, and is not a differentia under the specified account, because the quiddity has no genus whose other members it distinguishes it from.

It is surprising that Avicenna, as the author of the Maṭāliʿ reports, defines differentia in the Shifāʾ as the universal predicated of the species in answer to ‘What sort of thing is it in itself, within its genus?’—the essential universal distinguishing the species from other members of its genus. He seems to adopt al-Ṭūsī's basis, whose difficulty has been explained. Unless composition of a quiddity from coextensive constituents is itself impossible. Reflect. —ʿAbd al-Raḥīm

[A separate modern response attributed to al-Karmī and cited to al-Taqrīb p.34 follows; its position is preserved without reproducing its text.]


**Reading / scope note:** The digital phrase saying each constituent ‘is not a part’ appears contextually to require ‘is not a genus’; the translation makes the argument intelligible while flagging the reading rather than silently certifying an emendation.

On ‘the article is exhaustive’: do not object that muqawwim is an active participle, and that in active and passive participles the article is, according to the majority, a nominal relative rather than an article of determination. How could it then have exhaustiveness, supposedly a meaning of the latter?

Several writers, including the author in his commentary on the Talkhīṣ, expressly restrict that controversy to participles expressing an occurrence. Their reason for treating the article as relative is that such participles are verbs in nominal form, which is why they govern even without present or future reference. Where no occurrence is intended, as in ‘believer’ and ‘unbeliever,’ no one disputes that it is a determining article, as with a stable adjectival form. Even if the objection is granted, exhaustiveness is not confined to the determining article: a relative expression may also be exhaustive, as several investigators state. Understand. —Muḥammad ʿAlī

On ‘the higher intended here …’: earlier, highest meant a species with no species above it or a genus with no genus above it, while lowest meant a species with no species below or a genus with no genus below. Those absolute meanings are not intended here. ‘Higher’ means any species or genus standing above another universal, whether or not yet another universal stands above it.

The qualification applies to the general subject alternatively designated genus or species, not necessarily to each disjunct separately—otherwise one might object that a species must have a universal above it or it would not be a species. Alternatively understand a genus above another genus, whether or not it has a further genus above, and a species above another species, whether or not it has a further species above. **First-pass rendering** · [Qum 245](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/245?lang=ar)

You may object that ‘not every,’ like ‘some is not,’ quantifies a particular negative; how can that express a universal converse? I reply that ‘not’ supplies the negation in ‘not conversely’; what follows it expresses what is negated, namely the universal converse.

Why restrict converse to the universal and thus force a technical expression into its more remote linguistic sense? Because technical conversion is valid here and cannot be denied.

Why is the universal converse invalid? Why is rationality not constitutive of the higher as it is of the lower? Because the lower adds to the higher quiddity only its constituting differentiae. If those were shared with the higher, no distinction would remain between higher and lower. Moreover, not every part of a whole is part of a part; otherwise the whole itself, which is all its parts together, would become part of its part. Reflect. —ʿAbd al-Raḥīm

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-123"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-123 — local note 123

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 246](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/246?lang=ar)

Property and common accident each have three kinds. Either they embrace all instances of their subject or they do not; what embraces all is either necessary, inseparable from the subject, or separable. Some logicians reserve the unqualified name ‘property’ for an all-embracing necessary property. They must then put the other two kinds under common accident, or the fivefold division would fail. The glossator rejects that usage, expressly dividing property here into all-embracing and otherwise, and later into necessary and separable.
Avicenna is reported to have criticised that restriction in the Shifāʾ as confused: a universal is a property because it is predicated of only one reality, whether of all or some of its instances and whether permanently or not. Common accident contrasts with property and is common when predicated of that reality and another. Breadth within the subject and duration therefore do not determine this distinction.

Property also divides into absolute and relative. Absolute property belongs to its subject alone in relation to everything else, as writing to human; this is one of the five predicables. Relative property belongs to the subject alone in relation to some other things, as walking belongs to human in comparison with what is not animal. Later writers do not count this as property but as common accident.

There is also composite property: it combines features each individually a common accident, such as ‘winged and giving live birth’ for bat or ‘walking with upright stature’ for human. The glossator's present implication and later explicit statement, followed by most earlier and some later writers, admit both simple and composite property. Yet supplying ‘universal’ here, or stating it expressly as the Maṭāliʿ and Risāla do, seems inconsistent with that. The writers apparently do not apply ‘universal’ to a compound expression; some expressly say so. Otherwise definitions of the predicables themselves would undermine the exclusiveness of their definitions. Understand. —Muḥammad ʿAlī


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 246](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/246?lang=ar) · [Qum 247](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/247?lang=ar)

The generalisation indicates that property is not restricted to a species, contrary to those who define it as an external predicate exclusive to the individuals of one species, whether real or relative species. It also includes the property of a highest genus, as Avicenna and the Imam maintain. The Imam says that a property may belong to lowest, intermediate or highest species, or to highest genus. To be a property means only to occur in this subject and not another, whether the subject is a species or a genus. Reflect. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-125"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-125 — local note 125

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 247](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/247?lang=ar)

Using derivative predicates rather than abstract principles to illustrate the predicables indicates that their predication is univocal predication—‘it is this’—not predication through derivation or through a compound expression. A universal must be predicated of its particulars in the first manner. Abstract principles are not so predicated: one does not say ‘Zayd is rationality’ or ‘Zayd is laughter,’ but ‘Zayd is rational’ or ‘Zayd is laughing.’ Rationality and laughter apply to Zayd's, ʿAmr's and Bishr's rationality and laughter, not directly to the persons. They are universals in relation to those activities, not the persons themselves. Writers who nevertheless use the abstract principles as examples speak loosely and intend the derivative predicates; they do not thereby adopt a different kind of predication. Reflect. —Muḥammad ʿAlī

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-126"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-126 — local note 126

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 247](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/247?lang=ar)

On ‘understand’: there is no contradiction in a thing being a property relative to one subject and a common accident relative to another. Considerations differ, as one differentia may be proximate to one thing and remote from another. Walking is a property relative to animal, insofar as it is an external predicate applying only beneath the single animal reality. Relative to human it is a common accident, applying to human reality and other specific realities.

Walking is also sometimes called a property relative to human, but qualified as a relative property. ‘Understand’ may therefore point to the compatibility between calling it a common accident of human and calling it a relative property of human: in that usage the two are synonymous. The opposition is between common accident and absolute property. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-127"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-127 — local note 127

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 247](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/247?lang=ar) · [Qum 248](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/248?lang=ar)

An investigating glossator says that ‘its subject’ was used rather than ‘the quiddity’ to avoid the apparent objection that the subsequent division of the necessary divides a thing into itself—what is necessary to quiddity—and something else—what is necessary to existence but separable from quiddity. This explains the later phrase ‘what is necessary to the thing,’ not ‘to the quiddity.’

I say he rightly calls the objection merely apparent. Even if ‘quiddity’ were used, we do not grant that a necessary concomitant of existence is separable from the quiddity without qualification. It is separable from quiddity considered simply in itself; it does not follow that it is separable from that quiddity considered as existing.

The subject of division is what is inseparable from a quiddity in some respect, not necessarily insofar as it is just that quiddity. Inseparability in some respect includes inseparability both in itself and insofar as existent. Alternatively, take ‘quiddity’ to mean the existing quiddity. What is inseparable from it either is inseparable from it simply in itself, or not: the first is a necessary concomitant of quiddity, the second of existence.

Indeed, even the apparent objection does not arise for this glossator, since his division expressly supplies the qualification ‘insofar as,’ showing that the object divided is what is necessary to quiddity in some respect, embracing both kinds. Consider it. —Muḥammad ʿAlī

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-130"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-130 — local note 130

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 248](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/248?lang=ar)

On ‘this concomitant is established for it’: the thing cannot occur without that concomitant. Correspondingly, a necessary concomitant in respect of mental existence means that whenever the thing occurs in the mind, the concomitant is established for it: its occurrence without that concomitant is impossible.

‘Mental concomitance’ here is not the mental implication required for implicative signification, in which apprehending the thing without apprehending the concomitant is impossible. If it meant that, the divisions would not be mutually exclusive: a concomitant of external existence or of quiddity could also be mentally implied in that sense. Nor would the division be exhaustive. Mental attributes whose own existence follows only upon their subjects' mental existence—universality, genericity, specificity, differentiahood and the like—belong to neither of the first two classes, since their subjects can exist externally without these attributes existing externally. They must fall in the third. Yet apprehending their subject need not entail apprehending the attribute.

Thus the intended necessity is that the subject cannot occur in the mind without this attribute itself—not merely an image of the attribute—also occurring there. —ʿAbd al-Raḥīm

On ‘the non-evident is then the concomitant which …’: he departs from the usual definition, ‘the concomitant whose necessary connection requires an intermediary for mental certainty,’ because that would leave a third kind outside the division. An intermediary is what accompanies ‘because’ when one says ‘because it is such-and-such.’ In ‘The world is originated because it changes,’ changing is the middle, accompanying ‘because.’

But lack of a need for such a middle does not entail that conceiving the antecedent, consequent and their relation suffices for certainty of the connection. A connection may require no inferential middle yet not become certain from those conceptions alone—for example, matters known by intuition, experience or sensation. The glossator therefore gives the broader definition: a concomitant whose connection does not become certain merely from conceiving it, its antecedent and their relation, but needs either a middle or something else—intuition, experience, sensation or another source. —Muḥammad ʿAlī

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-148"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-148 — local note 148

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 251](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/251?lang=ar)

The passage answers the question why the author investigates the external existence of the natural universal but not that of the logical and intellectual universals. The proposed answer is that the latter two's nonexistence externally is already established among the writers, whereas the natural universal remains disputed.

In truth, the other two are also disputed, as theological works record. A better explanation is that investigating external existence is outside logic's proper art. Logicians investigate known contents leading to the conception of unknown contents; whether these universals exist externally is not itself part of that inquiry. Later writers nevertheless discuss the natural universal because they think some pedagogical explanations depend on it. It helps illustrate the art's rules: the example of animal being predicated of human, cow and horse becomes clearer when one knows that distinct external realities can be predicated of one another.

It is also said that those affirming the existence of relations affirm the logical universal's existence, while those denying relations deny it. The first implication is questionable: affirming that some relations exist does not mean affirming that every relation exists, including the logical universal. —Muḥammad ʿAlī


**Reading / scope note:** The digital source describes the genus example with ‘agreeing in realities,’ apparently at odds with the stated animal examples; the translation preserves the example's role without silently certifying that wording.

On ‘the absence of the part’—the logical universal—‘entails the absence of the whole’—the intellectual universal: the glossator explains that the intellectual universal is formed from logical and natural universal. Once the logical universal is held not to exist externally, the intellectual universal likewise does not, because absence of a part entails absence of the whole.

This account assumes the natural universal exists externally. If it does not, the explanation should instead be that when all the parts are absent the whole is absent, since the whole is only those parts.

The Imam argues for the intellectual universal's existence solely in the mind through the philosophers' account of what is qualified by universality. It must exist mentally or externally; otherwise it would be sheer nonbeing and could not be shared by many. It cannot exist externally: every external existent is determinate and individuated, no such individual is shared by many, and every universal is shared by many. Thus no external existent is universal. External existence excluded, mental existence remains.

An objection concerns ‘individual.’ If it means the quiddity together with its individuating accidents, the claim is certainly true. If it means the quiddity underlying those accidents, it is denied: abstracted from them and present to intellect, that quiddity can receive universality and be shared by many. —ʿAbd al-Raḥīm

<a id="HWN-MAFAHIM-153"></a>
## HWN-MAFAHIM-153 — local note 153

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 252](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/252?lang=ar)

One reply distinguishes two claims. If the consequence is that one numerically individual thing bears contrary qualities and exists in several places, we grant that this is impossible but deny that it follows. If the consequence concerns unity not numerical but specific or generic, we grant that it follows but deny that it is impossible. Whether one species or genus can exist in several places and bear different qualities is precisely the question at issue.

Do not answer that numerical unity is intended and argue: every external existent is intrinsically distinguished from others, so that once intellect considers its distinctive particularity it cannot suppose that particularity shared. If a nature existed externally it would be thus individualised, although shared by individuals in different places and with contrary qualities, producing the impossibility. We deny the premise that every external existent excludes possible sharing once its particularity is considered. That itself is the disputed starting point.

A further argument against external natural universals says: if one existed externally, it would be either outside its particulars, or within them as identical with them or as their part. All alternatives fail. Outside them, it could not be predicated of them. Identical with them, it would make every particular identical with every other: each would be identical with the natural universal, that universal identical with another particular, and identity is transitive. As a part, it again could not be predicated, since part differs from whole. Reflect. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

# Definition

**H-DEFINITION · printed pp253–262 · local notes1–29**


<a id="HWN-DEFINITION-001"></a>
## HWN-DEFINITION-001 — local note 1

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 253](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/253?lang=ar)

‘What a definition is composed of’ does not mean all five predicables. Later writers, including the author, do not admit common accident as a definition, as he will expressly say. Nor do they admit species, judging from their division of definition into essential definition and description, neither of which includes species or common accident. Those two were discussed incidentally, to exhaust the divisions of universals.

An investigating glossator suggests that all five may be intended. Species can be part of a definition, as in defining a Roman as a human of such-and-such character; common accident too can be part of a definition, as will follow, God willing. I say that this is true in itself, but does not fit the claim that the author has already finished explaining these materials. Reflect. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-DEFINITION-002"></a>
## HWN-DEFINITION-002 — local note 2

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 253](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/253?lang=ar)

On ‘to yield a conception of this thing’: this excludes a predicate not intended to yield conception. He abandons the familiar formula ‘that whose conception entails conceiving the thing,’ because it admits antecedents in relation to their evident concomitants, and also the defined thing considered precisely as something defined. Conceiving it under that consideration entails conceiving its definition, since that consideration is available only after the definition has been conceived.

It is therefore weak to deny the entailment on the ground that conceiving something in outline does not entail conceiving it in detail. Conceiving the defined as defined, even in outline, presupposes detailed conception of its definition. Its implication is like an effect's implication of its cause. Likewise weak is al-Dawwānī's objection that the quiddity of the defined may be conceived without the definition under the aspect available before acquisition.

Al-Sharīf answers the original counterexample by taking ‘entails’ to mean through discursive inquiry. The contextual indicators are the earlier designation of what leads through inquiry to conception as an explanatory statement, and logic's purpose of explaining how conceptions and assents are acquired. —ʿAbd al-Raḥīm


**Reading / scope note:** The Arabic distinguishes muʿarrif and muʿarraf by vocalisation not consistently printed; the English follows the argument's explicit causal sequence.

<a id="HWN-DEFINITION-004"></a>
## HWN-DEFINITION-004 — local note 4

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 254](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/254?lang=ar)

On ‘or under an aspect distinguishing it from everything else’: this broadens the account to include incomplete essential definitions and descriptions. They do not yield the whole reality, but distinguish the thing from everything else.

It answers a possible dilemma: either this definition fails to include all definitions, or the customary formula contains an unnecessary addition when it says ‘what entails conceiving the thing or distinguishing it from everything else.’ Here ‘conception’ is broader than in that formula, where it means conception of the entire reality. That formula consequently needs the additional alternative.

Do not object that conceiving the entire reality already distinguishes the thing from everything else, so ‘or’ improperly makes a thing a coordinate alternative to itself. The second alternative means distinction without disclosure of the entire reality. Thus one alternative gives distinction together with complete disclosure, the other distinction without it. Alternatively, the primary aim in the first is complete disclosure; distinction follows but is not primarily intended. In the second, distinction itself is the aim. Understand. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī

<a id="HWN-DEFINITION-006"></a>
## HWN-DEFINITION-006 — local note 6

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 254](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/254?lang=ar)

The claim has some force when the broader is essential and the narrower is conceived in its entire reality, as in the glossator's example. It can also hold when the broader is accidental and the narrower is conceived without its whole reality, provided definitions may combine a common accident with a differentia or property. Conceiving human as ‘walking and laughing’ or ‘walking and rational’ includes a conception of walking in one of the two relevant ways.

But when the broader is accidental and the narrower conceived in its entire reality, conceiving the narrower need not yield the broader: a complete definition of human does not require conceiving walking. Nor does it when the broader is essential but the narrower is conceived through a simple incomplete essential definition or an incomplete description. If conceived through a complete description or an incomplete essential definition combining remote genus and proximate differentia, it may again yield the broader.

After all these qualifications, saying that conceiving the narrower yields the broader remains weak. The broader was conceived before the narrower; what occurs later cannot yield the conception already present. Unless the intention is that seeking to conceive the narrower leads one to conceive the broader. Understand. —Muḥammad ʿAlī

<a id="HWN-DEFINITION-008"></a>
## HWN-DEFINITION-008 — local note 8

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 255](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/255?lang=ar)

On ‘because the narrower occurs less often …’: an investigator in the commentary on the Risāla argues that the narrower's mental presence entails the broader's, whereas the broader may occur without the narrower. Al-Sharīf objects in his marginalia that this requires the broader to be essential to the narrower and the narrower to be conceived in its entire reality. Otherwise mental presence of the narrower need not entail mental presence of the broader.

I accept the qualification but reject confining the entailment to those conditions. If the broader is essential and the narrower is apprehended through a complete description, or through an incomplete essential definition formed from remote genus and proximate differentia, the entailment also holds. Do not broaden ‘conceived in its entire reality’ to include these: that departs from customary terminology and would also admit a simple incomplete essential definition, where the entailment certainly fails. Moreover, if common accident may be combined with differentia or property in a definition, the entailment may hold even when the broader is accidental.

The commentary on the Risāla adds that the narrower has more conditions and incompatibilities: every condition or obstacle of the broader is one of the narrower, but not conversely. What has more conditions and obstacles occurs less often in the mind, and what occurs less often is less evident. Al-Sharīf replies that this holds externally—wherever the narrower is realised, the broader is realised—but not necessarily mentally, since the narrower may be understood without the broader, as already explained. Reflect. —Muḥammad ʿAlī

A separately introduced passage by Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm follows. If definition through a narrower term is forbidden, the definition of definition itself appears invalid. The expression used to define definition is one particular definition, narrower than definition generally: not every definition is that very expression ‘what is predicated of a thing to yield its conception.’

The reply distinguishes ordinary predication from a proposition about the nature itself. Narrower here means narrower in ordinary predication, as in ‘Every human is animal’ and ‘Some animal is not human.’ The definition of definition is not narrower in that sense. Every individual definition is something predicated of a thing to yield its conception, and every instance of that description is a definition. They are coextensive under ordinary predication. The negative proposition used in the objection is instead a nonstandard proposition about the nature. This is al-Dawwānī's answer. —Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥīm

<a id="HWN-DEFINITION-009"></a>
## HWN-DEFINITION-009 — local note 9

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 255](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/255?lang=ar) · [Qum 256](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/256?lang=ar)

On ‘from defining a definition as what is predicated of a thing …’: once definiens and definiendum are not identical—lest the thing be known before being known—their possible relations are four: equality, disjointness, unrestricted inclusion, or overlap. The last two have already been excluded. ‘What is predicated of it’ excludes disjointness, since what is disjoint from a thing cannot be predicated of it. Equality therefore remains.

Equality resolves into two universal affirmatives. A correct definition accordingly requires the defined term to be predicable of every instance of the defining expression, and conversely the defining expression of every instance of the defined. The first is called iṭṭirād or exclusion of outsiders; the second inʿikās or inclusion of all instances. Iṭṭirād means that no instance of the definition lacks the defined term; inʿikās means that no instance of the defined lacks the definition.

‘Converse’ here is not technical conversion, since an affirmative technically converts only to a particular. The first direction is treated as direct and the second as converse because what is being tested is the definition's equality with the defined: the definition is therefore appropriately made subject in the first universal, then the terms are reversed. Another explanation derives iṭṭirād from ṭard, exclusion, because it prevents outsiders from entering; its opposite then expresses inclusion of all the defined term's instances. Reflect. —Mīrzā Muḥammad ʿAlī

<a id="HWN-DEFINITION-019"></a>
## HWN-DEFINITION-019 — local note 19

**Visible prose rendered — SOURCE TABLE MISSING** · [Qum 257](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/257?lang=ar) · [Qum 258](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/258?lang=ar) · [Qum 259](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/259?lang=ar) · [Qum 260](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/260?lang=ar)

On ‘this is the upshot of their account’: the restriction of a definiens to four divisions summarises their statement that a definition proceeds either solely through essentials or otherwise. The first either contains all the essentials, such as the proximate genus and differentia, or only some, such as the proximate differentia alone or with a remote genus. These are the complete and incomplete essential definitions. The second either consists of proximate genus and proprium, or of the proprium alone or with a remote genus: the complete and incomplete descriptions.

There are two difficulties. First, none of the four divisions is confined to the combinations they name. A complete essential definition can contain the proximate genus and differentia together with a remote differentia, remote genus, proprium or common accident, among other additions. An incomplete essential definition can contain the proximate differentia with a proprium, common accident or remote differentia; or with a remote genus and a proprium, common accident or remote differentia, and so on. The same applies to complete and incomplete descriptions.

Here is the detailed account. The five predicables become seven when the two kinds of genus and differentia are separately counted. A definiens is either simple or composed of two, three, four, five, six or seven elements. There are seven simple cases, two valid and the rest invalid through excessive breadth or narrowness. Two-element combinations number forty-nine, from considering each of the seven with each of the seven. Some fail through breadth, narrowness, or placing the narrower before the broader, either alone or together with one of the preceding defects. Some reduce to simple cases. A table will distinguish the valid from the invalid and the relevant from the irrelevant, and also make the simple cases clear. [The searchable page announces the table here, but the retrieved text does not contain the table itself.]

Three-element arrangements number three hundred and thirty-six. The text first counts fifty-six three-element combinations. Take, for example, one combination of proximate genus, remote genus and proximate differentia, and another of remote differentia, common accident and proprium. These are two cases. Replacing each element of one combination with each element of the other gives eighteen more, making twenty. Replacing each element of either combination by species gives six cases. Replacing each of the remaining two non-species elements in these six by each of the other three gives thirty-six cases, which together with the preceding twenty make fifty-six. Each combination has six possible orders: six times fifty-six is three hundred and thirty-six.

Four-element arrangements are said to number three thousand three hundred and sixty. The text counts one hundred and forty combinations: two four-element combinations selected from seven must share at least one element, which may be any of the seven. This gives fourteen cases, seven for each combination. Replacing each of the three unshared elements in the seven forms of either combination by each of the three unshared elements in the other gives one hundred and twenty-six further cases. With the fourteen these make one hundred and forty. Each combination has twenty-four orders; the stated product is three thousand three hundred and sixty.

Five-element arrangements are stated to number five thousand four hundred. The text counts four hundred and fifty combinations: two five-element combinations from seven must share at least three elements, and those three have fifty-six forms according to the earlier calculation. This gives one hundred and twelve cases, fifty-six for each combination. Exchanging each of the two unshared elements in the forms of one combination with each of the two unshared elements in the other is said to yield four hundred and fifty. Each combination has one hundred and twenty orders, and the source gives five thousand four hundred as the resulting total.

Six- and seven-element arrangements are each said to number five thousand and forty. For six elements there are seven combinations, each with seven hundred and twenty orders: their product is five thousand and forty. For all seven there is only one combination, but its orders reach that number; multiplication by one leaves the number of orders unchanged. The rule for the number of orders is to multiply the number of orders in the preceding length by the number of elements in the following length.

Some arrangements are valid. Others fail through narrowness, as when species is an element; through breadth, as when neither proprium nor proximate differentia occurs; or through placing the narrower before the broader.

Do not reply that definition aims either at knowing the essence or distinguishing the thing from everything else, and that proximate genus plus differentia or proximate genus plus proprium already achieves this, making remote genus, common accident or remote differentia unnecessary. Each of those aims can be achieved in ways differing in completeness, detail and compression. When the fullest acquaintance or distinction is desired, a proprium may be added to an essential definition or a common accident to a description, and similarly in the remaining cases. A proprium alone already distinguishes; yet a proximate genus is added to it. Preserve this detailed account: I know of no one who preceded me in it.

The second difficulty is that, if an essence may consist of two or more coextensive constituents and we define it through one, that definition is neither an essential definition nor a description. The constituent is neither proximate differentia nor proprium. Proximate and remote differentiae belong to essences compounded of genera and differentiae, not to those compounded of coextensive constituents. And the constituent is essential, whereas a proprium is not essential. On the author's stated definitions—essential definition through a proximate differentia and description through a proprium—a middle case therefore remains. Our earlier discussion of distinguishing from what shares a proximate or remote genus is relevant; consult it and reflect.

<a id="HWN-DEFINITION-023"></a>
## HWN-DEFINITION-023 — local note 23

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 260](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/260?lang=ar) · [Qum 261](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/261?lang=ar)

On ‘an indication of what the earlier authorities allowed’: they say that definition aims at conception, either of the essence or under an aspect distinguishing the thing from something else—whether from everything else or only some of it. Distinction from every other thing is not obligatory.

At the beginning of the Book of Demonstration, the Shaykh says: ‘Acquired conception has degrees. One may conceive something through an accidental meaning peculiar to it or common to it and another, or through an essential meaning in either of those two ways. A specifically distinguishing conception may embrace the complete reality or only a portion. Similarly, an expression used to distinguish and define something may distinguish it from only some other things. If through accidents, it is an incomplete description; if through essentials, an incomplete essential definition. Or it may distinguish from everything else: through accidents it is a complete description, especially when a genus is included; through essentials, a complete essential definition. This is the account of the outwardly recognised logicians. For the thorough investigators, a definition is complete only if it embraces every essential constituent without omitting any; otherwise it is not complete.’

After quoting this, the commentary on the Maṭāliʿ observes that equality of extension is not required of definition without qualification, but of complete definition. Their intention is not to permit broader definitions indiscriminately. They permit one when the intended distinction from some other thing is achieved. If a human is confused with a stone or tree, calling the human an animal or a walking thing gives a conception distinguishing it from that object, though not from other animal natures. If a triangle is confused with a circle, calling it a polygonal figure distinguishes it from the circle, though not from all other polygons.

<a id="HWN-DEFINITION-024"></a>
## HWN-DEFINITION-024 — local note 24

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 261](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/261?lang=ar)

The restriction of a narrower defining term to an accident apparently implies, as some expressly state, that defining through a narrower essential term is not allowed. Apart from defining through something less evident, it would involve a circle. Defining animal through human makes knowledge of animal depend on knowledge of human, while human is rational animal and knowledge of a part precedes knowledge of the whole.

Two objections have been made. First, knowledge of human need not depend on knowledge of animal, since human might be known through an incomplete essential definition or incomplete description. Second, even granting the dependence, the argument only excludes defining a broader essential through a narrower essential, not a broader accident through a narrower essential.

But if human is known through an incomplete essential definition or description, conceiving it does not thereby give a conception of animal. Conceiving human as rational body or laughing body does not give us animal. It therefore cannot define animal under the previously stated definition of a definiens. This also answers the second objection: conceiving a narrower essential does not yield conception of a broader accident unless the former is conceived through that accident or something containing it. That would be circular and cannot serve as the definition. Reflect.

<a id="HWN-DEFINITION-028"></a>
## HWN-DEFINITION-028 — local note 28

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 262](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/262?lang=ar)

On ‘there is no acquisition of an unknown from a known in it’: you might object that a verbal definition gives a conception of the designated meaning as the meaning of this expression, which was not previously possessed. I reply that its purpose is not to conceive the meaning under that aspect, but to conceive the meaning itself. Someone hears ‘void is impossible,’ asks ‘What is void?’ and is answered ‘an imagined extension.’ This is a verbal definition. The listener seeks the meaning itself, not the meaning as assigned to this expression: his purpose is to obtain the judgment, which requires conception of its term, and he is not concerned with that further linguistic aspect.

Since the purpose is the conception of the expression's meaning, the author's classification of verbal definition among conceptual inquiries is preferable to the investigators' classification of it among assertoric inquiries. The latter rests on treating its purpose as knowledge of the word and assent to the proposition that it was assigned to a certain meaning, as a lexicographer does.

There is no fault in giving a synonym in a verbal definition: it principally employs synonymous simple expressions. If none is available, a compound indicating the concept is substituted. The detail conveyed by the compound is not itself the aim; the aim is simply to identify the relevant meaning among those already stored in thought. Nor is it objectionable to use an expression whose understanding depends on understanding the definiendum. The purpose is not to acquire knowledge of the definiendum itself, so that dependence does not constitute the circle objectionable in a real definition.
