<a id="HWN-CONDITIONAL-043"></a>
## HWN-CONDITIONAL-043 — local note 43

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 310](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/310?lang=ar) · [Qum 311](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/311?lang=ar)

Adding a connective removes an expression's independent completeness and immediate truth-evaluation because an actually asserted proposition cannot, without withdrawing its assertion, become a constituent of another proposition in the relevant conditional connection. If ‘The sun rises’ is already asserted, it cannot simultaneously be merely the judged-about or predicated component of that further conditional judgment. To place it within another, one abstracts from its assertion, and it loses independent completeness and truth-evaluability in that role.

The restriction is to the special relation between condition and consequent. An objection from a clause predicated of a topic—‘Zayd, his father stood’—does not straightforwardly apply. One can say the embedded clause is then treated like a simple predicate, as Arabic grammarians note, or interpret the sense as ‘Zayd's father stood.’ Understand the analogy without overlooking the difference.

# Contradiction

**H-CONTRADICTION · printed pp312–322 · local notes1–33**


<a id="HWN-CONTRADICTION-001"></a>
## HWN-CONTRADICTION-001 — local note 1

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 312](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/312?lang=ar)

This indicates the weakness of the argument that contradiction cannot occur between simple terms. That argument says: if assertion is included, they cease to be simple; if not, affirmation and negation—the constituents of contradiction—are absent. But affirmation and negation are required for contradiction between propositions, not for every broad use of the notion. The disagreement is verbal: those excluding simple terms mean assertoric contradiction, while those including them mean contradiction more broadly.

In that broader sense contradiction does apply to simple terms. The author's later definition of contraposition speaks of interchanging the contradictories of the two terms, or placing the contradictory of the second first. The terms are not necessarily propositions. Conditional components, though originally propositional, lose their independent completeness when connective particles enter. A categorical's first term is simple; even a clausal second term is treated like a simple expression in its predicative role. In any case, the simple first term alone suffices to establish the point, and the second often is simple too. All schools take the contradictory of the second term, and the earlier method also takes that of the first.

[A separately introduced modern al-Karmī/al-Taqrīb comment follows; it is identified but not reproduced as part of Muḥammad ʿAlī's text.]

<a id="HWN-CONTRADICTION-003"></a>
## HWN-CONTRADICTION-003 — local note 3

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 313](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/313?lang=ar)

The definition requires both implications intrinsically: the truth of either makes the other false, and the falsity of either makes the other true. It excludes cases where either or both implications depend on an external fact or the particular subject matter.

For an external fact, compare ‘Zayd is human’ and ‘Zayd is not capable of laughter.’ Their opposed truth-values depend on the coextension of human and capable-of-laughter, not merely on their form. One statement must be replaced by its equivalent for the contradiction to become explicit.

For special subject matter, the truth-to-falsity implication may fail to be intrinsic: ‘Some human is animal’ and ‘Some human is not animal’ have opposite truth-values, but two particulars can both be true, as ‘Some animal is human’ and ‘Some animal is not human.’ Or the falsity-to-truth implication may fail intrinsically: ‘No human is animal’ and ‘Every human is animal’ happen to oppose, but two universal contraries can both be false, as ‘No animal is human’ and ‘Every animal is human.’

The glossator explicitly explains the exclusion of the latter sort because it presents a more conspicuous challenge, or because exclusion of externally mediated equivalence is already clear. The omission does not mean the other sort escapes the qualification or counts as technical contradiction.

These examples show that quantified contradictories must differ in quantity: two particulars can both be true and two universals can both be false. One may object that the particular examples fail to contradict because the individuals differ—the animals judged human are not those judged nonhuman—not because quantity is the same. The reply is that logical rules concern the proposition's expressed content. ‘Some’ in each does not specify the same individuals, so their meanings do not contradict. Specifying individuals is extra to that content. Indeed, a universal refers to all individuals and its contradictory particular to some, yet contradiction still obtains.

The qualification ‘if they are quantified’ matters: contradiction is not confined to the four quantified forms. It also concerns singular and unquantified propositions. The requirement of differing quantity applies to quantified contradictories, not unrestrictedly.

<a id="HWN-CONTRADICTION-012"></a>
## HWN-CONTRADICTION-012 — local note 12

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 315](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/315?lang=ar) · [Qum 316](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/316?lang=ar) · [Qum 317](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/317?lang=ar)

The earlier authorities list eight required unities. First, subject: ‘Every human is animal’ and ‘Some stone is not animal’ can both be true because their subjects differ, and reversed claims can both be false. Second, predicate: ‘Every human is animal’ and ‘Some human is not stone’ likewise fail to contradict. Third, place: pearls may be surrounded by water in the sea and not in a chest. Fourth, condition: a body may disperse sight under the condition of being white but not under the condition of being black. Fifth, relative correlate: a father is father of his son, not of someone else's sons. Sixth, whole and part: some part of a man may be ʿawra while the whole man is not. Seventh, potentiality and actuality: wine in a vessel is potentially intoxicating but not actually causing intoxication there. Eighth, time: a person may be strong in youth and not in old age. Differing qualifications allow both statements to be true or, with the claims reversed, both false.

A separately introduced ʿAbd al-Raḥīm treatment explains that later writers reduce these eight to subject and predicate. They place condition and whole/part under subject, and the others under predicate. An objection calls that allocation arbitrary, since conversion interchanges subject and predicate. Better to say that all reduce to the two without rigidly allocating each. The objection is sound, though the allocation follows what is most natural. A subject denotes the bearer, which is directly qualified by white/black or part/whole; assigning these to the predicate-concept would require considering its bearer. Conversely, time, place, relation and potentiality/actuality naturally qualify the predicated concept; assigning them to the bearer would require recovering that concept.

Al-Fārābī is reported to retain only subject, predicate and time: it is immediately known that one determinate predicate's attribution and denial of one determinate subject at one determinate time cannot both be true or false. The other conditions are absorbed into the two terms. Al-Abharī objects that the argument absorbing place into predicate also absorbs time. ‘The moon is eclipsed when the earth intervenes’ and ‘The moon is not eclipsed at quadrature’ differ in temporally qualified predicate. Time therefore need not remain separate. The Imam likewise says in the larger Āyāt wa-l-bayyināt that time is included under predicate but is expressly mentioned for clarity concerning what contradiction requires.

Another report from al-Fārābī reduces all conditions to identity of the predicative relation. Altering subject, predicate, time or any other qualification alters that relation. By contraposition, identity of the relation requires identity of those conditions. What matters is that denial concern precisely the relation affirmed. That suffices for singular and quantified propositions. For greater explicitness one can list identity of terms and time, together with the appropriate modal opposition, and add quantity-difference for quantified propositions.

An objection gives ‘Zayd was ʿAmr's father yesterday’ and ‘He is not his father today’ as contradictories despite different times. They oppose only because of the particular subject matter: fatherhood established yesterday persists today, not because of bare logical form. Another objection adds unity of cause, instrument, object and specification: a carpenter works for the ruler but not the subjects; Zayd writes with one pen but not an iron instrument; he strikes ʿAmr but not Bakr; I have twenty dirhams but not twenty dinars. These all belong to predicate-unity, since the predicate includes its relevant complements.


**Reading / scope note:** The compressed quotations and grammatical transitions are retained as reports of competing reductions. No claim is made that the eight listed conditions alone replace the separately required quality/quantity/modal oppositions.

<a id="HWN-CONTRADICTION-013"></a>
## HWN-CONTRADICTION-013 — local note 13

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 317](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/317?lang=ar)

Several writers define a thing's contradictory as its removal. Al-Sharīf objects: negation is itself something, and its contradictory is affirmation; affirmation is not the removal of negation, though it entails it. Negation removes affirmation. Better to say ‘removing any thing gives its contradictory,’ unless ‘removal’ includes what is equivalent to literal removal.

An objection says that this revision makes ‘It is not the case that Zayd is not standing’ contradictory to ‘Zayd is not standing,’ although both appear negative and contradiction requires different quality. It would also give a negative two contradictories: its removal and the affirmative. One answer distinguishes considerations. To negate an already framed negative content, that content must be posited as a term: the original then functions as an affirmative with a negative predicate, and its denial as a negative with that predicate. If its negation is instead considered as an ordinary negative judgment, the positive affirmative alone is its contradictory. Thus the apparent duplicate depends on changing analysis.

Another answer denies that affirmation is the negative's genuine contradictory, calling only the removal of negation genuine and the affirmation figuratively equivalent; or asserts their identity. But genuine contradictory opposition should be reciprocal: if removal of affirmation genuinely contradicts affirmation, affirmation genuinely contradicts that removal. Nor is conceptual identity effortless: removing negation requires conceiving negation, while simple affirmation does not. Reflect carefully.

Each relation is reciprocal. Apply the same pattern to general actuality and perpetual propositions, and to every modal pairing. The statement ‘the contradictory of necessity is general possibility’ always carries these quality and, where applicable, quantity reversals.

One may object that sometimes only one component fails, so the negations are then genuinely exclusive and the weaker disjunction would be inappropriate. ‘An affirmative universal categorical with an alternative predicate’ is compatible with the earlier account: it is equivalent to the original compound's negation, not required to have the surface quality of literal negation.

The author and glossator do not spell out conditional contradiction, so a brief account follows. Contradictories differ in quality and quantity while retaining genus—connected or disjunctive—and type—implicative, intrinsically opposed or coincidental. A universal affirmative implicative has a particular negative implicative contradictory, and conversely; the corresponding rule holds for intrinsic and coincidental disjunctions.

Thus ‘Whenever the sun rises, day exists, by implication’ is contradicted by ‘Not whenever the sun rises does day exist by implication.’ ‘Sometimes, if something is black, it is sweet,’ under a specified kind of connection, is contradicted by ‘Never does that connection hold’ under the same kind. ‘Always, either this number is even or odd,’ under a specified disjunction, is contradicted by ‘Not always’ under that same disjunction. A particular affirmative disjunction is similarly opposed by the universal negative.

A separately introduced ʿAbd al-Raḥīm note distinguishes a categorical with alternative predicate from a disjunction resembling a categorical. With subject before the disjunctive expression—‘The number is either even or odd’—it is the former; with the disjunctive construction first—‘Either the number is even or it is odd’—it is the latter.

# Simple conversion

**H-CONVERSION · printed pp323–334 · local notes1–40**


<a id="HWN-CONVERSION-001"></a>
## HWN-CONVERSION-001 — local note 1

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 323](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/323?lang=ar)

The general reference to ‘the two terms’ allows simple conversion in both categorical and conditional propositions, unlike definitions confined to subject and predicate. A difficulty remains. If the genuine semantic terms are intended, categorical conversion does not literally exchange them: the true subject is its bearer and the predicate its description, whereas conversion takes the predicate's bearer as subject and the original subject-description as predicate. If the uttered terms are intended, disjunction too admits an exchange, though the logicians say it has no conversion.

Choose the latter and understand exchange as producing a relevant change of meaning. Reversing a disjunction leaves its substantive opposition unchanged. One may distinguish ‘evenness opposed to oddness’ from ‘oddness opposed to evenness’ in conceptual orientation, but both resolve into the same opposition between the two. No significant inferential benefit follows, so ‘no conversion’ means no conversion worth treating.

A separately excerpted ʿAbd al-Raḥīm remark similarly specifies that subject and predicate **titles**, not the actual bearer and predicated description as such, are interchanged.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-CONVERSION-002"></a>
## HWN-CONVERSION-002 — local note 2

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 324](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/324?lang=ar)

Defining conversion as an operation of exchange does not conflict with calling a particular affirmative ‘the converse’ of a universal affirmative. The first uses conversion as an action; the second names the proposition resulting from that action. The latter can be defined as the strongest proposition necessarily following through exchange, with the same quality and preservation of truth. One could also read the author's verbal noun as its result, or name the effect by its cause, but that is less apparent and contrary to some explicit explanations.

It is called ‘straight’ conversion by comparison with a clear, level path, unlike contraposition, which can mislead beginners. The Shaykh's reported omission of contraposition in the Shifāʾ is associated with the pedagogical principle that a wise teacher does not distort a beginner's understanding. Another explanation takes ‘straight’ to mean agreement with the original in truth and quality. That feature may occur in older contraposition too, but a naming resemblance need not be unique to the named operation.

<a id="HWN-CONVERSION-010"></a>
## HWN-CONVERSION-010 — local note 10

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 326](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/326?lang=ar)

Three methods establish conversion. First is supposition, to be explained at the end of contraposition. Second uses an already established conversion: negate the proposed converse and convert that negation into a proposition incompatible with the original. For an affirmative, denying ‘Some animal is human’ gives ‘No animal is human,’ whose conversion contradicts ‘Every human is animal’ or ‘Some human is animal.’ Conversely, to establish ‘No stone is human’ from ‘No human is stone,’ its negation ‘Some stone is human’ converts into ‘Some human is stone,’ contradicting the original.

These arguments would be circular only if both conversion laws were established through each other. That is not the procedure: one is independently established and used for the other. Books presenting both arguments offer alternative routes, not a jointly circular proof.

Third is reductio: combine the original with the negation of the converse in the first figure to derive denial of a thing of itself.

A subtle objection asks what ‘if the original is true, the converse is true’ means. If it means necessary implication, failure of implication does not immediately make the contrary actually true; the two might coincide without necessity. If it means only actual coexistence, it does not prove implication. The answer takes the first reading and makes the supposition the **possibility** that the contrary is true with the original. If implication failed, their joint occurrence would be possible; otherwise both truth and falsity of the converse would be excluded. But that joint occurrence entails an impossibility, and the possibility of an impossibility is impossible. Thus the converse must be true whenever the original is true.

On that reading conversion would seem possible even for him: what is possibly B can be supposed actually B, without converting possibility into real occurrence. If supposed actuality in both places, the general absolute's contradiction with the real perpetual becomes unclear: hypothetical affirmation does not oppose real perpetual negation, nor hypothetical negation real perpetual affirmation. <a id="HWN-CONVERSION-027"></a>
## HWN-CONVERSION-027 — local note 27

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 330](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/330?lang=ar) · [Qum 331](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/331?lang=ar)

Some claim that the universal absolute necessary negative converts with necessity preserved. One reductio assumes the contrary possible particular, uses it as a minor with the original necessary negative major, and derives necessary self-denial. But that proof assumes a merely possible minor is productive in the first figure; the later account requires actuality. Another proof converts the possible particular contrary and confronts it with the original, but this assumes general possibility itself converts, which has just been denied under the adopted account.

A third argument says ‘No C is necessarily B’ in the intended necessary-negative reading asserts incompatibility of C and B, and incompatibility is reciprocal. The reply distinguishes the bearers and descriptions: the original excludes the B-description from actual C-bearers; the proposed converse excludes the C-description from actual B-bearers. These are not automatically equivalent. Suppose Zayd's actual mounts are only horses. No actual mount of Zayd is necessarily a donkey, yet a donkey can become his mount, so the necessary reversed exclusion is false.

Under al-Fārābī's possible-subject account, however, the necessary negative can plausibly convert as itself. The possible minor and conversion of general possibility are allowed there, restoring the first two proofs. The third also works under the broader subject extension: if B could qualify a C-bearer, the original would fail; thus a B-bearer cannot even possibly be C. Under the Shaykh's actual-subject account, excluding actual identity does not exclude a bearer which is not now or ever actually C from possibly becoming C. Reflect carefully; this is difficult ground.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-CONVERSION-028"></a>
## HWN-CONVERSION-028 — local note 28

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 331](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/331?lang=ar)

Failure of the general conditioned negative to convert with its mode preserved is clear when the mode is necessity **during** the subject-description. Excluding B from actual C-bearers during their C-times does not necessarily exclude C from B-bearers during their B-times. Again, if Zayd's actual mounts are horses, necessary non-donkeyhood while being his mount does not show every donkey necessarily cannot be his mount while a donkey. The same difficulty occurs if necessity is ascribed to bearer-plus-description as a condition.

If, however, the predicate is necessary **because of** the description, so that the description itself grounds the necessity, reciprocal conversion appears valid. That grounds incompatibility in the descriptions themselves; either description then excludes the other in its bearer. The interpretation of descriptive necessity therefore changes the rule.

# Contraposition

**H-CONTRAPOSITION · printed pp335–340 · local notes1–26**


<a id="HWN-CONTRAPOSITION-001"></a>
## HWN-CONTRAPOSITION-001 — local note 1

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 335](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/335?lang=ar)

The earlier discussion of simple conversion, both ours and the principal glossator's, is relevant here.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-CONTRAPOSITION-002"></a>
## HWN-CONTRAPOSITION-002 — local note 2

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 335](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/335?lang=ar) · [Qum 336](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/336?lang=ar)

Once intrinsic preservation of truth is required, preserving quality in the older form of contraposition may be redundant except for clarification. A commentator denies the entailment, offering a materially true reversal with changed quality. But truth-preservation here is formal, not merely truth in a fortunate subject matter. Otherwise examples such as ‘Some non-white thing is non-human’ might count as contraposition of ‘Some human is white,’ although particular affirmatives do not uniformly contrapose.

One may object that, if truth-preservation entailed quality-preservation, the later method could not preserve truth while changing quality. The answer is that no unrestricted essential equivalence is claimed. The implication concerns the **older operation**, which exchanges both complemented terms. Under that operation, formal preservation of an affirmative's truth requires an affirmative relation between the complemented terms. The later operation complements only the original predicate and retains the original subject as the new predicate; under that operation truth-preservation instead requires a change of quality. The rule is relative to the transformation being defined, not an absolute equation of truth and quality. Reflect.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.


---


<a id="HWN-CONTRAPOSITION-003"></a>
## HWN-CONTRAPOSITION-003 — local note 3

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 336](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/336?lang=ar)

To prove it, suppose the proposed result false. Then some non-B is C. Simple conversion gives some C is non-B, contradicting ‘Every C is B.’ Alternatively, combine the assumed particular with the original to derive some non-B is B, which converts into a denial of a thing of itself and is impossible.


**Reading / scope note:** The digital second proof interchanges B/C in its displayed minor; the English states the consistent arrangement used by its own conclusion and flags the transcription problem.


---


<a id="HWN-CONTRAPOSITION-004"></a>
## HWN-CONTRAPOSITION-004 — local note 4

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 336](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/336?lang=ar) · [Qum 337](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/337?lang=ar)

The older method is the one used in the sciences, hence its priority in exposition. Later writers changed it because they objected to its standard proof. The literal negation of ‘Every non-B is non-C’ is ‘Some non-B is not non-C,’ a particular negative. It neither converts simply nor serves as a first-figure minor, which must be affirmative, nor major, which must be universal. Nor does it automatically yield ‘Some non-B is C’: a negative with a negative predicate need not entail a positive affirmative when its subject may be nonexistent.

One answer confines conversion to existent subjects, since logic serves philosophy's investigation of existents. Then the disputed implication holds. Even if the inquiry is general, a second answer distinguishes predicating a negative term from denying the positive. Take the complemented terms as denials rather than positive assertions of negative attributes. The older contraposition then uses the later writers' ‘negated-term’ analysis, which they themselves say need not require subject-existence. If the corresponding denial of denial is true, its embedded denial is false, and under that analysis not because the subject is absent; the positive must therefore hold. The proof can then be completed. — ʿAbd al-Raḥīm.


**Reading / scope note:** This is a historical proposed defence relying on a disputed analysis of negated terms, not an independently certified modern proof.

<a id="HWN-CONTRAPOSITION-007"></a>
## HWN-CONTRAPOSITION-007 — local note 7

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 337](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/337?lang=ar) · [Qum 338](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/338?lang=ar)

Al-Sharīf says that the older meaning of contraposition is the one used in scientific discourse; the later definition is not the customary scientific operation. The later writers nevertheless changed it because the standard proof seemed defective. Negating the proposed older converse gives a particular negative with negative predicate, not immediately the affirmative ‘Some non-B is C.’ The particular negative does not simply convert and cannot occupy either required first-figure position.

The reply that the affirmative is an indirect consequence encounters the subject-existence problem: a negative can be true without an existent subject, whereas either a positive or negative-term affirmative requires one. Two answers have been offered. First, restrict the conversion discussion to existent objects, as philosophy's instrument; then negative-with-negative-predicate and positive affirmative coincide under that assumption. Second, retain generality but follow the commentary on the Maṭāliʿ: the misunderstanding treats the contradictory of B as affirming non-B, whereas it is denying B. The contraposed affirmative has terms formed by denial; once its meaning is analysed, denial of denial gives affirmation in the intended construction. The proof therefore takes the affirmative equivalent on that analysis.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 338](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/338?lang=ar)

A negative, universal or particular, contraposes only particularly, not generally universally. The author's ‘because it may be …’ explains the failure of universal strength; the particular consequence is taken as evident.

Strictly, the proof could state the relevant particular premises directly without the emphatic ‘let us suppose the subject-bearer to be D.’ The supposition answers an opponent asking how the selected D is known to instantiate C: the original particular assertion already provides some bearer in reality itself, and D is a label for that bearer or whatever stands in its place. # Syllogisms

**H-SYLLOGISM · printed pp341–371 · local notes1–157**


<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-001"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-001 — local note 1

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 341](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/341?lang=ar) · [Qum 342](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/342?lang=ar)

On ‘that is, a compound’: qawl originally meant any utterance, whether assigned a meaning or not; ordinary usage restricted it to meaningful utterances, simple or compound; this discipline restricts it further to a compound, conceived or spoken. The definition can therefore define either a conceived syllogism or a spoken one: in the first, both ‘discourse’ and ‘propositions’ are conceived, and in the second spoken.

An objection says that uttering premises does not entail the further discourse called a conclusion. The reply is that the spoken compound is considered as an expression whose parts are intended to indicate the parts of its meaning. It counts as a spoken syllogism only insofar as it signifies that meaning. When such a syllogism is present, its conceived counterpart is present too; the alleged separation does not occur. Someone who pronounces premises without knowing their lexical assignments does not possess a syllogism relative to himself, although the utterance can be a syllogism relative to a listener who understands it. Likewise ‘Zayd is standing’ is discourse for someone who understands the language, not for someone ignorant of it.

You may object that the further discourse then follows from the spoken syllogism only through the conceived syllogism, whereas the definition requires it to follow intrinsically. But the spoken syllogism is already defined as meaningful expression. The consequence follows from it precisely under that defining respect, without another consideration being added. Even conceding an intermediary, ‘intrinsically’ excludes dependence on an extraneous premise, as in the equality argument discussed below; it does not exclude every consideration whatever.

The further discourse which follows is, in any event, conceived, whether the definition concerns conceived syllogisms, spoken syllogisms, or both. Neither entails the actual utterance of its conclusion, but rather its intellectual apprehension and assent to it.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-002"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-002 — local note 2

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 342](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/342?lang=ar) · [Qum 343](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/343?lang=ar)

Calling a compound ‘broader than an ordered composition’ answers the objection that ‘a discourse composed of propositions’ redundantly means ‘a compound which is compounded.’ Composition in the narrower sense requires an appropriate connection among the parts, whereas a compound as such need not. Al-Sharīf makes this distinction in his marginalia on the Kashshāf. It is consequently an accepted specification of a general term by a narrower one. It also signals that the formal component—the configuration satisfying the forthcoming conditions of the four figures—is essential. ‘Composed’ suggests agreement and linkage of parts. The author accordingly uses a masculine pronoun in ‘there follows from it intrinsically,’ referring to the composed discourse, rather than a feminine pronoun referring simply to the propositions. A conclusion follows not from any premises indiscriminately but from their matter together with their arrangement. It is surprising that the critic recognised this reason for the pronoun yet called the definition redundant.

Another commentator answers that qawl here means the ordinary meaningful utterance, including simple expressions, rather than the logician’s compound; ‘composed’ then excludes simple expressions and supplies the nearer genus. Both answers face an objection: specifying the general by the particular is appropriate only when the general concept is not already included in the particular. ‘Rational animal’ is acceptable, but ‘bodily rational animal’ repeats what animal already includes. The narrower composition on either account includes meaningful compound expression. The objection is not peculiar to the first answer. The reply is that even granting the rule, the narrower determination may be abstracted from the general element already stated; then there is no forbidden repetition.

A further question concerns using an equivocal qawl in a definition. Context makes its third, technical meaning immediately understood: a writer explaining this art’s technical expressions should use its established senses where these exist, rather than the ordinary or original senses. This consideration also reveals the weakness in the second proposed answer.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-004"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-004 — local note 4

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 343](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/343?lang=ar)

Qawl, covering conceived and spoken compounds, functions as a genus because it includes complete compounds and certain incomplete ones. If the definition concerns the conceived syllogism, the compound is conceived; if the spoken syllogism, spoken. The former is properly a syllogism, while the latter receives the name because it indicates the former.

An objection says that the spoken syllogism entails the sought conclusion only through the conceived syllogism, not intrinsically. The answer is that it is not mere sound but sound considered as indicating meanings. The Shaykh expressly says that a spoken syllogism is not syllogistic as bare expression, since expression as such does not necessitate another expression, but insofar as it signifies an intelligible meaning. The meaning is consequently a defining qualification, not an extraneous inferential intermediary. The further compound may be considered intellectually or linguistically; one must not suppose that spoken premises necessarily entail the actual speaking of a conclusion.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-005"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-005 — local note 5

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 343](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/343?lang=ar) · [Qum 344](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/344?lang=ar)

‘Composed of propositions’ means more than one proposition, thereby including a syllogism of two premises. If actual propositions are intended, as the wording naturally suggests, poetic syllogisms seem excluded: they consist of imaginative presentations rather than assents. If potential propositions suffice, a conditional proposition would enter the definition in relation to its own conversion: it potentially contains propositions and entails another statement. For a spoken syllogism, one might choose the first alternative and say that poetic premises are propositions as understood by the hearer, though not actually assertoric in their true character.

Alternatively, choose actual propositions and treat poetry, sophistry and similar forms as incidental discussions rather than parts of the argument which acquires assent. That argument consists of certain or probable premises, such as demonstration and rhetoric. A third response chooses potential propositions but restricts the entailment in the definition to acquisitional reasoning; a proposition’s mere conversion is not included.

## HWN-SYLLOGISM-007 — local note 7

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 344](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/344?lang=ar)

The second part of a compound modal proposition is not an explicit proposition. But one can replace ‘not perpetually’ with its explicit meaning, and the resulting pair would then satisfy the definition while merely converting a proposition, not forming a syllogism. The same objection applies to any two conjoined propositions.

The answer supplies the aspect-condition: a syllogism is composed discourse from which another discourse follows intrinsically insofar as it is composed. Simple conversion and contraposition follow from the proposition, not from its being so composed. Some express this by saying that the entailment must operate through discursive acquisition.

Another answer takes the indefinite singular ‘another discourse’ to mean exactly one, whereas conversion of a compound proposition yields two statements. That answer fails for affirmative temporal and existential compound modalities whose conversion, as already stated, is a single statement.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-008"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-008 — local note 8

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 344](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/344?lang=ar) · [Qum 345](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/345?lang=ar)

‘There follows from it’ excludes induction and analogy, whose explanations will come shortly. It also excludes arguments whose further statement happens to be true because of their particular matter rather than their form. ‘No horse is rational; every rational being is human’ happens to yield the true statement ‘No horse is human.’ Likewise ‘Every human is an animal; some animal is rational’ accompanies the true statement ‘Every human is rational.’ Neither truth is a necessary consequence of that arrangement. Change the first major to ‘Every rational being is an animal,’ and ‘No horse is an animal’ fails. Substitute ‘Some animal neighs’ in the second example, and the corresponding conclusion about humans neighing fails.

Another objection is that requiring entailment excludes rhetorical, dialectical, poetic and sophistical syllogisms, since they do not yield certainty, although they are counted among syllogisms. Earlier authors therefore qualified the definition: ‘a discourse composed of propositions which, whenever conceded, necessitate another discourse.’ One commentator rejects this qualification by interpreting entailment as the premises’ being such that knowledge of them brings knowledge of the conclusion. But that interpretation is not conveyed by the unrestricted wording and should not simply be assumed in a definition.

A preferable reply invokes the aspect-condition: the further statement follows from the discourse considered according to its verbally expressed content, apart from the actual extramental relations and the speaker’s condition. Reports have decisive assertoric content in that respect, as indicated by the Shaykh’s description of a report as decisive discourse. Thus the five arts can fall under the definition. Reflect.

A separately introduced gloss by ʿAbd al-Raḥīm restricts the exclusion to incomplete induction and analogy which does not produce certainty. Complete induction is the divisive syllogism. An analogy whose effective ground is certainly established can be reduced to a syllogism—for instance, the judgement about nabīdh through its intoxicating character and the rule governing every intoxicant. Such cases are not excluded merely because they are called induction or analogy.


**Reading / scope note:** The source’s second substitution shifts its example’s conclusion from universal to particular; the underlying invalid-form test is preserved. The account of all five arts is the glossator’s proposed interpretation, not a certification that their premises are factually true.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-009"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-009 — local note 9

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 345](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/345?lang=ar)

The restriction ‘intrinsically’ seems to exclude the second, third and fourth figures, since their conclusions are established by reduction to the first. The answer is that entailment includes both evident and non-evident entailment. These figures intrinsically entail their conclusions in every appropriate matter, although their entailment is not immediately apparent. Reduction is needed to obtain knowledge of their productivity, not to make them productive. An equality-chain argument is different: its supposed consequence can fail in other relational matters, showing that the consequence is not intrinsic to that form.

Even if one treats the reduction as an intermediary, ‘intrinsically’ need mean only without an alien premise. An alien premise is one not entailed by the two premises, or one entailed by a premise but whose two terms differ from that premise’s terms. This preserves the difference between a legitimate reduction and a genuinely additional relational rule.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-010"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-010 — local note 10

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 345](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/345?lang=ar) · [Qum 346](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/346?lang=ar)

The equality argument is usually defined as two propositions such that the correlate of the first predicate is the subject of the second. One objects that the correlate includes a preposition and its governed noun, whereas the second subject is the noun alone. The earlier grammatical discussion answers that the correlate is the governed noun; the particle is not itself part of that correlate.

The definition seems confined to chains arranged like the first figure and to omit differently oriented equality arguments which become productive by reduction. The answer takes the required arrangement either as actual or as obtainable after transformation. It need not be already explicit in the original order.

Nor is the argument confined to equality. It includes ‘A entails B; B entails C,’ ‘A depends on B; B depends on C,’ and similar relations. The familiar name comes from its best-known example, reportedly the equality example given by the First Teacher.


**Reading / scope note:** One lettered example in the digital Arabic repeats the proposed conclusion among its premises. Its letters are not silently reconstructed; the general definition and response are translated.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-011"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-011 — local note 11

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 346](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/346?lang=ar)

The conclusion requires an external premise. From ‘Two is half of four; four is half of eight’ one cannot conclude that two is half of eight. Nor does disjointness from something disjoint from humans establish disjointness from humans. Half of a half is not a half, and what is disjoint from a disjoint thing need not be disjoint from the original. Equality and entailment chains yield their intended conclusions only when the appropriate external relational rule is granted. Without it the intrinsic result is merely ‘A equals something equal to C,’ ‘A entails something entailing C,’ or ‘A is contained in something contained in C,’ rather than the intended direct relation.

An objection invokes dependence: divorce depends on marriage, and marriage on the consent of both parties, yet divorce can occur without the wife’s consent. The reply fixes the time and object of the dependence. The consent meant is that required for the marriage, not consent at the time of divorce. Divorce presupposes that marriage and hence its antecedent conditions. It resembles a roof depending on a wall which depends on a foundation.


**Reading / scope note:** The marriage example reports the historical glossator’s assumptions and is not current legal guidance.

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 346](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/346?lang=ar)

Thus ‘A equals B; B equals C’ gives ‘A equals something equal to C.’ Add ‘Everything equal to something equal to C equals C,’ and infer ‘A equals C.’

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-013"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-013 — local note 13

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 346](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/346?lang=ar) · [Qum 347](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/347?lang=ar)

Calling the equality argument ‘not intrinsically productive’ concerns its intended direct conclusion, such as ‘A equals C,’ not every conclusion whatever. It intrinsically yields the intermediate conclusion just described, and in relation to that conclusion it meets the definition of a syllogism.

But then the usual division appears incomplete. It is neither exceptional nor a conditional conjunctional syllogism; if categorical conjunctional, it should belong to one of the four figures. Yet those figures require a repeated middle term in the conventional sense, which this argument lacks. A reply places it under categorical conjunctional reasoning by definition: the conclusion’s matter, but not its form, is present, and both premises are categorical. The requirement of a repeated middle is then said to concern knowledge of productivity rather than productivity itself. The restriction to four figures applies to forms satisfying the conditions for knowing that they produce a conclusion.

The glossator objects that even this answer is insufficient. We know the equality argument produces the stated intermediate result although it lacks a repeated middle in the conventional sense. Perhaps some repetition in a broader sense is required, but conventional repetition has not been shown indispensable for knowledge of productivity. Reflect.

## HWN-SYLLOGISM-015 — local note 15

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 347](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/347?lang=ar)

The ‘matter’ of the conclusion means its subject and predicate, whether their connection is affirmative or negative. This explains why an exceptional syllogism can contain either the conclusion itself or its contradictory.

Neither is present there as an independently asserted proposition. Otherwise the conclusion would already be known before the inference, contradicting the requirement that the result differ from each premise; or its contradictory would already be assented to, precluding assent to the conclusion. What is present is the conclusion’s terms, or its contradictory’s terms, in the relevant arrangement within a larger conditional—not an independently asserted judgement capable there of truth or falsity on its own. The glossator’s phrase ‘its two terms’ points to this distinction.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-017"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-017 — local note 17

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 348](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/348?lang=ar)

Negating the conjunction of ‘matter and form present’ leaves three possibilities: matter without form, form without matter, or neither. Only the first supplies the conjunctional syllogism. Form cannot occur without its matter, just as an attribute cannot occur without its bearer. Nor can a conclusion arise from an argument containing no trace of either its matter or form.

One apparent counterexample is ‘Every C is B; every B is B; therefore every C is B.’ Its conclusion already appears with both matter and form, although it looks conjunctional. The reply denies that it is a syllogism at all: the conclusion is already known in the first premise and is not newly acquired. Moreover, the relevant definition concerns the presence of the conclusion’s terms within another assertion, not the whole conclusion itself as an already asserted premise.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-030"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-030 — local note 30

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 349](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/349?lang=ar) · [Qum 350](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/350?lang=ar)

The commentator explains the second and following conditions but leaves the first—affirmation of the minor—to be understood by comparison. Its reason is that the major’s judgement, affirmative or negative, applies to what possesses the middle. If the minor denied the middle of the minor term, that term would not have been placed among the bearers of the middle. A judgement about one of two disjoint things does not entail the same judgement about the other.

For example, ‘No human is a stone; every stone is inanimate’ accompanies a negative conclusion about humans and inanimate things. Replace the major by ‘Every stone is a body,’ and the corresponding true judgement is affirmative. Different conclusions under the same arrangement show that the arrangement itself does not necessitate either.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-032"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-032 — local note 32

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 350](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/350?lang=ar)

If the minor only asserts that the middle belongs possibly to the minor term, the major’s predicate cannot automatically be transferred. The major judges what is actually middle, while the minor term is only possibly middle; a possibility may never be actualised. Suppose Zayd actually rides only horses and ʿAmr only donkeys. Everything ʿAmr rides may possibly be ridden by Zayd, and everything Zayd rides is necessarily a horse, yet it does not follow that anything ʿAmr rides can be a horse: his actual mounts are necessarily donkeys, and no donkey is necessarily a horse.

This condition rests on the usual interpretation of the Shaykh’s actuality as actuality in reality itself. On the interpretation that it means actuality under intellectual supposition, whether or not realised, the condition does not follow in the same way: remaining merely possible in reality does not prevent hypothetical actuality. The author here appears to require real actuality both for predicate-connection and, in the Shaykh’s doctrine, for subject-connection. But, as noted earlier, that interpretation does not straightforwardly cover mental propositions without actual instances. Reflect.


**Reading / scope note:** The riding example is a stipulated modal countermodel, not a universal fact about riding. The source’s final animal contrast is translated according to its evident intended incompatibility.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-034"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-034 — local note 34

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 350](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/350?lang=ar) · [Qum 351](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/351?lang=ar)

What possesses the middle is judged of the minor term at least in some cases, because the minor is among the bearers of the middle at least in some cases.

Abū Saʿīd objected to Avicenna that this first figure, the foundation of the other three, is circular. Knowing its conclusion depends on knowing its premises, including the universal major. But knowing the major requires knowing the major predicate’s affirmation or denial of every individual of the middle, among them the minor term. That already requires knowledge of exactly the conclusion sought.

The Shaykh distinguishes implicit or comprehensive knowledge from explicit and detailed knowledge. The conclusion is known within the major in an undifferentiated manner; after extraction from the premises it is known distinctly. The dependence of the latter on the former is not vicious. The same thing can be known under one respect and unknown under another: under the first respect it is presupposed, under the second acquired.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-037"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-037 — local note 37

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 351](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/351?lang=ar)

If both conditions are absent, the minor is neither necessary nor perpetual, and the major belongs to the seven forms whose negatives do not convert. Among the minors, the most restrictive relevant forms are the special conditioned and the temporal: the former is narrower than the general conditioned and the two customary forms; the latter is narrower than the remaining eight. The temporal form is the narrowest relevant major. Combining these restricted minors with a temporal major is unproductive because the same form admits opposite material results.

For example, an eclipsed thing is necessarily non-luminous at a specified time but not perpetually, and every moon is necessarily luminous at a specified time but not perpetually. Yet even a generally possible negative conclusion between eclipse and moon is excluded by the stipulated necessary connection. Replacing moon with sun yields the opposite material result. If these stronger combinations do not produce a conclusion, weaker combinations cannot do so either.


**Reading / scope note:** This is the historical modal argument with its astronomical examples and assumed subject-domains; it is not an independently certified modal theorem.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-042"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-042 — local note 42

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 351](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/351?lang=ar) · [Qum 352](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/352?lang=ar)

If the minor is possible, the first condition has already ruled out a major among the seven forms whose negatives do not convert. Apart from the three necessary forms, only the perpetual and two customary forms remain. The possible–perpetual combination fails because a property may possibly belong while being perpetually absent. One can stipulate a subject which might be dark but is never dark, then use that same subject in both premises; a negative conclusion denying the subject of itself is impossible. Replacing the second subject by a disjoint class can instead make a negative conclusion true.

Failure with the perpetual entails failure with the broader general customary. The special customary has two components: the general customary, already unproductive, and non-perpetuity. The latter has the opposite quality to its principal component, and so agrees in quality with the possible minor. Since the second figure requires premises of different quality, that component is unproductive too.

If the major is possible, the first condition restricts a non-necessary minor to the perpetual. That pairing also fails: something may perpetually possess a property while its absence remains possible. Using the same subject gives an impossible negative self-predication, while using an appropriately disjoint class gives the opposite result.


**Reading / scope note:** The original examples employ ethnic labels and colour stereotypes. Their purely logical role is rendered with stipulated classes rather than endorsing those descriptions of real populations.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-043"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-043 — local note 43

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 352](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/352?lang=ar)

Ibn Hishām in the Mughnī says ghayr requires an understood genitive complement and may omit that complement in wording only after laysa when its meaning is understood. He calls lā ghayr an error and condemns it emphatically in his commentary on the Shudhūr. Al-Sīrāfī similarly restricts the omission to its attested occurrence after laysa, not other negatives.

Muḥammad ʿAlī replies that al-Zamakhsharī records both lā ghayr and laysa ghayr in the Mufaṣṣal, accepted by al-Andalusī. Ibn al-Ḥājib also records lā ghayr without objection from his commentators. Abū al-ʿAbbās reportedly used it with a fixed final ḍamma, like qablu and baʿdu. Ibn Mālik adduces a verse using lā ghayr in his discussion of oaths. Surprisingly, Ibn Hishām himself uses the disputed expression repeatedly in the Mughnī and other works.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-044"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-044 — local note 44

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 352](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/352?lang=ar) · [Qum 353](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/353?lang=ar)

The conditions can be justified briefly. If neither perpetuity of the minor nor convertibility of the negative major is present, the minor is among the thirteen forms other than the necessary and perpetual, and the major among the nine whose negatives do not convert. The special conditioned is narrower than the general conditioned and the customary forms; the temporal is narrower than the remaining forms, because necessity throughout the duration of a description entails necessity at some time of the subject, not conversely. The temporal is also the narrowest relevant major.

A special conditioned minor and a temporal major still fail: stipulate that an eclipsed thing is necessarily not luminous while eclipsed but not always, and that every moon is necessarily luminous at a specified time but not always. A possibly negative conclusion excluding the moon is impossible under the assumed necessary eclipse–moon relation. Replace the major’s subject by sun, and a negative conclusion is true. The same arrangement thus permits opposite outcomes. Failure of the stronger combination entails failure of its weaker variants. This analysis of the special conditioned follows the author’s definition, necessity while the description holds. Under the alternative definition, necessity on the condition of the description, the enumeration must instead state separately the special conditioned’s relation to the general conditioned and customary forms, and the temporal’s relation to the remaining eight.

For the second condition’s first alternative, a possible minor cannot combine with the nine non-convertible negative forms. Outside the necessary and two conditioned forms, the remaining major options are perpetual and the two customary forms. Possible–perpetual fails: a property can be possible yet never actual, producing either impossible negative self-predication or a true negative between different classes depending on the chosen subject. The general customary is weaker and therefore also fails. The special customary’s principal component fails for the same reason; its non-perpetuity component agrees in quality with the minor and so violates the second figure’s required opposition of quality.

For the second alternative, a possible major with a non-necessary minor must, by the first condition, have a perpetual minor. A property can belong perpetually while its absence is possible. Once again a same-subject example and a disjoint-subject example yield opposite material results, disproving formal productivity.


**Reading / scope note:** Historical counts and modality relations are reproduced without claiming a new proof certificate. Ethnic/colour examples are treated as schematic subject-classes, not empirical assertions.

The author’s wording here is insufficiently precise. By saying that the four moods produce their stated conclusions ‘by reductio, or conversion of the major, or conversion of the minor,’ he seems to suggest that the alternatives are available in each case. In fact reductio applies to all four, conversion of the major not to the second and fourth, and conversion of the minor only to the second. The wording should specify which method belongs to which mood, or replace ‘or’ with ‘and.’ A conjunction would state that the collection of methods covers all the moods without requiring every method to cover every mood.

Alternatively ‘or’ may be used in the sense of ‘and,’ an attested usage illustrated by al-Nābigha’s calculation of the pigeons: the next line gives ninety-nine, and another transmission has wāw. The same criticism concerns the author’s listing of proof methods in the later figures.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-083"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-083 — local note 83

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 358](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/358?lang=ar) · [Qum 359](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/359?lang=ar)

Five modal conditions are traditionally stated for productivity in the fourth figure.

First, both premises must be actual. If one is possible, productivity does not follow. A negative possible premise falls under the next condition. An affirmative possible premise fails whether major or minor, because the same form admits opposing results. Suppose Zayd’s actual mounts are exclusively horses. ‘Every mount of Zayd is necessarily a horse; every donkey can be a mount of Zayd’ gives a negative relation between horse and donkey, whereas replacing donkey by a neighing animal gives an affirmative relation. If the possible premise is minor, ‘Every braying animal can be Zayd’s mount; every donkey necessarily brays’ gives one result, while ‘Every animal can be Zayd’s mount; every neighing animal is necessarily an animal’ gives the other.

Second, a negative premise must belong to the six forms whose negatives convert, not to the nine which do not. The most restrictive among the latter is the temporal, and even it is said to fail whether minor or major. The example combines the moon’s not being eclipsed at quadrature, but not perpetually, with a necessary relation involving the lunar disappearance or dark phase. The proposed possibly negative conclusion is contradicted by the corresponding necessary affirmative. If the strongest excluded form fails, the weaker forms fail.

Third, in the third mood the minor must imply perpetuity—being necessary or perpetual—or the major must imply the general customary, belonging to the six negative-convertible forms. If neither condition holds, the negative minor must be one of the four general/special conditioned and customary forms, while the major is one of the nine other forms. Even the strongest special conditioned minor with the strongest temporal major is said to fail: an eclipsed thing is necessarily non-luminous with lunar illumination while eclipsed, but not always, and every moon is eclipsed at the relevant interposition, but not always. The proposed particular possible negative between lunar illumination and moon is false.

Fourth, in the sixth and eighth moods the minor must be one of the two special forms, and the major one of the six negative-convertible forms. The sixth is established by converting its particular negative minor to reduce it to the second figure. Such a negative converts only in the two special forms. Since the converted minor does not imply absolute perpetuity, the second figure also requires the specified major. The eighth is established by exchanging the premises to obtain the first figure, then converting the result. Its transformed major must therefore be a special form capable of yielding a convertible particular negative, and its transformed minor one of the six forms. In the original order these requirements attach to the minor and major respectively.

Fifth, the seventh mood’s major must be one of the two special forms. Its productivity is established by converting that particular negative major and reducing the argument to the third figure. The conversion is available only for those special forms. This summarises the received account.

However, the demonstrations of the second and third conditions are incomplete. To establish failure by divergent material outcomes, one must exhibit a matter where affirmation is impossible and another where negation is impossible. No matter has been found here where affirmation is impossible. That would require the universal necessary exclusion of the major from the minor, blocking a particular generally possible affirmative. But a temporal premise makes an extreme coincide with the middle at one time and separate at another. Where the other extreme necessarily accompanies the middle, their coincidence at the relevant time prevents universal necessary exclusion. Consequently, if the argument establishes the impossibility of the negative, a general-possible affirmative may remain a necessary result of those combinations. The stated counterexamples therefore do not prove the full claimed barrenness.


**Reading / scope note:** The note reports the five conditions and then explicitly challenges proofs of two of them. The lunar examples preserve the source’s stipulated astronomical relations. This translation is not a certificate of the disputed fourth-figure modalities.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-088"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-088 — local note 88

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 360](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/360?lang=ar)

The moods here are ordered by their premises rather than the dignity of their conclusions. Thus a particular affirmative-producing mood precedes a universal negative-producing mood, although a universal is considered nobler than a particular. The first has two universal affirmatives and the premises of the first figure’s first mood. The second shares affirmation of both premises and approximately the first figure’s second-mood material, so the universal-premise negative moods are not inserted between them. The third reduces to the first figure by exchanging the premises. The fourth and fifth reduce through conversion of both premises and precede the others; the fourth precedes the fifth because its minor is universal affirmative rather than particular affirmative. The sixth and seventh contain a universal affirmative unlike the eighth; the sixth precedes the seventh because conversion of its minor reduces it to the second figure.


**Reading / scope note:** The digital text calls the fourth ‘inferior’ while immediately giving a reason for superiority over the fifth. The ordering rationale is translated with that apparent textual slip noted.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-089"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-089 — local note 89

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 360](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/360?lang=ar) · [Qum 361](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/361?lang=ar)

For the first two moods, take the universal contradictory of the particular affirmative conclusion as a major and the original affirmative minor as a minor, as in third-figure reductio. The first-figure result converts into a contradiction of the original major. Thus ‘Every B is C; every A—or some A—is B’ requires ‘Some C is A.’ Otherwise ‘No C is A’; with ‘Every B is C’ this gives ‘No B is A,’ whose conversion contradicts the original assertion of A as B.

For the third mood, use the affirmative contradictory of the conclusion as minor and the original universal major as major. From ‘No B is C; every A is B,’ deny ‘No C is A’ by assuming ‘Some C is A.’ Together with ‘Every A is B’ this gives ‘Some C is B,’ converting to ‘Some B is C,’ contrary to the original minor.

For the next two moods either procedure is available: their minors are affirmative and the contradictories of their conclusions universal; equally, those contradictories are affirmative and their majors universal. There is therefore no basis for restricting all three final negative-producing moods of this five-mood group to the second procedure.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

The contradictory of its particular negative conclusion is universal affirmative; combining it with the universal affirmative major gives a universal affirmative, whose conversion is merely particular affirmative. That does not contradict the original particular negative minor: affirmation and denial may concern different individuals.

In the seventh, only the first route could be attempted because the major is not universal. Again the two universal affirmatives yield a universal affirmative which converts to a particular affirmative, not contradicting the original particular negative major. In the eighth neither route is available: the minor is not affirmative and the major not universal.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-135"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-135 — local note 135

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 367](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/367?lang=ar)

Calling the special conditioned the narrowest remaining minor follows the author’s account of conditioned necessity as necessity throughout the duration of the description. On that account it is narrower than the general conditioned and the two customary forms, and also than the temporal, which is narrower than the other eight: necessity throughout all times of the description entails necessity at some time of the subject, not conversely.

On the more familiar account, necessity conditional upon the description, one should instead say ‘the special conditioned or the temporal.’ Those two overlap rather than one containing the other. They coincide when the relation is necessary given the description and the description is itself necessary to the subject at some time, as in the eclipsed thing’s darkness. The special conditioned can occur without temporal necessity when the description is never necessary to the subject, as fingers moving while someone writes. Temporal necessity can occur without the requisite descriptive condition, as the moon’s eclipse at interposition but not always.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-140"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-140 — local note 140

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 368](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/368?lang=ar)

‘And excellent is the trustee’ admits several grammatical constructions. It may be coordinated with the preceding nominal sentence, either because a performative expression can be coordinated with a report or because ‘He suffices me’ here, in the setting of supplication, effectively means ‘God, suffice me.’ The particular subject of praise is then omitted, as in the scriptural ‘Excellent is the servant.’ It may instead be analysed through an implicit subject and an implicit ‘it is said of Him,’ with different grammarians allowing the preceding implicit or explicit pronoun to supply the subject specifically praised. If coordinated only with the predicate through an understood ‘said of Him,’ the earlier pronoun can similarly supply that subject according to al-Raḍī and others; the majority instead supplies an omitted predicate.

Alternatively the praise is a parenthetical sentence introduced after the preceding statement is complete, as Najm al-Aʾimma explains the parenthetical ‘and no boasting’ in the reported saying ‘I am the master of Adam’s children, and no boasting.’


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-141"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-141 — local note 141

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 368](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/368?lang=ar)

Each of the five conditional combinations requires a common component serving as middle. It may be an entire antecedent or consequent in both premises, an incomplete component of an antecedent or consequent in both, or a complete component of one and incomplete component of the other. These three patterns occur in the combinations of two connectives, two disjunctives, and mixed connective–disjunctive premises. In combinations involving a categorical premise, only incomplete sharing is available, since neither categorical term is itself a proposition.

A categorical–connective pair further has four arrangements: the categorical may be minor or major, and its shared component may belong to the connective’s antecedent or consequent. A categorical–disjunctive combination may yield one categorical result, called a divisive syllogism, or fail to have that unifying form. For the divisive case, there is a categorical premise for each disjunctive member, each categorical shares the appropriate member, and all branches yield the same conclusion. For example: an animal is rational, neighing, or neither; rational animals are sentient, neighing animals are sentient, and the remaining animals are sentient; therefore every animal is sentient. Different numbers of categoricals and disjuncts, different sharing, or divergent conclusions belong to the non-divisive alternatives. Extended works such as the commentary on the Maṭāliʿ give their details.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-142"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-142 — local note 142

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 368](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/368?lang=ar) · [Qum 369](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/369?lang=ar)

The author omits a new definition of exceptional syllogism because it is already known from the preceding division. Exceptional and conjunctional arguments can be transformed into one another. Al-ʿAḍudī explains the first direction by making the antecedent a middle: its affirmation supplies the minor, and its entailment the major. For a disjunctive example, ‘Two is even or odd; it is even; therefore it is not odd’ includes the connection ‘Whenever even, not odd.’ It can be recast as ‘Two is even; every even thing is not odd; therefore two is not odd.’

Conversely, a conjunctional argument becomes connective by treating the middle as entailing the sought result. For a disjunctive reconstruction, introduce the incompatible alternative to the middle beside it. In the even-number example, oddness supplies the alternative to evenness.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-150"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-150 — local note 150

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 369](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/369?lang=ar)

Denying the antecedent does not establish denial of the consequent. One may object that verses by Abū al-ʿAlāʾ and a poet in the Ḥamāsa appear to infer a consequence’s absence from the absence of its condition: enduring dynasties would leave their members ordinary subjects, or a hoofed creature’s earlier flight would permit the imagined animal to fly, yet the condition is absent.

The logical claim concerns knowledge: knowing the antecedent absent does not, from the stated connection alone, entail knowing the consequent absent, since a consequent may be broader than its antecedent. The author’s commentary on the Talkhīṣ distinguishes ordinary linguistic usage from logical usage. Ordinary law may explain that the real cause of the consequence’s absence is the condition’s absence, without investigating how that absence is known. Logicians use the connection to show that knowledge of the consequent’s absence gives knowledge of the antecedent’s absence, or knowledge of the antecedent’s occurrence gives knowledge of the consequent’s occurrence. The verses concern the first, causal-explanatory usage, not a demonstration that denial of an antecedent is generally a valid inferential form.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-151"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-151 — local note 151

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 370](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/370?lang=ar)

Three conditions govern productivity of exceptional reasoning. First, the conditional must be affirmative. If it denies a connection or a disjunction between two things, affirming or denying one does not by itself require affirmation or denial of the other.

Second, a connective must be implicative and a disjunctive genuinely exclusive in the relevant sense, rather than accidental. An accidental conjunction gives no rational connection licensing affirmation of the consequent from the antecedent or denial of the antecedent from the consequent. An accidental disjunction likewise supplies no intrinsic incompatibility. Moreover, knowledge of the truth of such an accidental conditional already depends on knowing one component true or false. Inferring that very component’s truth or falsity from it would be circular.

Third, at least one of three conditions must hold: the conditional is universal; the exceptive affirmation or denial is universal; or the time and situation of the implication or incompatibility agree with those of the exceptive premise. If all three fail, affirming or denying a component does not secure the corresponding result.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-152"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-152 — local note 152

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 370](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/370?lang=ar)

Khulf, with ḍamma on the first consonant and a silent lām, originally denotes failing to fulfil a statement about what one will do; lying denotes falsely stating what one has done. The former thus originally concerns the future and the latter the past. The term was then transferred to what is false or impossible.

ʿAbd al-Raḥīm adds that calling an argument a ‘syllogism of impossibility’ names the cause from its effect: it shows the contradictory of the desired proposition to be impossible. It does not mean the argument itself is invalid. This is the majority’s explanation of the name. A second explanation is supported by calling an argument which reaches its goal directly, without first refuting its contradictory, ‘straight’ or direct.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.

<a id="HWN-SYLLOGISM-156"></a>
## HWN-SYLLOGISM-156 — local note 156

**First-pass rendering** · [Qum 370](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12170/370?lang=ar)

The conditional premise may itself need demonstration. For example, to convert ‘No C is B’ into ‘No B is C,’ suppose the latter fails. Its contradictory, ‘Some B is C,’ would hold, and that contradictory would imply an impossibility. Thus ‘If the desired result is not established, an impossibility is established; but no impossibility is established; therefore the desired result is established.’

To prove the conditional, combine the supposed contradictory with the original: ‘Some B is C; no C is B,’ yielding ‘Some B is not B,’ which is impossible because a thing cannot be denied of itself. The word ‘may’ recognises that the relevant conditional is sometimes evident and does not need an additional demonstration.


**Reading / scope note:** Working first-pass English rendering of the cited digital note. Technical arguments are sometimes rendered economically; this is not a certified unabridged critical translation.
